en: The first book:
Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable reality of speech;
it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds.
That which is traditionally taught as one alone, by virtue of its dependence on diverse powers,
appears as if distinct from those powers, even though it is not separate from them.
Depending upon whose power of time, which has superimposed its portions,
there arise the six transformations— birth and the rest— which are the sources of the differentiation of existence.
Of this single seed of all, there exists this manifold state in the form of the enjoyer,
the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment.
The Veda is the means of attaining that [Brahman] and its imitation; though it is one, it has been handed down by the great seers as if it had many paths, each separately.
The multiplicity of paths for the various divisions, the unity of action in a single [act],
and the fact that words possess their respective potencies— these are observed in its branches.
And the various Smṛtis, which have purposes both seen and unseen,
were formulated by those learned in the Veda based on that very [Veda] through its indicative marks.

Based upon those [Vedic texts] which are of the nature of explanatory statements (arthavāda), the various doctrines of both monists and dualists have emerged in many ways, born of their own conceptual constructions.
In that context, purity is said to be truth, which is the single-footed Vidyā;
it is joined with the form of the *praṇava*, which is not in conflict with any philosophical doctrine.
The various branches of knowledge, which serve as the causes for the refinement of wisdom, extend from that Creator as the structural components and subordinate parts of the worlds.
The wise say that grammar is near to Brahman, the highest of all austerities, and the first limb among the Vedic meters.
This is the direct path to that most meritorious light, which is the supreme essence of speech once it has attained its full differentiation of forms.
Words alone are the basis for the reality of the operation of meanings;
the comprehension of the reality of words does not exist apart from grammar.
That [Veda] shines forth as the gate to liberation, the remedy for the impurities of speech,
the purifier of all sciences, and the science beyond [all others].
Just as all real universals are invariably based upon forms,
so too in the world this science is the ultimate resort of all sciences.
This is the first station for those ascending the steps of accomplishment;
this is that straight royal road for those seeking liberation.
Here, one who has transcended all error perceives the Self alone—
the source of the meters, consisting of the meters, as the body made of meters— within the desire that is the origin of the meters.
Or rather, that which is the supreme form of speech, whose distinctions have subsided,
and which, even within this very darkness, unfolds as a pure light.
Having transcended the visible activity of forms and having passed beyond light and darkness, they worship that which is the manifestation of the transformative.
In that [state], the indicators of speech— like signs for the recollection of phonemes—
appear, through a connection preceded by sound, like reflections.
In which [speech] there are the various high and low phonemes belonging to the Atharvans, the Aṅgirases, the Sāmans, and the Ṛg and Yajus, each maintained in its distinct position.
That which is one, yet is divided manifoldly through various methods of analysis—
by resorting to that grammar, the supreme Brahman is realized.
In that regard, the great seers— the authors of the Sūtras, along with their Anutantras, and the Bhāṣyas— have declared that the relationships between words and their meanings are eternal.
Those items which are extracted [from the sentence], those meanings which possess established characteristics,
those words which are to be explained grammatically, and those which are expressive [of meaning].

Those relations which exist among correct and incorrect words— whether as cause and effect or as suitability— with respect to the dharma, the cognition, and the constituent parts [of speech], [are what constitute the connection].
In this treatise, they have been described by means of their indicative marks and their own specific words;
however, only some of them are here followed for the sake of memory, in accordance with tradition.
Correct words, established through tradition from the learned, are the means for accomplishing dharma;
they are correct because there is no difference in their conveying meaning, whereas incorrect words are the opposite.
Whether they are eternal or produced, no beginning of them exists;
and this very arrangement of theirs is called "eternality," just like [the eternality] of living beings.
No one ought to establish this convention as being purposeless;
therefore, the traditional rule (smṛti) concerning grammatical correctness is recorded by the learned.
And dharma is not established by reasoning apart from scripture;
even that knowledge which belongs to the seers is preceded by scripture.
Furthermore, no one can subvert by means of logic those uninterrupted paths of Dharma that have been established, because they are well-known to the world.
When the potencies of entities differ due to variations in state, place, and time,
their establishment through inference is exceedingly difficult.
When a substance whose capacity is already known is connected with a particular substance for the sake of various specific causal functions, that capacity is obstructed.
Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents may be established in a completely different way by others who are more proficient.
The discernment of gems, silver, and so forth, which arises for experts through practice alone and cannot be described to others, is not inferential.
Established beyond both perception and inference,
the supernatural powers of the ancestors, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas arise solely from their past actions.
For those whose light has become manifest and whose minds are unclouded,
knowledge of the past and future does not differ from direct perception.
Those who perceive with the vision of a seer (ārṣa-cakṣus) entities that transcend the senses and are not accessible to ordinary cognition—
their word is not sublated by inference.
How could anyone else turn back that person who, like his own property, does not doubt another's knowledge or vision, and who stands firmly on the side of direct perception?
Regarding these two categories— "this is merit" and "this is evil"—
the utility of the scriptures for human beings is minimal, extending only as far as the outcaste (caṇḍāla).
That which exists without interruption, like consciousness itself—
the tradition (āgama) that one who relies upon is not subverted by arguments based on logic.
For one who relies primarily on inference, a fall is not difficult to encounter— just like a blind man running on an uneven path by means of the touch of his hands.
Therefore, relying upon the uncreated scripture and the Smṛti together with its foundational basis,
the learned initiate this Smṛti concerning grammatical correctness.
Those who know words recognize two kinds of words within the category of "words":
one is the cause of words, and the other is employed for the sake of meaning.
Indivisible, it arises from the divided [phonemes] as the designator of the meaning;
therein, the word—whose essence is the form of the meaning—enters into a relationship [with that meaning].
Some who recite the Purāṇas say that there is a difference in essence between those two;
others declare that the one who is non-different appears divided due to a difference in cognition.
Just as fire residing in the fire-stick is the cause of other manifestations of light,
so too the word, when present in the intellect, is the distinct cause of various auditory perceptions.
That [word-meaning], which was previously reflected upon by the intellect and fixed upon some object,
is assisted by the sound manifested from the articulatory organs.
Because sound is produced in a sequence, it is neither prior nor posterior;
though itself devoid of sequence, it appears as if possessed of differentiation through its sequential form.
Just as a reflection, though situated elsewhere, follows the movement of the water due to the action of that [water],
so too does that property [of the sphoṭa] follow the activity of the articulations and sounds.
Just as the form of the self and the form of the object of knowledge are perceived within cognition,
so too the form of the object and the word's own form are manifested in speech.
The sacrifice, which is designated by the word [“sacrifice”], has entered, as it were, into the state of an egg;
its function, consisting of action, assumes a sequential order part by part.
Just as a form is fashioned on a cloth as the object of a single cognition,
so too is a triad observed in the case of a word with respect to another form.
Just as the speaker’s prior cognition operates toward the words themselves,
so too does the determination of the perceivers arise with respect to those very same words.
People do not perceive those [words] which have become subordinate to the meaning as having fulfilled their purpose within certain denotable objects, because they exist for the sake of another.
Just as light possesses two powers— namely, the state of being the object of apprehension and the state of being the apprehender—
in the very same way, these two [powers] exist separately in all words.
An object is not revealed by words that have not themselves entered into the state of being objects;
for those [words], when unperceived, do not manifest objects merely by their existence. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 1.57)
Therefore, because its form is not yet known, it is asked, "What does it say? Just so, the intrinsic nature of the sense organs is not grasped with respect to the object to be illuminated.
Two properties of the word, grasped as distinct and extracted [from the whole],
function as causes for the various forms of differentiation without contradiction.
Just as words such as *vṛddhi* and others, which are based on their own forms,
enter into a relationship with the named objects (*saṃjñin*) through the words made known by the [technical] markers *āT*, *aiC*, and *auC*.
In the same way, this word "fire" is based on the word "fire";
through the auditory perception of the word "fire," it enters into a relationship with that which is denoted by the word "fire."
Whatever word is uttered is necessarily not itself the bearer of the action;
its capacity to convey another [meaning] is not obstructed.
Because it is dependent on its utterance, the phoneme (guṇa) is not connected with grammatical operations;
therefore, the connection of the operations with their meanings is postulated.
Whatever common property is relied upon between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison,
another property of that [commonality] is distinguished within the standards of comparison.
When a quality that is the cause of excellence is taught as being independent,
its state of excellence is understood to arise precisely from the quality upon which it depends.
The word that exists as the denotative form of that [meaning],
its own form is also distinguished from that [meaning] when it is uttered.
Prior to its connection with the named object, the name has as its referent its own form;
it thus serves as the basis for both the genitive and the nominative case endings.
In that case, because it possesses meaning, the nominative case is prescribed after a word that is a name;
its distinction [from other cases] arises precisely from that meaning.
However, according to some, "its own form" (*svarūpa*) refers to the individual instance (*vyakti*) as a name;
the universal (*jāti*), being conjoined [with that instance], undergoes the grammatical operations belonging to the universal. (Vākya-kāṇḍa 1.69)
Others, however, maintain that in the Sūtra the individual instance (*vyakti*) endowed with a name is what is intended to be grasped;
the individual instance, having been made known by the genus (*jāti*), presents itself in the specific rules (*pradeśa*).
Regarding whether [the word] is an effect or eternal, some are proponents of unity;
regarding whether it is an effect or eternal, some are proponents of plurality.
Even when there is a division of words, the unity of the phonemes does not cease;
and a single word is perceived even within sentences that are themselves distinct.
Apart from phonemes (varṇa), no other word (pada) exists;
nor does a sentence (vākya) exist apart from phonemes and words, for there is no distinction whatsoever [between them].
Phonemes do not exist within words, nor do parts exist within phonemes;
there is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and the sentence.
Relying upon divergent perspectives, linguistic usage is followed;
therein, what is primary for some is the opposite for others. (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-vārttika 1.75)
They declare that for the *sphoṭa*, which is itself devoid of temporal divisions yet conforms to the duration of the sounds (*dhvani*),
there is a distinction in its manifestation due to the differences in the conditions of its apprehension.
Because of the difference in their intrinsic nature among short, long, and protracted [vowels], the duration of the natural sound (dhvani) is metaphorically attributed to the word (śabda). 1.77.
The natural sound (dhvani) is held to be the cause for the perception of the word-sound; the modified sound (vaikṛta) serves as the cause for the differentiation of its duration.
After the manifestation of the word-sound, however, the various modifications of its function are brought about by the articulated sounds (dhvani);
yet the essence of the sphoṭa is not differentiated by them.

The three theories of those who maintain that [the word] is manifested are as follows: the embellishment (saṃskāra) is produced either in the sense organ alone, or in the sound alone, or in both; by means of articulated sounds (dhvani). (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 1.80)
The refinement of the sense organ itself is achieved through concentration, collyrium, and so forth;
whereas the refinement of the object is for the sake of perceiving its fragrance.
If the eye functions by reaching its object, then a refinement (saṃskāra) of both the object and the sense-organ is desired through light; that same sequence applies to sound.
Some maintain that the perception of sound (*dhvani*) occurs without distinction from the form of the *sphoṭa*;
others postulate that sound is imperceptible and exists as an independent entity. (Vākya-kāṇḍa 1.83)

Just as an *anuvāka* or a verse reaches a state of mastery through repetition, yet that text is not re-examined with every single repetition; [so it is with the cognition of meaning]. (Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 1.84)
When a word is manifested by sounds that are themselves inexpressible yet conducive to apprehension, its own form is determined.
When the intellect, in which the seeds have been sown by the preceding sounds, reaches a state of full maturation through repetition, the word is apprehended along with the final sound.
And those words which one considers to exist in the interval between non-existent [entities], that is merely the incapacity of the cognizer; it is simply a means of apprehension.
The imitation of distinctions is a constant affliction of both cognition and speech;
speech has a form conditioned by sequence, while cognition is dependent upon the object of knowledge.
In worldly discourse, cognition does not exist without an object of knowledge;
nor is any meaning expressed by speech that has not acquired its sequential order. (Brahma-siddhi 1.89)

Just as the apprehension of the first number is the means for the comprehension of other numbers despite their difference, so too is the hearing of another word [the means for the comprehension of its meaning].
Those manifestors which belong individually to the distinct phonemes, sentences, and words,
even though they are absolutely different, their powers appear as if intermingled.
Just as by means of previous perceptions, even from a distance or in deep darkness,
one determines an object in one way after having initially apprehended it otherwise.
Likewise, when a sentence is being manifested by the causes of its manifestation,
the cognition first proceeds in the form of grasping its constituent parts.
Just as there is a fixed sequence of transformation in the case of milk and a seed,
so too is the order of cognition fixed for those who understand.
Even in those [phonemes] which are parts of the word, there is a differentiation of form in the sound (*dhvani*) according to its sequence;
or else, since they are indivisible, one must employ the conceptualization of a distinction between parts as a means.

The genus (*jāti*) manifested by many individual instances (*vyakti*) is known as *sphoṭa* by some; others have conceived these very individuals themselves as being the "sounds" (*dhvani*). (Bṛhad-vākyapadīya 1.96)
The sound (dhvani), though modified by its causes, serves as the means for the perception of the unchanging word,
just like light.
Furthermore, manifestation is not invariably established in things that are impermanent;
nor is the manifestation of eternal universals admitted to depend upon their substrata.
A connection with place and other factors is observed even for those possessing bodies;
yet, despite the conceptualization of differences in place, there is no difference between the sound and the word.
Just as the fixed capacity between the grasper and the grasped is established,
so too is it in the case of the manifested and the manifestor, such as between the *sphoṭa* and the sounds.
Furthermore, in the world, there exists for each individual substance a specific cause that illuminates the corresponding perceptions of odor and so forth.
The object to be manifested conforms to the differences among the manifestors;
this is directly perceived in the case of reflections in oil, water, and so forth.
In objects of contradictory dimensions, such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror,
there is no possibility for entities possessing the same form as mountains and the like to exist.
Therefore, in the case of phonemes, sentences, words, and so forth, which exist at non-distinct times,
the time of their manifestation and their own [inherent] time are distinguished by the difference in the sounds (nāda).
That which is produced by conjunctions and disjunctions through the organs is the *sphoṭa*; others have declared that the sounds born from the [original] sound are the *dhvanis*.
Whether the sound is small or great, the duration of the *sphoṭa* does not differ;
rather, it is the subsequent series of sounds that consists of increase and decrease.
Just as from a distance one perceives only the light of a lamp,
so too among the sounds of bells and the like, a distinct difference is observed.
Due to the impact of a substance, two accumulated [sounds], though distinct as long and protracted, arise when the vibration has ceased;
these sounds are the differentiators of the function (vṛtti).
Even when the articulatory organ is not in a state of fixed vibration, other sounds arise from the *sphoṭa* itself,
just as flames arise from another flame.
Some maintain that air, atoms, and cognition undergo the transformation into sound;
indeed, the diversity of philosophical views is not fixed among various doctrines.
The air, having acquired its activity through effort that follows the speaker’s intention, attains the state of being sound when it is struck against the articulatory locations.
By the power of its cause, which possesses the property of an accumulation of momentum,
even substantial material forms are split apart through their conjunction.
Because they possess all powers, atoms function through both differentiation and conjunction;
they undergo transformation into the forms of shadow, heat, darkness, and sound.
When one's own capacity is being manifested, the atoms called "sounds," impelled by effort, accumulate like clouds. (BVaky_1.114)
Now, this internal knower, abiding within the subtle speech-self, undergoes a transformation into the form of sound (*śabda*) for the sake of manifesting its own nature. (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 1.115)
Having attained the state of mind and reached maturity through its own radiance,
it enters the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and is then fully aroused.
The wind has become the substratum of the principle of the internal organ;
permeated by its quality, it evolves through fire alone.
*Dividing the knots of its own self through various forms of revealed scripture,
the vital breath manifests the phonemes and then merges back into those very phonemes.* (Brahma-sūtra-vārttika 1.118)
The self, having empowered the objects through the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the bodily fire, which impels the vital air.
That word which has an unceasing existence is not perceived because of its subtlety;
like wind [unperceived] due to a fan, it is recognized through its own cause.
That power which resides in his vital breath and that which is established in the intellect,
as it evolves through the various stations, attains differentiation.
The power residing in words alone is the bond of this entire universe; for it is through them as its eyes that this world, which consists of manifestation, unfolds in the form of differentiation.
Since the distinction between sound and so forth is explained by means of sound itself,
all varieties of meaning are therefore dependent upon the mere elements of sound.
Those who know the sacred tradition understand that this [universe] is a transformation of the Word; from the meters alone does this entire world first proceed. (Brahma-vākya 1.124)
Having divided himself in many ways, that Prajāpati Chandas entered him in many ways through the measures consisting of the meters.
In those persons in whom virtuous speech is firmly established,
the merit of Prajāpati’s form exists in greater measure.
The great splendor belonging to Prajāpati, as if gathered within vessels,
returns to its own source upon the dissolution of the body of the wise.
This radiant orb, which is the locus of manifold prosperity,
having attained its true state, dissolves into primordial wisdom.
In this world, every course of action depends upon words;
even a child understands it through the impressions deposited in the past.
The initial arrangement of causes, the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa),
and the impact against the articulatory locations do not occur without the latent impression of sound (śabdabhāvanā).
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by speech.
If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from cognition, then illumination would not be manifested; for that [nature] is what effects reflective awareness.
She is the binder together of all sciences, arts, and crafts;
by her power, every object that has come into being is differentiated.
This very consciousness of transmigrating beings exists both externally and internally;
it is the pure sentience that has not transcended the subtle elements (tanmātra) within all classes of beings.
Speech impels all embodied beings toward purposeful actions;
when it departs, this person is seen to be unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall.

Speech alone, having acquired its formal aspects through the transformation of the apprehension of distinctions, is declared in all branches of knowledge to be the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vākyapadīya 1.136)
Not transcending oneness, and being bound to speech, the various divisions of speech such as "cow" and so forth appear as distinct entities. (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 1.137)
Those who indeed worship Speech— which has six gates, six foundations, six awakenings, and is sixfold and imperishable— truly transcend death.
Just as the agent proceeds toward the action through differentiation,
so too does that very same [agent] abide as the action itself through non-differentiation.
Having divided himself by himself and created various kinds of entities,
the Lord of All, who consists of all things, proceeds as the enjoyer in a dream.

Just as a word is introduced by its own etymological derivation (*śruti*) or by a supreme [conventional] derivation (*paramātrā*), so too does it attain established usage (*rūḍhatā*); for by that [usage], the meaning is enjoined.

When the cause is absolutely non-existent, the determination of the form of an object is seen to occur through reliance on verbal testimony, as in the case of a fire-brand wheel and the like. (Brahma-siddhi 1.142)
They say that the speaker’s own self, which abides within as sound, is the Great Bull, with whom union is sought.
Therefore, that which is the refinement of speech is the perfection of the Supreme Self;
he who knows the true nature of its operation partakes of that immortal Brahman.
Having transcended the function of the vital breath and being established in the reality of speech,
one withdraws the self into the Self by means of the yoga of sequential withdrawal.
Having applied refinement to speech and having established speech within knowledge,
one should analyze its bonds and render it free from those bonds.
Having reached the internal light and severed the grasp of the knots,
one proceeds after cutting through the knots and attaining oneness with the causal light.
No one ever accepts a scripture that is without an author;
therefore, when all other scriptures have fallen away, the triple Veda alone remains established as the seed.
When debates have ceased and other authors no longer exist,
the world does not transgress the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.
If knowledge were innate, there would be no purpose whatsoever for the scriptures;
if dharma is the cause of knowledge, then the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is its foundation.
And logic that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures is the eye for those who lack vision;
for the meaning of a sentence does not rest upon the mere form [of the words] alone. (BVaky_1.151)

"The intention not to speak despite possessing knowledge, the subservience to another's purpose, and the inferential manifestation of meaning"—this manifold principle is analyzed through reasoning. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vākya 1.152)
That power belongs to words alone; reasoning (tarka) which relies upon man is a logic (nyāya) that follows words, and it has no foundation in those things that are beyond verbal testimony.
If even a great quantity of yellow *udumbara*-colored water from jars,
when drunk, cannot lead one to heaven, how could that which is offered in a sacrifice do so?
Just as visible forms and other objects are observed to possess their respective capacities for their intended purposes,
so too are words observed to have such power in cases such as the neutralization of poison.
Just as their capacity is understood in that [ordinary] case, so too should it be recognized regarding the Dharma;
therefore, the virtuous should speak with the virtuous for those who desire prosperity.
Everyone understands objects whose fruits are not perceived through scripture;
moreover, it is possible to state the opposite in every case regarding scripture.
This grammatical tradition (vyākaraṇasmṛti) has as its object the knowledge of correctness; it is the basis for this tradition among the learned (śiṣṭas), which has continued without interruption.

This is the wonderful, supreme reality beyond the threefold speech— consisting of Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and Paśyantī— which, through its various divisions into numerous sacred paths (tīrthas), leads to the highest goal.
Like a cow, the goddess of speech, possessing a pure smile, flows with the most excellent essence; she is both divine and non-divine in form. (Brahma-vākya 1.160)
"Behold the interval between these two subtle, vibrating [winds]: there exists eternally within the space between prāṇa and apāna that one [consciousness] which abides in all."
But another [speech] exists even without being impelled by breath,
for from that [other speech], breath is born again, nourishing the voice.

Nourished by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that very [speech] which is the basis for linguistic usage never speaks at any time unless it has obtained exhalation (*ucchvāsa*). (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-vākya 1.163)
The articulate [speech] proceeds as that which has produced sound and that which is without sound;
and between these two, the soundless alone is more weighty than the articulate.

When the air is manifested in the [articulatory] places, speech in its manifest form (*vaikharī*)—which assumes the form of phonemes—is produced by speakers and is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (Vākyapadīya 1.165)
Following the sequence of forms assumed by the intellect as its substrate,
the intermediate speech (*madhyamā vāk*) proceeds after transcending the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*).
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all sequence withdrawn;
it is the light of its own nature within, the subtle, imperishable Speech. (Brahma-sūtra-vārttika 1.167)
Though it is constantly being filled with adventitious impurities like nectar, the final stage of the moon is not said to be completely [defiled]. (1.168)
They call that immortal digit the sixteen-fold Puruṣa, upon the perception of whose true nature one's qualification [for worldly action] ceases.
Having acquired a form colored by the accompanying disturbances,
that *vaikharī* speech is not intermingled with them, just as pure *sattva* is not intermingled with the [other] *guṇas*.

The capacities of words for denoting entities are observed by those who know their true nature to be established as being manifested through both the differentiation and non-differentiation of those entities.
They say that the sacred revelation (śruti) is beginningless, uninterrupted, and without an author;
as for the tradition (smṛti), though it is composed by the learned, it is not interrupted.
The manifestation of evolved entities occurs without division, as is heard [in scripture] and as in a dream;
however, having discerned the true nature of existence through its indicative marks, the Smṛti has been prescribed.
The impurities that reside within the objects of body, speech,
and intellect are purified by the medical sciences and the inner treatises (adhyātmaśāstra) which have the characteristics of healing.
That word which, being devoid of correct grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), is intended to be used as "gauh" (cow),
they consider to be an *apabhraṃśa* (corrupt form) when it is applied to a specific meaning.
Words such as *aśvagoṇī* and others are correct in a different sense;
correctness is established everywhere according to the difference in the underlying cause (*nimitta*).
In the case of the virtuous, these [words] become the causes for the arising of cognition through inference;
as if they had attained identity with it, they manifest the meaning of the word.
Since they are not followed by the learned— just as correct words are not followed by synonyms— they are therefore not directly expressive according to the Smṛti treatise.
Just as a child learning to speak utters indistinct sounds like "ambvaṃbu," those who know the truth reach a certain conclusion regarding the clear word through that indistinctness.
Thus, when a correct word ought to be employed, if an incorrect form (apabhraṃśa) is used instead, some meaning is expressed by it only through the mediation of that correct word.
Through successive transmission, corrupt forms have attained common usage among speakers who lack proficiency; consequently, for them, the correct form is no longer expressive.
This divine speech has been thrown into confusion by incompetent speakers;
however, regarding this doctrine, those who perceive it as non-eternal experience a perversion of intellect.
Because both [the primary and secondary meanings] are uninterrupted, when another word is employed with the intention of expressing something else,
that other word is not the denoter of that [intended] meaning.
It has been stated that a word is an aggregate of sounds, or it is a genus residing in an aggregate; or else, the word is a single partless entity, while sequence is a mental synthesis.

Regarding the sentence, the views of those who perceive the principles of logic are diverse in many ways: some hold that every word is distinct [from others], while others maintain that every word is dependent [upon others]. BVaky_2.2 //
Whatever has been formulated as a technical rule (paribhāṣā) in the treatise for the purpose of establishing the application of elision (nighāta) and so forth,
does not apply to everything that possesses the same formal characteristic, provided its constituent parts require further specification.

A sentence is said to consist of parts that require mutual expectancy, contain words that do not require further external words, have the action as its primary meaning, possess subordinate elements (guṇas), and expresses a single unified sense. (Brahma-vākya 2.4)
And whatever is a vocative word is a qualifier of the action; likewise, they say that a verbal form (tiṅanta) is a qualifier of another verbal form.
Just as even a single word ending in the suffix *ktvā* can be a qualifier of a verb ending in a finite suffix (*tiṅ*),
so too they say that a verb ending in a finite suffix can be a qualifier of another verb ending in a finite suffix.

Just as the single light that illuminates all objects is differentiated according to the diversity of the things perceived, so too is the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence [differentiated]. (BVaky_2.7)
Just as a single variegated form is designated by means of distinctions such as blue and so forth, which possess distinct characteristics, [so too is the universal designated].
In the same way, the designation of a single sentence that is entirely free from expectancy is followed by other words that possess expectancy.
Just as in a word, the base, the suffix, and so forth are analyzed,
so too is the extraction of words from a sentence possible.
A similarity to other phonemes is observed within the constituent parts of phonemes;
likewise, the constituent parts of words stand as if they were similar to other words.
The bull, water, and barley-meal are associated with useless parts;
rather, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is the basis for linguistic usage.
There is no division in the word; how then could there be one in the meaning?
It is the ignorant person who, through divisions, arrives at a distinction in grammatical derivation.
Just as there is no such thing as the "meaning of a Brahmin" in the case of a "Brahmin’s blanket," so too would [names] such as Devadatta be rendered meaningless within a sentence.
The general meaning, having vanished, does not persist in the particular;
how can there be the abandonment of what has been grasped, and where could that which has ceased abide? (Brahmavidyā-vākya 2.15)
If the meaning of a sentence were not denoted by words, then the meaning of a word would likewise not be so;
and this being the case, the connection between a word and its meaning would be lost.
Certain particularizing words, which are counter-forms of universals,
are manifested to cognizers through their connection with other words.
But for them, the entire meaning of the sentence is completed with each individual word;
the manifestation of the meaning in the hearers is accomplished through both the explicit words and their secondary implications.
That manifest, sequential sound which one recites in a whisper is *vyakta*; but that which is without sequence, where the intellect remains as if having expanded [it], is *akrama*.
Just as a difference in action is not perceived even when there is a specific upward movement,
so too is the genus manifested through repeated actions such as revolving and the like.
In this way, the auditory perception of phonemes, sentences, and words— which possess similar secondary characteristics—
is perceived as if identical in form, despite the absolute difference in their underlying reality.
And in the case of eternal things, how could there be "prior" or "subsequent" in the ultimate sense?
It is simply the power of that single entity itself which causes it to appear in such a way.
Just as the cognitions "long" and "short" appear at different times despite there being no difference in time [in the object itself],
so too does that property [of duration] appear in the case of short and long vowels.
Time, being eternal, cannot undergo differentiation here merely through its constituent measures (*mātrā*);
for in the absence of distinct measures, what kind of sequence could there be? (BVaky_2.24)
The single cognition that arises from those [two] is devoid of parts;
for, by its own power, it appears as if divided while reflecting upon the sequence.
Because a seed has been sown within that [speech] through the continuous succession of sequential utterances,
no definitive explanation of its unity or plurality can be established.
But at the time of cultivation, this sequence is non-sequential;
for by its power, an object whose distinctions have been set aside is perceived as possessing distinctions.
If the words in a sentence are indeed those same phonemes that exist in the word,
then within the phonemes there would have to be a division of phonemic parts, just like atoms.
Due to the lack of contact between the parts, there would be neither phoneme nor word;
since they are indefinable, what else could be defined? (Brahma-vākya 2.29)
That single essence of sound which is manifested through its constituent parts— others call that "the word" (śabda), and likewise maintain its unity within the sentence.
In this way, the internal meaning of those [words] is revealed through their respective portions of meaning;
word and meaning are two divisions of the one Self alone, existing inseparably.
The relationship between the illuminator and the illuminated, as well as the nature of cause and effect,
always belongs to that essence of sound (śabdatattva), which consists of the internal measure (mātrā).
Its existence and non-existence are established as its capacity,
appearing in a sequence despite being non-sequential, serving as the basis for conventional discourse.

Since the existence of word-meanings is postulated on the basis of the authority of cognition, if one were to abandon that [cognition] when adding further word-meanings, it would follow that [the word] is meaningless. (BVaky_2.34)
The meaning of "king" is understood through the word *rājan* in its distinct form;
however, in a compound (*vṛtti*), another word resembling a verb is employed. (BVaky_2.35)
Just as when "aśvakarṇa" is uttered, a certain specific object is understood even without [the presence of] a horse, so too is the cognition [of the meaning] in all cases.

In certain sentences, when a similarity is conceived based on a meaning other than the literal one, the status of these as conventional (*rūḍhi*) words is understood from the grammatical treatise itself. (Vākya-kāṇḍa 2.37)
Those things which are to be abandoned even by means of [certain] means are called "means";
moreover, the restriction of such means does not necessarily remain fixed.
A certain person somehow arrives at the meaning [of a sentence];
for the distinctions based on sentences are either combined, separated, or differentiated. (BVaky_2.39)

When the connection "this is that" is undertaken by means of the intellect regarding the meaning of a sentence, then even a single phoneme may, in some cases, be expressive [of that meaning]. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 2.40)
Whatever meaning is expressed by a word alone,
they say that [the word], when situated in a sentence, is the denoter of that much meaning.
When a relationship exists, that further excellence which arises is said to be the very meaning of the sentence, which rests upon many words.
Although it resides in many words, it is completed with each individual division;
like a genus, it is conceived by others as residing even in a collection, just as number is.

Others, however, understand the universal (*sāmānya*) to be that which conforms to all particular instances (*bheda*); through its association with other objects, it assumes the form of those particulars. (BVaky_2.44)
The relation, by establishing itself in a specific [particular], cuts off that state of oscillation belonging to it which arises from its desire for further distinctions.
The relationship is to be inferred from its effect; it possesses no form of its own. Therefore, they declare it to be absolutely non-existent in nature.
The goal is necessarily accomplished by the means, and the action has necessary means;
that restriction is manifested merely through their proximity.
In that context, a noun functions with expectancy as a subordinate element (guṇabhāva),
while the verbal form requires the causal factors (nimitta) as that which is to be accomplished (sādhyatva).
Those very particulars which are not manifested within the word-meanings are apprehended sequentially; the sentence, however, is not the expressive unit.
And since there is no other expressive word apart from the mere sequence of sounds,
and sequence is a property of time, therefore no sentence exists [as a single entity].
And those possible distinctions among word-meanings that remain unmanifested [in isolation] become manifest when they are brought together; however, this process does not apply to phonemes.
The designation "word" and the name "sentence," which apply merely to the sequential arrangement of phonemes and words respectively,
are not accepted as being the essence of "word-ness" (śabdatva) for those two.
However, although the nature of being a word (śabdatva) is the same [in each phoneme], comprehension is observed to arise from the word (pada);
this does not occur for each individual phoneme. Therefore, the wise know that the meaning belongs to the word.
Just as phonemes, though possessing parts, are meaningful when combined even without some denotable object, so too is a sentence held to be [meaningful] in this same way.
They say that words, whether meaningless because they lead to undesirable consequences or meaningful through their individual referents,
when uttered in sequence, convey the sentence-meaning which has a distinct characteristic.

Whether one postulates that groups [of words] are eternal, or that it is the universal (jāti) that is so, they say that the non-deviating capacity of a single sentence to convey a single meaning is established. (BVaky_2.56)
Those who maintain the theory of the sentence (vākyavādins) consider non-differences to be preceded by difference as mere conceptual constructs;
however, those who perceive the word (padadarśins) regard non-differences as being preceded by difference.
The original form of the word is described according to the different types of grammatical operation (*vṛtti*);
the *saṃhitā* is the source of words, or rather, the *saṃhitā* rests upon the words.
And if the traditional recitation of words (*padāmnāya*) were something distinct from the *saṃhitā* that indicates it,
then how could the word-form be established as eternal therein, given that it is observed through grammatical rules?
Just as the cognition of the meaning of a word is not perceived with respect to each individual phoneme,
so too the determination of the sentence-meaning is not perceived within the words themselves.
Just as the meaning of a sentence resides in words that function together,
so too does the meaning of a word reside in phonemes that function together.
Just as a subtle object of perception, when mixed with another, is perceived together with it, so too a phoneme, when connected with another phoneme, is expressive [of meaning]. (BVaky_2.62)
Just as a certain meaning is determined from the utterance of a word,
so too that same meaning is cognized from the proximity of the phonemes.
If, by the power of that which has already been obtained, a subsequent scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction,
then the general rule is completely set aside by that specific one.
From the injunction "one should sacrifice," the substance [required] is obtained by implication;
that [substance] would be set aside by the explicit mention of *vrīhi* (rice), and thus there would be no substitute.
Therefore, the word "rice" (vrīhi) should establish the property of being rice (vrīhitva) as something additional;
since it is not contradictory, it does not sublate the property of being a substance (dravyatva), which serves the purpose of [the word's] application.
And when that co-occurring substantiality has been excluded by that [word], other particulars are not perceived there because they are impossible [in that context]. (BVaky_2.67)
Nor are all particulars indicated by the action-word as if they possessed a universal; for a word is not the designator of every existent thing.
Just as existing qualities such as whiteness and the like are not intended to be expressed there [in the word "cow"],
so too are the distinctions concomitant with substantiality not intended to be expressed.
Let there be no substitute for a permanent rite when its materials are absent;
however, it is logical that there should be an omission of a rite performed for a specific desire if its materials are missing. (Brahma-vākya 2.70)
If a specific action is conceived as the meaning of the sentence,
then in the absence of the substance, that [action] would become a different action in its substitute.
And when a word whose meaning is already known has its referent established, why should one inquire, "What is this [word] such as 'pika'? regarding that which is not understood? (BVaky_2.72)
And that which is obtained through implication and is subsequently supplied for the sake of the individual instance—
the direct statement (śruti) itself, by means of such supply, sublates both indicative power (liṅga) and syntactical connection (vākya).
But that which, such as "white" and so forth, is not already present and is understood through proximity—
whether it is brought about by effort or occurs within the sentence— is distinct from the property of direct audition (*śruti*).

If it is maintained that a sentence is indeed indivisible only when its meaning is indivisible, then all such [sentences], being of the nature of direct revelation (*śruti*), will not contradict revelation itself.
Furthermore, regarding that collection of sentences which exists for the sake of establishing a single meaning and whose parts are mutually expectant,
even the meaning of the sentence does not exist [as a distinct entity].
This task is incidental; this is accomplished through the *tantra* (the method of brevity);
here, sublation and combination occur through repetition and differentiation.
In this matter, modification (ūha) is appropriate; its connection is not sublated.
This is an extension (atideśa) of the general rule, yet here a specific detail is extended.
In this context, "desire" (arthitva) refers to capability; the meaning here does not differ from that in the treatise.
This person has obtained the qualification through the scripture, and his exclusion applies only to other actions.
"This sequence is obtained through direct revelation (śruti), while this other is from explicit utterance (uccāraṇa);
therefore, this [former] sequence is stronger here, whereas that [latter] is not intended to be significant."
This [word] is connected with the subordinate members (parāṅga) and is not itself prompted by them; rather, it is that which prompts them, and this [prompting] is inseparable from it.
"This is the primary [element], this is the subordinate; this is the sequence of application: this assists it directly, while this distinguishes it indirectly. (BVaky_2.82)
In this case, there is a distinction between the capacity and the operation; however, it is the result that differs here.
This distinction, which arises from the relationship [between word and meaning], is not intended to be expressed in that context.
"This is a non-presuppositional negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), this is an exclusionary negation (paryudāsa) here;
this is secondary (gauṇa), this is primary (mukhya); this is pervasive (vyāpin), and this is heavy (guru) or light (laghu). (Bhāṣāvṛtti 2.84)
Through its differentiation, the relationship of part and whole (aṅga-aṅgin) of this [sentence] is conceptualized in many ways;
it is thus regulated that the fitness for this [part] arises in relation to that [whole].
The distinction of this [word-meaning] is inferred from the indicative mark (liṅga) observed in other sentences;
this word-meaning is analyzed by being abstracted through words. (BVaky_2.86)
Thus, whatever properties in sentences are based upon the meanings of words would all be rendered impossible if the word were non-expressive.
Even though the meaning of a sentence is indivisible, when it is extracted through a distinction of powers by means of the division of other sentences, what has been stated is not contradicted.
Just as there is a conceptual differentiation of a single odor according to its presence in flowers and so forth, so too is a difference in meaning attributed to a sentence.
Just as in the case of a gavaya or a man-lion (narasiṃha), when they are perceived through a single cognition,
one perceives a part that is similar to another species.
But when a fool perceives a portion that is unestablished, unseen, and not observed, he assumes a lack of awareness regarding that very extent in all cases.

Likewise, in a sentence that is entirely distinct [from its parts] through the connection of words such as "pika" and so on, one considers there to be a cognition of a non-existent object as if it were similar [to the parts]. (BVaky_2.92)
Similarity is perceived in one part and difference in another part of the partless light by means of a partless mind alone. (Brahma-vākya 2.93)
In the very same way, similarity is determined in one part and difference in another,
even though sentences whose properties are entirely distinct lack any such parts.
If words were destroyed [upon utterance], how could there be the conception of a limit?
And if the word is not grasped as having a limit, how can its meaning be distinguished?
Just as in the case of the blending of colors, a form situated elsewhere is perceived in sound;
likewise, that form is held to be distinct within various forms by means of the tantra.
Within that non-difference, the forms of the various distinctions exist as if in a state of conjunction;
therefore, a form is distinguished from another form while remaining non-different from it.
In the treatise, the unity of the signifier is sometimes relied upon with respect to the signified;
in other cases, a distinction between the apprehender and the apprehended is established.
Relying on non-difference through the syllable *ū*, [the forms] are conceived according to their respective numbers;
yet, in the inclusion of *lṛ* and *luṭ*, a distinction is conceptually constructed by the two things to be grasped.
The form *yasya* is the designator of those things to be designated (*saṃjñin*) that possess the suffix *aṇ*; for it is not possible to grasp [an object] by means of what is merely being implied.
The particle *ū* is both non-different and based on different sentences;
its apprehension as distinct is like the "other form" (*pararūpa*) of two [sounds].
By rejecting the expansion of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of a protracted vowel (*pluta*) as well as their combination (*samāhāra*),
one instead relies entirely upon a distinction (*bheda*) among words.
Just as there is a difference in form among words such as *ardharca* and others according to their sequence, so too,
within the framework of a single word, the perception of distinct [meanings] occurs differently through the power of the system (*tantra*).
In the context of the *saṃhitā*, phonemes remain unchanged in their essential form;
yet, by assuming different capacities, they appear as if they were becoming distinct words.

The perception [of objects] among graspable things through a modification of the sense faculties and so forth is distinct from the abandonment of the self; that is the sequence [of cognition] taught in the Śruti.
Due to the difference in the act of denotation, even though the words themselves remain unchanged,
that very same single form appears as if it were absolutely distinct.
The *sāman* is either the *ṛc* itself or merely the melody; it is not a separate substance.
However, due to the differences in melody, those very same *ṛcs* are perceived as modified forms.
In the compendium of the Vedas, when those [words] that have been split apart by means of a specific method remain as a single residue,
their grammatical correctness is stated in the treatise when they are uttered by way of *tantra*.
Having grasped a single grammatical rule (śruti), even for those [words] that possess different forms, a simultaneous utterance (tantra) must be performed; otherwise, they would not be correct.
And when sentences are identical in form, although not explicitly taught by the grammatical treatise,
a single correct form is obtained through the principle of *tantra* (economy of effort) due to their simultaneous utterance.
Just as a single entity assumes multiple forms through its connection with things such as tubes and so forth,
in the same way, according to the Tantra, many entities may possess a single form.
Just as there is the possibility of sentences that resemble individual words,
so too would these possess separate meanings even in the absence of other distinct sentences.
For one for whom the meaning of a word is the denotable object and the meaning of a sentence is the purpose,
no connection between sentences is logically possible.
In that case, it is the verbal roots alone that mutually require one another;
however, the relationship [between nouns] is understood as being connected to those verbal roots.
In the conceptualization of the distinct meanings of words, there is either repetition or restatement;
for while the meaning is complete in each individual word, it functions [as a whole] when they occur together.
Regarding the meaning of a sentence as being free from conceptual construction, various conceptualizations based on mental cultivation arise;
in this matter, the arguments of former teachers have been held in many ways.
Others maintain that every word is a cause of intuition (*pratibhā*) due to repeated practice, as is observed in the communication of meaning to children and animals. (Brahma-sūtra-vārttika 2.117)

And some maintain that this convention (*samaya*) is a practice (*abhyāsa*) devoid of a prior source (*anāgama*), which indicates that "this effect must immediately follow from this [cause]. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 2.118)
"There is an object for all words"—this is the definition of that which is to be signified;
they say it is the same as in the case of *apūrva*, deities, and heaven, even with respect to words such as "cow."
However, that apprehension of form which arises from the practice of observing usage is not the object of the word, for it depends upon a different effort.
Some distinctions are manifested by words that denote them; however, it is held that certain word-meanings arise as concomitants [of the primary meaning]. (Vākyapadīya 2.121)

When a word conveys a universal (jāti), the individual (vyakti) is necessarily concomitant; however, the word denoting the universal does not depend upon the specific differences residing in that individual.

A denotative word does not convey the specific forms of jars and the like, because it is restricted to the mere entity; therefore, the cognition of those forms is necessarily dependent on something else.
An action impelled by a word is not observed to occur without its employment;
therefore, it is understood that the meaning of a word is the employment which follows as a consequence.
However, others maintain that those applications which are fixed and that means which is fixed possess the status of being denotable by words. (Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 2.125)

Some maintain that the meaning of a word is either a collection (*samudāya*)— whether it be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or a simple aggregate (*samuccaya*)— or else it is a relation (*saṃsarga*) that is unreal.
Either that reality which is qualified by an unreal adjunct becomes the basis for words,
or else the word itself, having attained the state of conceptual identification (*abhijalpa*), enters into the status of being the denotable object.
Because of the connection "this is that," form is unified with the object; they call that word *abhijalpa*. (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 2.128)
Since these two are not distinct in essence, their conventional usage is non-deviant;
in certain cases, a particular form alone remains predominant.
In common worldly usage, a word functions as having the nature of the object;
however, in the scientific treatise (śāstra), it possesses both natures, distinguished according to the speaker's intention.
Whether due to incapacity or because [the word] possesses all powers, the fixed conceptualization of action and so forth for a single object is constructed by words alone. (BVaky_2.131)
Alternatively, that object which is the domain of the intellect and is based upon an external thing,
being known as "the external thing," is understood to be the meaning of the word.
These [objects] appear as possessing forms, being perceivable, and serving as the basis for manifestation and memory; pure consciousness, however, is otherwise than this.
Just as the sense organ, when coming into contact [with its object], manifests [its perception] in various ways,
so too is the comprehension of meaning from a word manifold.
Furthermore, when there are diverse understanders who have set out with different intentions, the meaning of a word is differentiated according to their own respective cognitions. (BVaky_2.135)
Even regarding a single visible object, perceptions differ individually;
and even a single person perceives it differently again at another time.
And even for a single word, its meaning is conceptualized in many ways—by one person through unstable causes, and by many others as well. (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 2.137)
Therefore, for those who have not perceived reality, their vision or even their speech is always flawed, full of fallacies, and entirely unstable.
And as for that vision of the seers which is established in some degree of reality,
there is no linguistic usage based upon it, nor is it dependent upon words.
The sky appears as if it were a surface, and a firefly like a fire;
yet there is no surface in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vākya 2.140)
Therefore, even when perceiving an object through direct perception, the wise person should examine it through reasoning;
one should not postulate the existence of an object merely on the basis of the validity of its perception.
Just as worldly people provide designations for things whose true nature is inexpressible during conventional discourse, the wise person should not conceptualize those designations.
When the meanings of words are apprehended as distinct, another intuition arises;
they call that "sentence-meaning" (vākyārtha), which is brought about by the word-meanings.
"This is that"—in this way, it cannot be described by others in any manner whatsoever;
established as a function within each individual self, it cannot be defined even by its own agent.
Unexamined, that [cognition] brings about, as it were, a close contact with objects;
having assumed, as it were, a universal form, it functions as the objective domain.

No one can transcend that [capacity] regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), whether it is produced by the word directly or through the accompaniment of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). (BVaky_2.146)
The entire world follows that [speech] as its authority;
even the undertakings of animals proceed by virtue of it.

Just as the powers of intoxication and so forth are seen to arise without effort from the ripening of specific substances, so too do the creative intuitions (*pratibhā*) of those who possess them [arise].
Who transforms the vocal activity of the male cuckoo in spring?
And how are living beings instructed in the construction of nests and the like? (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya 2.1.49)
In activities such as aversion to food, affection, and swimming— those established by species and lineage— who is the agent among beasts and birds?
This [distinction] arises from scripture itself, following from its cultivation;
however, scripture is distinguished by proximity and remoteness.

They know that intuition (*pratibhā*) is of six kinds: that which arises from the appearance of the obstruction of intrinsic nature, that which is produced by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and that which is endowed with excellence. (BVaky_2.152)
Just as the word "cow" is employed when an object is characterized by substances possessing conjunction, yet that word does not reveal those specific qualities themselves.
Even though a word functions with respect to cows and the like, which are composed of shapes, colors, and parts, it does not admit those [components] as its own object.
A word is applied to an object qualified by configuration, color, and parts; its application to those individual parts is not observed.
For anyone in this world, it is difficult to perceive all the parts [of an object] at once;
rather, when certain parts are perceived, the whole object is inferred.
Likewise, the determination of qualities such as those of the *jāti* jasmine and other flowers— which coexist with their fragrance and are seen to be eternally connected— is observed.
Independent of number, measure, and configuration,
the expressive word for "water" and the like functions both with respect to a single drop and to a collection.
That which is established in oil and the like, which are delimited by their conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth,
refers to a single part as being the reality itself, by means of that which resides in its constituent parts.
When a designation is employed because it is connected with a certain meaning,
its employment ceases once that meaning has departed.
However, a word that is employed while implicitly including those properties that are possible [to be expressed] does not necessarily require the presence of those [properties].

Just as the word "cow" is seen to apply even when there is deviation regarding the presence of hair on the feet and so forth, it does not function in that same way in the absence of the universal (jāti).
Therefore, when there is a comprehension of a possible object from a word,
that [object] is understood as being connected [to the word] for the purpose of excluding what is not perceived.
The case endings (vibhakti) expressing duality and so forth may either be expressive of the number itself,
or the entire aggregate [of the word and its ending] may be the denoter of the object possessing that number.
Alternatively, words such as "cow" and others denote certain objects— endowed with numerical distinctions— even without the explicit mention of a number, by means of a distinction in their own form.

Those words whose relationship is eternal and whose expressive powers are known through discrimination have their meanings distinguished by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

As long as it is possible to conceive of those two [the word and its meaning] through an invariable relation, a restriction applies there; however, such a restriction does not exist in the case of suffixes such as *nuṭ* and *śa*.
The status of being a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is not possible for a name when it is [merely] present;
for the powers of words, which are relative, are restricted to their specific associations.
No semantic connection is observed among the meanings of *kūpa*, *sūpa*, and *yūpa*;
therefore, it is understood that the composite whole alone expresses a distinct meaning.
Explanations diverge in the processes of word derivation;
when many meanings are possible, some specific cause is required [to determine the correct one]. (BVaky_2.170)
Vairava, Vāsiṣṭha, Giriśa, as well as Ekāgārika and others,
have been designated by some in various ways through a confusion of causes and limits.
Just as the description of a path by means of trees, anthills,
and mountains is not contradictory, so too is [the description] of cows and other things by means of distinct concomitants.

Furthermore, those who perceive the differences in states provide alternative designations for the *kiṃśuka* tree and others, based on the determination of its various parts. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 2.173)
By some, different etymologies for the word *gauḥ* have been presented here: from the roots *gṛ* (to swallow), *garj* (to roar), *gam* (to go), *gav* (to seek), or *gad* (to speak).
The word "cow" (go) applies to cows either by its own nature as the form "cow" or through etymological derivation; some maintain that all words function in both ways.
And in the treatise, a general instruction is adopted for the sake of brevity;
the specific features of another [word] are established as being like those of a different class.
And they know that which occurs in a different meaning to be a different primary form;
it does not, while retaining its identical form, become attached to another conventional meaning.
The two roots *ij* and *jī* are distinct, yet they are restricted to different domains;
they have been taught by some in various ways, for the methods of exposition are indeed diverse.
And in this way, one should treat the *vālavāya* and other such [sounds] like the *jitvarī*;
when both difference and non-difference are accepted, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

In the grammatical treatise, the separate conceptualization of roots and prefixes is for the purpose of establishing the rules regarding *aṭ* and so forth; however, in reality, it is the root alone that is of such a nature.
For it is thus that the rule is recorded for the root *sam-grām-ayati* when preceded by a prefix;
such specific actions are undertaken within a composite formation.
In this way, the internal relationship between the verbal root and the prefix is such that the action,
being of that very nature, enters into connection with the factors of accomplishment (sādhana).
When established for the sake of application, the object to be divided is specified;
moreover, prior to its connection with the means of accomplishment, the action itself does not yet arise.

Just as the status of being a verbal root and the state of being an object are established through the application of a future accomplishment of the root's meaning, so too should other cases be understood.
Just as lac-dye and other substances, through their connection at the time of the seed, assist the fruits by means of a transformation of color and so forth; [so too does the word].
From the connection with the root, as well as from that with the prefix,
a distinction that was internalized becomes manifest at the time of the word-division.
In some cases, distinctions that are possible but not indicated by the verbal roots alone are manifested through their connection with prefixes such as *pra*, *ni*, *ā*, and so forth.
That [prefix] is either the denoter of specific qualities because they are possible [therein], or it is an illuminator;
or else, it is employed as an auxiliary to the verbal root (dhātu) for the purpose of imparting its capacity.
And since movement and so forth are not perceived by means of the verbal roots *sthā* and others used in isolation,
the action [of standing] and so forth is said to possess that property [of being inferred] on the basis of two kinds of inference.
When there is no application [of another action], and as long as another action is observed in the presence of the prefixes *adhi* and *pari*,
the verbal root (*dhātu*) that denotes that [action] is meaningless when accompanied by those two prefixes.
In the same way, certain suffixes added for their own sake (svārthika), occurring within a different compound, when conjoined with a meaningless element, merely restate the meaning of the base form.
Some particles are indicators when conceived as having distinct meanings, while others, like grammatical augments (*āgama*), accomplish the meaning collectively. (BVaky_2.192)
Whether placed above or before, their function as illuminators does not differ,
even when they are employed in all ways with distinct meanings.
Particles such as *ca* and so forth are not employed in isolation when they possess the status of a word;
likewise, even though it possesses expressive power, an affix is not employed in isolation.

But when there is the expression of a collection [of meanings], no exclusion (vyatireka) exists; moreover, a state that has not yet become a real entity (asattvabhūta-bhāva) is expressed by verbal suffixes (tiṅpada).
Even when there is a collective expression, words that denote qualified objects are connected with their respective qualities; however, particles such as *ca* and others are dependent on those words.
In some cases, having produced a certain relation, the action ceases;
in other cases, when an action-word is heard, a relation is brought into being.
In that context, the genitive case is prescribed at every step for the purpose of precluding compound formation;
however, it is cited as an example with respect to a *kāraka* for the sake of illustration.
And that relation which has arisen when the verbal action is ceased is regulated in various instances by a *karmapravacanīya*.
That which implies a verbal action is joined with case endings of the *kāraka* relations; for example, as in "likha," where it is devoid of a prefix (*anupasarga*).

The non-employment of the verb *tiṣṭhati* is also observed, as in the expression *apratyajayan*; furthermore, the root *abhi* is employed even alone in the sense of "facing toward," as in *sunv abhi*.

The status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed when there is a connection with an action, for the purpose of precluding [the application of] rules such as the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, in the case of words like *sva* and others which possess different properties.

When the connection between cause and effect has been delimited by the particle *anu*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) characterized as a cause—which would otherwise apply—is superseded by the rule governing the introduction [of the particle]. (BVaky_2.203)
This [particle] is neither an indicator of an action nor an expresser of a relation;
nor does it imply a verbal form of action, but rather it serves to differentiate the relation.

A collection of meaningless [phonemes] is meaningful, and likewise, it is meaningless; a word is composed of phonemes joined with meaning, but the constituent parts do not possess meaning within the word.
Furthermore, the combination of words whose meanings are already connected is split apart by the comprehension of another meaning and by the dissolution of their mutual relation. (Brahma-vākya 2.206)
Some maintain that the meaningful and the meaningless do not attain a relationship when distinct;
others, however, hold that they do attain it, citing examples such as the word *kuṭīra*.

A compound arises from meaningful elements as something possessing a distinct meaning; however, some maintain that it does not arise [as a separate entity] in the case of nominal suffixes (svārthika) and the like within compounds.

For some words have meanings established as separate entities whose capacities are known through their distinctness, while others have capacities that are merely conceptualized through the methods of agreement and difference.
The meaningfulness of phonemes has been demonstrated precisely through the meaning of the treatise;
for pure roots and the like possess no worldly meaning.
The meaning of primary derivatives (kṛt) and secondary derivatives (taddhita), as well as that of isolated words, is unreal (*alaukika*);
likewise, the meaning of a word ending in such an affix does not exist prior to the addition of an inflectional suffix.
That meaning which is perceived as more clearly manifest at the end of suffixes is of such a nature that it is resorted to on account of the section concerning meaningfulness.
If there is no distinct entity [such as a sphoṭa] other than the phonemes in words and sentences,
then the phoneme would be the signifier through its capacity, by virtue of mutual dependence.
If a word-formation that expresses [an object] is deficient by some phoneme, it is not a different word; therefore, it is understood as being non-deficient [in its expressive power]. (BVaky_2.214)
Fixing a memory of the meaning upon that expressive word by means of its cause,
he brings forth the meaning— which is actually mediated— by the word as if it were directly present.
Just as there is no object denoted by the word in cases such as "white-ass" (*gaura-khara*), even though a cognition certainly arises, nothing at all is understood in the aggregate. (BVaky_2.216)
When the essence of an object is perceived as if endowed with the meanings of its constituent word-meanings,
the perception of those word-meanings therein is likewise of no assistance.

And when the aggregate and its constituent parts have different meanings within the grammatical operations (*vṛtti*), difference and relation—which are mutually contradictory—would follow simultaneously. (BVaky_2.218)
And who would postulate *adhi* and the others as having the meaning of a mere instrument (*sādhana*)? Furthermore, how could there be a meaning for an unapplied word within a *bahuvrīhi* compound?
Nor is there a determination of meaning through the parts, such as the prefix *pra-* and the verbal root;
therefore, the aggregate alone is the basis for the specific meaning.
The word *garga* is a single entity that functions with respect to many referents; even as a collective known as a *dvandva*, this aggregate denotes many individuals.
Just as in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, the action of eating and so forth resides in each individual [member],
so too, in the meaning expressed by a *dvandva* compound, the action itself is distributed individually.

And that dependence of the referent of a dvandva compound upon the word *tat* (that) is also a case of a pronoun having the same form [as its antecedent], provided the object has a distinct form. (BVaky_2.223)
And just as the act of cutting proceeds sequentially through the parts when cutting a piece of khadira wood,
so too is the sequential perception [of meaning] observed in the parts of a compound word.

Just as those who have departed from a portion of the Saṅgha are still considered followers of the Saṅgha, so too do they consider specific ritual actions [to belong to it]; such is the sequence regarding a member of a dual compound.

While explaining that the function [of speech] for those who have not understood it is preceded by the sentence, the predominance [of the sentence] is demonstrated in the commentary through the differentiation of word-meanings. (BVaky_2.226)

In a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), because the referent is non-different [from its absence], the primacy [of the negation] is described in various ways in the *Bhāṣya*; however, the faults pertain only to the process of grammatical derivation.
And by one who maintains that in the *jahatsvārtha* alternative all meanings are abandoned,
the abandonment of the entire referent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound is demonstrated.
In some instances in the grammatical treatise, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is expressed by the suffix (pratyaya),
and when the base has ceased [to function], the meaning of the suffix is expressed by verbal roots (dhātu).
The single meaning that two distinct suffixes express together,
that same meaning a verbal root sometimes expresses alone— as in "they cook" (*pacanti*)— and sometimes it expresses without them.
And those meanings of the suffixes which are established as the basis for the traditional grammatical treatises (*anvākhyāna-smṛti*),
have been cited in another tradition as being the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*).
"It is taught thus in the treatise that it causes vomiting because of its notoriety;
for they consider the formal procedures of the treatise's meaning to be for the sake of conventional usage. (Brahma-vākya 2.232)
In the treatises, it is ignorance alone that is described through various systematic analyses;
however, true knowledge manifests of its own accord, free from traditional authority and conceptual construction.
Just as a fruit that is unattached to its causes is beyond description,
so too is knowledge indescribable, though it is perceived through the means provided by the treatises.
For speech strives to convey meaning according to habitual practice;
and this beginningless false practice is established as if it were its very nature.
The unwise imagine an atom to possess parts,
and likewise imagine a composite whole to be joined with further constituent parts.
Because of the perception of jars and other such things, the world is determined to be finite;
and because of the production of entities, Brahman is eternal yet possesses a beginning.
The skillful means of those in training are for the sake of instructing the ignorant;
by abiding on the path of the unreal, one subsequently strives for the real.
Having understood a meaning otherwise by first grasping the words,
one subsequently understands that very same meaning in a different way within the sentence.
Even many meanings that have been adopted, when a negation is subsequently applied to them, they are turned back; therefore, one should not rely upon them in that context.
And the statement "there is no tree" is characterized by the absence of a qualified entity;
the exclusion [of that entity] does not reside in either the object or the cognition, as there is no connection [between them].
And if, in the case of the cognition of cessation, it is determined that "it exists," how could that established cognition— which is not denotable by words— be negated?

Now, if that cognition which has arisen is rendered false by the negative particle (*nañ*), then how can there be an apprehension of non-existence when this function of the negative particle is distinct? (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 2.243)
And if it were to function without a substratum, the negative particle would have to function prior [to its association with the word];
or else, that very [word] must be its substratum, and the scriptural statement would serve the purpose of restriction.

Or, it may be for the purpose of indicating a restriction, or it may be a restatement (anuvāda); in that case, only one word would be meaningful, while the remaining words would be redundant. (Brahma-vākyapadīya 2.245)
Furthermore, when a contradiction has been established by means of the examples and so forth, one understands the meaning of the sentence differently once the sentence is completed. (BVaky_2.246)
In sentences where praise or censure predominates, the meaning is not such as it is imagined to be through the separate division of the words.
Now, the meaning that is indeed uncombined resides within the individual words;
