this is the means for the comprehension of a single sentence-meaning.
That which was previously unconnected with words and is gradually accumulated, they know to be more distinguished because it is like a string of pearls that has been cut and restrung.
Some investigators say that a single word has multiple meanings;
for that single word, its capacity to signify all objects is differentiated according to the difference in the causal conditions (*nimitta*).
Having transcended simultaneity, it settles upon succession,
either through the meaning and the context, or through connection, or by means of another word.
Just as a physical body possessing a dewlap and so forth is denoted by the word "cow," so too that very same word "cow" is established even for a Vāhīka.
However, because that very word possesses manifold properties and all capacities,
its status as primary or secondary arises from the difference in conventional usage.
A single mantra exists with its powers differentiated for all purposes, without confusion, according to the internal self, the deity, and the ritual act. (BVaky_2.254)
Some maintain that the attachment of the universal "cowness" to a Vāhīka occurs due to a specific cause;
[in this view], it is only the object that is mistaken, while the word remains established in its own primary meaning.
In the same way, the own-form (svarūpa) of words is attached to all objects;
while the mere object is inverted, the audition (śruti) remains fixed upon the own-form.

Those who perceive the path of distinction, however, declare that there is identity between the secondary and primary words because they possess the same form, even though there is absolute difference between them.
And in this way, it is attached to the repetition following the *sāmidhenī* verses;
and the mantras, through their application, acquire differentiation just like the *ūha*.
Those very other traditions are indeed recited; however, there is only a certain portion that is meaningless, while the rest is understood as something else.

The nature of the word is [the same], but the meaning is described by others as being different in each recitation; there is absolute difference among all [meanings], yet they appear as identical because of their connection with that [word].
One *sāvitrī* is employed for ritual acts involving formal preparation (*saṃskāra*), another for the continuous recitation of prayers (*japa*); yet it is perceived as being one and the same.
For one who maintains that words function toward the nature of their referent by virtue of their own form,
the sentence as a whole functions toward the sentence-meaning independently of anything else.
For those who follow the view that a single word possesses multiple meanings,
the distinction between the primary and secondary senses is determined by whether [the meaning] is established or not established.
Others know that word which, depending on the context of the meaning, or joined with other words, causes the meaning to be understood as secondary (gauṇa). (Brahma-vākya 2.264)
When a word is uttered in its pure form, that meaning which is understood as its well-known sense should be known as its primary meaning; it is based solely upon the word's own form.
But that which is applied with effort as if by the operation of another, they consider that to be unestablished, being intent upon a figurative meaning.

Even when operating in its own primary sense, that which one relies upon for the sake of a particular meaning is considered the primary cause (nimitta) therein, while the thing possessing that cause is regarded as secondary (gauṇa).
When two words with contrary meanings occur in a context where the sense is divided,
their specific determination depends upon the meaning and the context.
When the meanings of words are conceptually extracted from the meaning of the sentence,
with which single [meaning] could a connection to another word be logically established?

Furthermore, when a single word is observed in some instances to possess the function of expressing an action, they say that it is actually a distinct sentence; it cannot be construed with another [word].

And when, in response to the question "What is this?", it is said "It is a cow" or "It is a horse," the very act of questioning there consists of the previously initiated operations such as seeing and so forth.
Neither the excess nor the deficiency of properties is what determines [the status of a word];
for people consider even an excess as [standard] due to common usage, and in some cases, they consider even a deficiency as such.
Others know that word to be figurative (gauṇa) where a genus-word is employed even in the absence of the genus, due to a property similar to that which is related [to it]. (BVaky_2.273)
Where, as if due to a misconception, people perceive the object as having a different nature than it actually has— such as the word "cow" and so forth— that is sometimes called secondary (gauṇa).
Just as ploughs, swords, maces, and so forth are understood to be employed in ritual acts as fixed means, endowed with their specific forms and capacities; [so too are words].
Nor do these [words] lack the capacity for other actions;
rather, their subservience to that specific purpose is understood with necessity from their very form alone.
In the very same way, a word that is established by its production through both form and power,
having a fixed denotation, is employed elsewhere by virtue of its [latent] power.
That meaning whose capacity is determined by the mere hearing [of the word] is considered the primary meaning; that which is established through effort is considered secondary.
O Venerable One, when the suffix *cvī* is used in the sense of "becoming" (*svārthāt arthāntare sthitau*) for great beings,
the state of that [new] quality (*tadbhāva*) is seen there as being primary (*mukhya*), even though it is a figurative usage.
Nature (prakṛti) attains both greatness and the state of being white;
yet, when it is perceived through differentiation, it establishes its subordinate status.

Words such as *agni* (fire) and *soma*, which denote their own essential forms (*svarūpa*) as their referents, are employed in connection with the bearers of those names (*saṃjñin*); because [the primary sense] is not established in that context, they are used figuratively (*gauṇatā*).
But as for the fire that belongs to Agnidatta,
in that case the word [for fire] assumes a secondary (gauṇa) status because it functions with the meaning of "given" (datta) as its subordinate element.
When the process of deriving word-meanings has commenced based on a distinction of causes,
the presence and absence of the augment *suṭ* are established in cases such as *hariścandra*.
When a word that has already undergone grammatical refinement in relation to its primary referent (such as a seer) is subsequently joined with another [element],
the internal refinement does not cease even when an external meaning is involved.
Even when an object is determined to be utterly contrary [to its actual state],
the word is employed there in its primary sense according to that very cognition.
Although the determination of the true nature of an object depends upon cognition,
not every cognition regarding it arises as if it were already established.
The perception [of water] in a body of water is equal to the perception of a mirage and the like;
however, because touch and other [sensations] differ, a mirage is not water.
Since the specific effects of a rope and a snake are well known, their distinction is determined even though the perception of them is identical. (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 2.288)
And whatever is seen as a cause for the reversal of a well-established meaning,
the distinction that is perceived from that [reversal] is declared to be unreal.
And just as in a painting there are forms such as depressions and elevations along with mountains and so forth, yet no action such as obstruction occurs therein— so it proceeds in that case.
Just as the continuous succession of touches by the hand [is perceived] in the case of a wheel,
it is not so in the case of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), for that is indeed touched in a fragmented manner.
And just as those [obstacles] do not exist in cities due to the obstruction of touch by means of ditches and ramparts, so too they do not exist in gandharva-cities.

To whatever extent a purpose is accomplished by means of actual animals, cattle, and so forth, that same extent does not exist in their clay-made counterparts; therefore, the suffix *kana* applies to them as objects [of comparison].
A vast region is covered by well-known mountains and other such features,
yet a reflection is seen as situated within a very small portion of that space.

And just as poison and the like are primary causes for death and so forth, they do not accomplish their own respective effects in dreams and similar states; such is the case with the object [in cognition].
Whatever is perceived differently due to variations in place, time, and sense faculties,
that is determined in accordance with the common consensus of the world.
There is no linguistic usage based on those two kinds of cognition— that which arises from injury and that which is supramundane— because words are grounded in worldly convention.
Just as a lamp, when employed for a purpose such as [illuminating] a jar or the like, produces illumination for other things as well due to their proximity. (Bhāṣya-vākya 2.298)

In the same way, when a word is employed with respect to objects that are associated [with it], it causes those other [objects] to be understood as well, distinct from the primary motivator of its usage.

Just as the friction of two fire-sticks, prepared for the purpose of obtaining fire, produces even smoke—which is unintended—by means of that same single instrument; so too [is the case with the means of knowledge].
Likewise, even when a word is intended to convey a specific meaning, it reveals a meaning that was not intended to be conveyed due to its proximity [to other words]. (BVaky_2.301)
Just as an object that is completely intermingled cannot be abandoned,
so too a word that is related [to its meaning] cannot be separated.
Even when objects are present and even when they are manifested,
it is understood that the object is the motivator of the word, despite there being no difference in its form.
In some cases, the status of being subordinate or primary among meanings is not intended to be expressed;
in other cases, even their mere presence is not a cause for comprehension.
And that which is not directly expressed by the word is understood in some cases;
in other cases, the primary meaning itself becomes the definition of another. (Brahma-vākya 2.305)
Whatever verbal form indicates the meaning of a secondary derivative (taddhita), a reversal of the status of the subordinate and the principal is observed therein. (Brahmavidyābharaṇa 2.306)

In a grammatical exposition, the proximity of gender and number is not a cause [for restriction]; a measure such as "half-a-short syllable" (*ardhahrasva*) is understood even when it is not explicitly mentioned. (BVaky_2.307)

And that which is observed as half of a short [vowel] is designated in the same way even when that [short vowel] is not present, because it serves as the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of the short vowel. (BVaky_2.308)
Its distinction may be by means of length and prolation, or by its measure;
or it may serve as a defining characteristic of the genus, in every way like the *saptaparṇa* tree.
"When it is the characteristic of time [to indicate], 'The sun should be seen; it must be gone to,' this is expressed as a means for knowing the time. (Brahma-vākya 2.310)
In the expression "he pierces without a bow," a specific instance is demonstrated;
it serves as a basis for the general principle that any [entity] whatsoever can be a communicator of power.
Even a child, when instructed that "the ghee must be protected from crows," does not protect it from dogs and the like, since the statement is intent upon [excluding] those who would cause harm.

Even though it is not explicitly mentioned by its own form, the wiping of the place [where the bowls were kept] following the washing of the bowls is understood, because it is an integral part of the act of eating.
Words and their meanings are distinguished through context, the situational framework, the purpose, propriety, and place and time; they are not determined by form alone.
Association, dissociation, co-occurrence, opposition,
purpose, context, indicative mark, and the proximity of another word [are the factors that determine the specific meaning of a term].
Capacity, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth, are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined. (Vākya-kāṇḍa 2.316)

Even on the view that words are distinct, meanings that are different [from one another] become restricted for cognizers due to similarity; these words attain manifestation through context and other such factors.
Those words which have the same form as nouns or verbs and are based on other grammatical operations— the meaning of the sentence is not understood from their form alone.
The skillful practitioner understands that the conceptualization of praise and blame intended for the purpose of inciting activity or cessation is not in accordance with reality.
When an action being enjoined— which has a visible or invisible purpose—
is praised, that praise serves as an incentive specifically for its performer.
Just as a child is deterred by the mention of a tiger or the like,
even though it is unreal, so too is a certain transgression (pratyavāya) described.
Even after making arrangements, no learned person would engage in an action that is prohibited by the scripture and results in such a transgression. (Brahma-vākya 2.322)
Even after taking precautions against snakes by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, one should not act otherwise; one should not allow [the snake] to bite. (BVaky_2.323)
In some cases, the designation of reality is made for the purpose of praise or censure;
even there, engagement and withdrawal are taught.
The form (rūpa) of all word-meanings (padārtha) is that which is bound to the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha).
However, those sentence-meanings which are dependent [on others] are equivalent to word-meanings themselves.
They consider even that to be a sentence which consists of a single word whose action is already accomplished,
because we observe the occurrence of duality at the beginning of a sentence even without an explicit verbal action.
Where, in a verbal form (ākhyāta-śabda), a specific means (sādhana) is invariably understood,
that too is called a single sentence whose meaning is complete.
Cognition mediated by words, which rests upon unuttered words, is said to be the cause for the comprehension of their meaning; it is called inference.
Others, however, maintain that this very meaning belongs to the word itself,
established independently of its connection with other words. (Brahma-siddhi-vākya-kāṇḍa 2.329)
When a particular meaning is understood upon the utterance of a word, that alone is said to be its meaning; there is no other definition of meaning.
Just as an action is understood for the original verbal roots when words denoting an action are present as upapadas,
so too in a compound with *nir-* and other prefixes, the meaning of "gone beyond" and the like is cognized.
These are indeed other words, like synonyms used in common parlance;
however, their specific meaning is restricted by context and purpose.
However, those means of awakening which are directed toward this or that particular person are not necessarily connected with the object to be known through the words themselves.
Even when there is no actual comprehension, or when the instruction is erroneous,
those various words remain established through their own inherent meanings with which they are eternally connected.
In this scriptural statement regarding action, "the door," according to the context,
is understood through the means [of expression] to signify either "fasten" or "give."
In that regard, a word whose function is to establish [an object] and which is based on its existence does not denote the primary object that is to be proven. (BVaky_2.336)
Having manifested its own meaning alone, this [word] ceases to function as something dependent;
however, its related object brings about its presence [in the mind].
Since the state of being for another's sake is not distinct [in either case], there is no proximity of word to word from the word itself;
nor is there proximity of the word to the meaning from the meaning, nor proximity of the meaning to the word from the word. (Brahma-siddhi-vākya-kāṇḍa 2.338)
If both the action (bhāva) and the substance (sattva) were to attain primacy simultaneously, then the word denoting the action would be cast aside as if its form were lost. (BhV 2.339)
However, the verbal form of this [word] is described as being identical in form to the noun;
through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), its usage is distinguished.

Nor does the capacity to denote cease even when there is doubt regarding its form; for it is understood through contextual implication (sāmarthya), just as in the case of the expression "half of the animal."
If every locus of a being is pure when bound by its own formative nature, and if its meaning is not separate [from that nature] even when it is distinguished within a complex aggregate; 2.342.
"Verbs have action as their primary meaning, while nouns have substance as their primary meaning;
[these are] the four classes of words—all this is contradicted [by your position]. (Brahma-vākya 2.343)
Having observed that sentences are eternal in the intellect and possess worldly connection with meaning, Audumbarāyaṇa asserts that there is no fourfold nature [of speech].
And linguistic usage, which is pervasive and concise, rests upon words;
it is conceived through differentiation alone for the sake of practical function in both worldly life and the treatises.
In the world, established conventions do not arise for speakers through their connection with external objects;
therefore, nothing other than the sentence exists that is non-worldly (alaukika).
And those [meanings] indicated by signs and sentences heard elsewhere are understood as being their own meanings alone; they remain unperceived because there is no difference in their form.
That which was abandoned in the statement of general exclusion, though appearing wordless as it were,
is heard in the subverting statements and is understood elsewhere.
The Vedic revelation of the Brahmins has commenced with curd, excluding Māṭhara;
yet Māṭhara, through his connection with buttermilk, explains its true meaning therein.

Even when there is a connection with multiple verbs, some maintain that a sentence is indeed one, though it appears as if it were divided in form, depending on whether it follows the general rule or an exception.
In that case, restriction and prohibition are supplementary to a positive injunction;
they know that when elision (*luk*) is prescribed in the second [case], the non-elision (*aluk*) is its supplement. (BVaky_2.351)
Since they are independent of one another regarding their completion and are primary,
how could there be a single syntactical unity among them, given that they do not render mutual assistance?
Because there is a requirement for a specific injunction, a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is inferred;
therefore, the expectation [for such a supplement] is equal regarding both the object to be enjoined and the object to be excluded.
There is no elision of that which is a part of a name-word; that name, having been formed with its specific form, does not cease to exist.
Furthermore, no designation other than "Datta" and the like is perceived;
how then could the word "Datta" denote the bearer of that designation known as Devadatta? (Brahma-vākya 2.355)
Some maintain that all individual word-forms possess a relationship with all their denotata that is equal to the relationship of the entire aggregate.
The meaningfulness of phonemes occurs through their relationship with the things they name; a constituent part that is not connected [to its referent] cannot function as a name when it is isolated.
When there is a simultaneous connection with all the individual forms of the named object,
it is impossible for that object to be conveyed by means of those [forms] which resemble it only in part.
However, from a single part [of the word], a memory of certain [parts] arises within the aggregate;
and from the word, which is the object of that memory, the meaning of the aggregate is understood.
How could memory be restricted to a specific part within a composite whole that is distinct [from its parts]?
And how could a word, being perceived in this way, be the designator of an object?
But words that share a common form in part, yet are endowed with various specific distinctions, exist as designations established through their co-occurrence [with the primary term]. (BVaky_2.361)
Because they are common [to all], they are ambiguous; yet by virtue of their capacity, they have fixed substrata.
Among those [words], it is for the sake of those that are correct that elision and other operations are taught in the treatise.
When the co-arising [of grammatical operations] is equal, forms such as *jye*, *drā*, and *ghā* are incorrect;
for there is no traditional authority (*smṛti*) regarding them in the explanatory treatise, as there is in the case of *datta* and others.

And those words that have been formed with the suffix *kṛt*, such as *kharaṇasa* and others, which are eternal because they are taught as denoting a single substance— these they declare to be correct.
But they say that these [words] are indeed *gotras* (generic entities), because they are endowed with the capacity for denotation;
it is not necessarily required that they depend upon external causes (*nimitta*) for their own meaning.
The restriction of names to a named object is for the sake of conventional usage;
however, the relationship is indeed eternal, as in the case of "Dittha" and so forth, just like "cow" and so forth.
Because it is produced, the impermanence of the relationship is established;
for in the case of a name, it is applied by persons according to their own will.
For just as names such as "bee" and so forth are applied by children to lines drawn in the dust, this very same conceptualization applies to all names.

Furthermore, in this treatise, the relationship between *vṛddhi* and the others is indeed uncreated (*akṛtrima*), characterized by the delimitation of their capacities, just like that between a qualifier and a qualified.
Based on its own essential nature, worldly cognition functions in some cases when a causal sign is present, and in other cases even in the absence of a causal sign. (Brahma-vākya 2.370)
In the treatise as well, the great designation is based upon the essential nature [of the object];
inference is recognized when the cause is present.
In that case, inference is understood either from recurrence due to similarity of form,
or as an inference from the difference of words, or as the comprehension of a difference in capacity.
In some cases, an artificial [distinction] is established through a difference in objects;
however, regarding number, the establishment [of the distinction] pertains to a single object for both [the individual and the collection].

Even when uttered in some cases by a worldly person, a word reaches its object even from afar; for indeed, in the case of perfect cognition, there is the apprehension of both [the word and the object].

Regarding the cases of the collective (saṅgha), the remainder (ekaśeṣa), and the dual (dvandva), some maintain that actions reside in each individual substratum by virtue of their functional capacity.
The meal is completed by means of both the fruit and the form in each individual case; for otherwise, if they were established separately, that purpose would not be accomplished.
And all individuals experience the act of eating, which consists of the taking of food and so forth, as resulting in the fruit of satisfaction individually; it is not like a theatrical performance.
Like water for the feet, it remains distinct according to its capacity;
the verb *bhuj* performs the action for the sake of the object to be enjoyed, not simultaneously [for all], like a lamp.
But even a single action such as "seeing" may, when applied to such objects of action,
pertain to a collection [of instances] even without repetition.
When one observes linguistic usage and other such activities, the agents whose modes of operation are distinct are seen to act separately, yet they accomplish their purpose through cooperation.
Since the object to be characterized is established in common worldly usage, and since the indicative mark is seen in the technical treatise,
the designation "vṛddhi" is completed by distinguishing it among those who seek [the result] and those who perceive it.
Because the act of punishment has "a hundred" as its primary object when it consists of the action of taking a hundred,
the number to be counted does not differ among the objects, even though there is a difference in the qualities of the claimants.
Because it is subordinate to the Saṅgha alone, when conveying that which possesses an action,
there is a connection by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application) in that case for the technical designations of *samāsa* and *abhyasta*.
For those for whom the Vedic revelation has as its purpose the definition [of dharma] with respect to some specific action,
that dharma is characterized by them, both individually and collectively.
Just as in the case of the rule "Śūdras must not enter this house," the entry of both individuals and those acting in concert is prohibited.
However, when there is instruction regarding the prohibition of the desire for gain and so forth by acting together,
activity is not contradicted because such [individual] activity is not prohibited separately.

Because the meaning [of the rule] is characterized by separation (*vyavāya*), the substitution of *ṇ* is not prohibited by the presence of *a*, *ṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, or *āṅ*, either individually or collectively. (BVaky_2.387)

When the act of eating is undertaken for the sake of favoring those who eat, yet it does not favor them due to differences in place, time, and so forth; [then that eating is not truly beneficial]. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka-vākya 2.388)
The multiplicity of a single entity is taught on account of the distinctions of its vessels and so forth;
conversely, the unity of that which is divided is conceptually constructed.
Even when acting together, they are presented as being distinct;
having each obtained their own respective food, they enjoy it collectively by sharing it out.

Because there is no scope for distributive repetition (vīpsā), because of contradiction with another number, and because completion in two ways is impossible, the number "one hundred" resides in the group (saṅgha). (BVaky_2.391)
Where a single remainder is taught through either a copulative compound (*dvandva*) or a remainder-formation (*ekaśeṣa*) together with other [words],
there too, because it serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the sentence is completed in two ways.
Some maintain that each of the other sentences possesses its own completion;
by this [principle], there is a subsumption of sentences joined with different forms.
There are no distinct sentences that constitute the denotata of a sentence; rather, when that [sentence] is uttered, one understands various distinctions within it.
For those for whom the entire meaning of the sentence is completed at each individual word, what purpose would there be at that time for the existence of a distinct word-meaning?

Alternatively, if that object produced by those very [phonemes] exists in distinct [individuals], then there would either be a contradiction with the previous object or a coexistence with it. (BVaky_2.396)
If they were to exist together, there would be a contradiction between the qualified and the unqualified;
however, if the object is abandoned, the relationship becomes inconstant. (Brahma-vākya 2.397)

The single, common denotative essence (arthātman) resides within each individual word; it is present in the aggregate and among the members of that aggregate, serving as the indicator of their proximity.
Just as ownership of wealth is common [to all heirs], as is the fruit of its renunciation and undiminished joy, so too is the connection with that object for those who possess it.
When the phonemes possess meaning, that [meaning] resides in the aggregate of those [phonemes] by virtue of that very same meaning;
yet, because of their distinctness, unity does not remain established within that aggregate.
Just as all people see common property by means of a single lamp, in the same way, number is denoted by a single suffix.
Thus, the meaningfulness of words, phonemes, and sentences does not differ;
however, a different sequence resulting from repetition appears as if it were contradictory.
Apart from its application (viniyoga), a word does not reveal its own meaning; they declare that the connection for the denotation of meaning has speech as its medium. (BVaky_2.403)
Just as an eye, when directed toward it, serves for seeing, so too a word, when intended [for a specific purpose], becomes the designator of an object.
A connection mediated by an action is observed between instruments and objects;
therefore, there is a fixed rule for the expression of both the signifier and the signified.
When many things are denoted by a single name and all of them perform a single function,
the word remains fixed upon that which the speaker intends.
Some say that the words of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) are meaningless when used in repetition;
others say they function solely as their own forms for the purpose of conveying other things.
Those who perceive [the word] as a single entity consider those very [words], which convey the meaning through their connection with the act of denotation, to be distinct injunctions (*niyoga*).
Those who employ conventional discourse regarding diversity declare that there is absolute non-difference among them,
because they are associated with a single genus, just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth.
In these cases, no intention other than the actual application is found;
for since one acts according to one's capacity regarding the object, that [intention] is established therein.
The cognition of diversity itself [is determined] by means of context, purpose, and so forth; for words whose meanings are otherwise never function with a different meaning in any way whatsoever.

And as for that word which is a sentence having the form of a *pada* and serving as the basis for existence, let this investigation apply to it; it does not apply to a *pada* that is a constituent part of a sentence.
Just as a qualified meaning is expressed by means of meaningless phonemes,
so too is a qualified meaning expressed by means of meaningless words.

The cognition that arises with respect to objects in the interval [between the initial perception and the final ascertainment] is a means to comprehension, because the final determination has not yet been reached. (BVaky_2.414)
Just as the ultimate nature of each subsequent object is followed by its preceding meanings,
so too does association proceed with respect to other objective entities.
But when some means of proof have already been accepted as establishing the object to be proven,
the repeated mention of those means of proof serves solely to satisfy [the listener].
Since there is no restrictive rule regarding the substratum (ādhāra), there is no implication of it [by the verb];
its possibility arises from contextual capacity (sāmarthya), while the explicit mention (śruti) serves to exclude other [substrata].
An action is distinct from other actions and possesses a fixed substratum and means;
these distinctions, as they are undertaken by practitioners, are the causes for full comprehension.
But for others, that sentence and its meaning appear as indivisible from the words, even though the words possess a sequence; thus it appears without a sequential order of words. (Brahma-vākya 2.419)
The self of that which possesses its own intrinsic nature cannot be defined;
however, the self of that which lacks an intrinsic nature is indeed defined.
Others understand the determination of the form of an object to be wordless;
and memory, which has the appearance of the object as its form, arises from words.
In one way, one who is burned perceives the burning through contact with fire;
in another way, the meaning of "burning" is understood by means of the word "burning."
Just as for the sense faculties— which are established as distinct entities and pursue distinct objects— no activity is possible apart from the body.
Likewise, for all words that are established as having individual meanings,
once they are separated from sentences, no possessiveness of meaning is found.
The nature of conjunction is perceived in objects that are conjoined;
however, the reality [of the whole] is not described here, because it is seen to be a non-entity (*apadārtha*).
Even that which is the truth of perception does not exist as perception;
for the object, in its form of association, is determined to be formless.
Since an object is denoted as being either connected with existence or situated within its own nature,
a sentence is employed for that purpose.
A word-meaning is not cognized without its connection to an action;
whether it be real or contrary [to reality], such a thing does not exist in linguistic usage. (BVaky_2.428)
However, this sentence "It is existent" (sad iti) does not convey its meaning— whether as "it was" or "it exists"—
without a connection to the expression of an action.
When the meaning expressed by a verbal form is connected with its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*),
the expectancy [for further information] does not cease without the expression of a substance (*sattva*).
But because of its predominance, action is analyzed first, prior to the object;
the constituent parts are employed for the sake of what is to be accomplished, and the fruit is that which motivates it.
The speaker alone intends the nature of the goal and the means,
and he likewise endeavors to conceive the connection between the meanings.
That which "performs the act of cooking" is designated as the object (*karman*);
however, the act of cooking (*pakti*) itself, being of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), is perceived as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Whatever portion of an object is intended by the speakers through whatever specific assistance,
that portion remains established exactly in that way, because the object possesses all powers.
In the case of remote operations, a connection is sometimes expressed;
that which is embraced [by the operation] but not directly joined is sometimes perceived.
The state of being divided belongs to things that are mixed, while the state of being mixed belongs to those that are distinct;
unity belongs to things of diverse nature, and diversity occurs in the opposite case.
Because an object consists of all things, or because it is devoid of self-nature,
it is established that sound alone is the basis [of cognition], since its power is absolutely unrestricted.
A word that merely indicates an object does not express a benefit;
therefore, it is not possible for it to touch upon the inherent power of things.
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is a property of related things, is denoted by its own specific term;
however, inherence (*samavāya*) is understood only through its status as a relation.
Objects are established by their defining characteristics, but not in reality;
that very object is somehow understood through its functional utility.

The meaning of a sentence is the relation [between word-meanings]; its essence does not reside anywhere [independently]. In linguistic usage, they describe that very essence as the "meaning of the words. (BVaky_2.441)
Whether it be completed in a single word-meaning or in a collection [of meanings],
its essence is never divided anywhere according to the distinctions in the forms of those word-meanings.

The distinction that serves as the basis for comprehension for the sake of grammatical exposition is described as something distinct [from the sentence], consisting of parts that stand in mutual expectancy.
The differentiation of the many powers of a single [sentence] is observed;
for the unity of meaning of a sentence is indeed perceived even by a slight degree.
An external object, whether existent or non-existent, is differentiated on the basis of its being the object of cognition;
however, this differentiation, having been made external, is characterized by the extraction of its functional powers.
The powers, which are restricted to their own respective meanings within the suffixes, are not fixed elsewhere;
nor is their form perceived apart from them.
Even when there are many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) that are mutually expectant, they constitute a single sentence;
thus, the prohibition of the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) by one finite verb with respect to other finite verbs becomes meaningful.

For one for whom a sentence in the grammatical treatise is defined by having only one finite verb (*tiṅ*), there is no need for the mention of "non-finite" (*atiṅ*), because such a definition does not apply due to the diversity of sentence types.
Furthermore, when joined with other finite verbs, or even with those joined [to them],
as in "Look, the deer is going," neither difference nor non-difference remains.
Where the sense of what ought to be done is expected through implication,
that which lacks a verbal indicator for such expectation and has its meaning complete is called "concluded."

But when there is merely the restatement of a fact, whatever meaning follows as a consequence, the sentence is completed by the Vedic revelation even without the employment of that [meaning]. (BVaky_2.451)
While walking, study here; while muttering, perform the walking.
Although the purpose is the same, a distinction is perceived through the words.
The various actions that possess results, which are based upon other actions and are innumerable due to their sequential indications, are shown to be presented by means of a single verb.
Every action, including all its concealed distinctions, is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*);
it is impossible for the Veda to conceive of a detailed differentiation of these distinctions.
"Kings will sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice; Brahmins are performing a sacrificial session"—from such expressions, no distinction [between the two classes] is perceived. (BVaky_2.455)
An action that is heard only once, even though it is not repeated, undergoes differentiation by virtue of its capacity within the *prājāpatya* offerings. (BVaky_2.456)
In cases such as "Devadatta and others," the verb *bhuji* (to eat) resides with each [individual];
or rather, each sentence is understood separately as being independent.
In the utterance of sentences, no other form is perceived; however, in the comprehension of distinct [sentences], another form is cognized.
A single statement of apprehension is expressed in a general sense, such as "the agent"; and that [general term] is then divided among specific instances, such as cattle and the like.
If the expectancy were satisfied upon the single hearing of that which has come into being,
it could not possibly enter into a connection with anything else in any way whatsoever.
It is of a single form yet possesses manifold meanings; therefore, it is the basis [of language] and the source of analytical statements, existing as if non-different from them. (BVaky_2.461)
In some cases, action proceeds toward assistance through its individualized parts; in other cases, it is the universal aspect alone that accomplishes the purpose of this [action]. (BVaky_2.462)
Furthermore, the distinctions that differ in time, as well as those found in expressions such as *uṣṭrāsika* (a camel-sitter),
do not differentiate the essence of the word from its generic portion (*jātibhāga*) within the context of the discourse.
In the case of individual instances that are numerically one, actions differentiated by genus and other factors are applied separately when that word is heard only once.
Just as the distinct actions of eating, breaking, and playing with dice and so forth remain separate for each individual, even though there is no difference in the time of their performance.
The "string" (*tantra*) of those who possess strings is the means; it is their state of uniformity.
The sequence of these [strings] when divided is their connection, while their simultaneous hearing is their unity. (BVaky_2.466)
Two methods for the employment of words are established:
either succession or simultaneity, neither of which the world transgresses.
Form is divided according to sequence, but it is not differentiated in simultaneity;
however, action, even in simultaneity, follows the form of sequence.
The two powers of differentiation and connection remain as if distinct from the word;
even when they occur simultaneously, the auditory perception is differentiated by the employment of multiple [words].
When a single object intended to be expressed is not differentiated by its various forms,
the whole is understood through the properties of its parts.
Regarding the definition of its division, however, the word is either completed with each individual object,
or it remains as a distinct utterance when there is a division of the sentence.
In that case, the word *akṣa* is employed either in the singular number,
or it is divided into a plurality for each individual according to the literal expression.
Even in those sentences which reside in two [entities], for those who perceive their unity,
the inherent power of the one— which possesses manifold capacities— is divided.
Or, in the case of two [words] that are absolutely distinct, there may be a method characterized by *tantra* (simultaneous application) in their usage;
in that case, the connection [of the meaning] varies among the perceivers.
Having previously understood two words of identical sound as distinct, the hearers are now led by the speaker to comprehend them simultaneously through the method of *tantra*.
Even when there is an intention to express only one [meaning], the other follows as a consequence;
the word, whose nature is power (*śakti*), manifests even without a deliberate intention.
In some cases, multiple powers of a single entity are heard of simultaneously;
for example, fire is employed in both illumination and burning even in a single instance.
When a sentence has a meaning differentiated by the power of repetition (āvṛtti), even when it is heard only once,
the distinction [between its parts] is established either through indicative mark (liṅga) or through the principle of common application (tantra).

In the definition of *saṃprasāraṇa*, a distinction between a phoneme and a sentence arises in the very same manner as it does within a single grammatical rule (*sūtra*), based on two indicative marks.

Likewise, regarding the doubling [of a consonant] by the rule *aco ra ṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.105), the indication [of the term *ac*] as being without a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*) is shown in the Bhāṣya itself through the method of ellipsis (*tantra*) and through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa*.
Generally, when the *Saṃgraha* had disappeared, grammarians were encountered who took pleasure in brevity and possessed only a limited grasp of knowledge.
Then, when the teacher Patañjali, who perceives the sacred truths, had composed the Mahābhāṣya— a compendium containing the seeds of all systems of logic— *Vākyapadīya* 2.482.
Because its depth has not been fathomed due to its profundity, and because it appears superficial due to its elegance,
those of unrefined intellect have no settled conviction regarding it.

When the scriptural text, which serves as the protective covering for the *Saṃgraha*, has been corrupted by the Vaiśeṣikas, the followers of Saubhava, and the Haryakṣas— who rely upon dry logic— [the following occurs].
The tradition of grammar that had fallen away from the disciples of Patañjali remained,
over time, among those of the South as nothing more than the written text.
Having received the tradition from the mountain, it was further developed into many branches by Cāndrācārya and others who followed the seeds of the Bhāṣya.
Having studied those systems of the path of logic as well as our own philosophical view,
this compendium of scriptures has been composed for us by our teacher.
In this [work], only the mere substance of certain paths has been illustrated;
in the third book, there will be a detailed investigation.
Wisdom attains discernment through the various perspectives of the scriptures;
for how much can be extracted by one who merely follows his own reasoning?
For those who speculate on this and that without the ancient scriptures and who have not served their elders, knowledge does not become fully clear.
3.1: Regarding the exposition of universals (*jāti*), some maintain that a word is divided into two parts, or into four, or even into five,
by extracting them from sentences just as one extracts stems, suffixes, and so forth.
When words are analyzed into their constituent meanings,
it is described that for all words, the word-meanings are either the universal (jāti) or the substance (dravya), both of which are eternal.
For some, the genus (jāti) serves as an indicator of capacity through association;
when items such as the khadira wood are incapable, that which is capable is substituted as a proxy.
Bondage has as its fruit a lack of independence; it is taught [to exist] like the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
Therefore, even when a genus (*jāti*) is denoted, that which is devoid of causal power is not apprehended.

If what is intended to be expressed is merely the act of binding through conjunction, then gender, number, and so forth are taught as being based on the substratum of the capacity [of the word]. (BVaky_3.1.5)
One's own genus is denoted by all words first of all;
thereafter, there arises the conceptual construction of superimposing that [genus] upon the forms of the genera of objects.

Just as the reality of the quality "red" is designated in the dye-stuff (kaṣāya), and it is also perceived in clothes and other objects due to contact with that which possesses the quality; so too [is the universal perceived].
Likewise, through the relationship between word and object, the universal resides in the word;
it serves to effect the function of the universal for the various classes of objects during their designation.
In the case of a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) of genus-words (*jātiśabda*), that [genus] is intended as the genus of the genera;
in the expression "the genera of words" (*śabdajātayaḥ*), that genus [resides] within the word-genera.
That universal which exists in words and is characterized as distinct from individual words,
that universal exists without deviating from its nature as a "word-universal."
Even when a word denotes a universal (jāti), all words denote universals,
because word-meanings are established as being characterized by activity (vyāpāra).
Since, in the case of an object that is a genus, either the genus or a particular is expected by words just like the genus itself, therefore those [words] are denoters of the genus.
In the case of a category (padārtha), however, every meaning is said to reside in the substance (dravya) as its property;
because it is the substratum of the properties of substance, substance is therefore accepted as being all meanings.
Or else, *jāti* may be a property of recurrence (*anupravṛttidharma*) among all classes;
or it is accepted as a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛttidharma*) within a particular (*viśeṣa*). (Vākya-pada 3.1.14)
When space is conceptually constructed as having distinct locations based on the differences in the properties of the objects conjoined with it,
the universal of space exists even within those various locations.
Just as there are locations belonging to objects such as jars which themselves have no location,
so too there are locations belonging to space, even though space itself has no location.
Cognition based on distinct objects persists among things that are conjoined;
however, among things that are inherent, the apprehension of distinction ceases.

Therefore, the status of being secondary is attributed to the locations of the conjoined [substances], while the status of being primary belongs to the inherent [qualities], due to the non-discrimination [of the former] from their locations. (BVaky_3.1.18)
Some know that *ākṛti* (form) to be the manifestation whose nature is persistence;
others, however, describe it as having the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), [identifying it] with substance (*dravya*).

"Distinct" or "non-distinct"—this conceptual proliferation regarding the nature of entities arises only when they are associated with external limiting adjuncts (upādhi). (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vākya 3.1.20)
Neither unity nor plurality, neither existence nor non-existence is found in the true nature of things,
which are entirely unconditioned.
When it is determined that the nature of all powers resides in one alone, the postulation of a difference in the self-nature of entities would be purposeless. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vākya 3.1.22)
Therefore, all powers such as substance and the rest, which possess distinct characteristics,
accomplish the purpose of the person when combined, but not when isolated.
Just as the integrity of the sense organs and so forth constitutes their very self,
so too is it perceived in the connection between related entities through their mutual association.
Nothing whatsoever is produced for which birth does not exist;
birth is the motivator of causes for the manifestation of the self.
Having established their footing within causes— both eternal and non-eternal— these generic properties (jāti) repeatedly manifest themselves in certain effects.
In the case of an object being produced (*nirvartya*), the genus (*jāti*) is also the means (*sādhana*);
it is that [genus] which instigates the actions for the sake of bringing its own substratum into existence.
Whether in an injunction or a prohibition, the means of proof is Brahminhood and so forth;
the genus of number, which depends on or does not depend on the individual, serves as the qualifier of the genus.
Just as the face itself is designated when it is manifested by water and so forth,
so too the universal (jāti) itself is designated when it is manifested by substances.
Just as the distinction residing in the sense organ [is perceived] despite the absence of the apprehension of the sense organ itself, so too,
although it is invisible within the objects of the senses, it serves to produce a distinction in cognition.

Likewise, for some, individual instances—even in the absence of [perceived] forms—become the cause of the various cognitions of universals, because they grasp the nature of the self [of the universal]. (BVaky_3.1.31)
Regarding each individual entity, there exist two portions: the real and the unreal.
That which is real therein is the universal (jāti); the individuals (vyakti) are considered unreal.
Existence itself, being differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference in its correlates, is called "universal" (jāti); all words are established in that [existence].
They declare that [Bhāva] to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self (mahān ātmā), and they say that suffixes such as -tva and -tal denote it.
That same activity, when its sequence has been reached in relation to specific particulars, is designated as such;
when the form of that sequence is withdrawn, it is called "Being" (sattva).
That very [Brahman] undergoes six states among the modifications of existence;
thus it manifests itself sequentially through its own powers.
Even the sequence inherent in this [speech] appears as its very self, wherein this perception of time exists,
situated as if divided by way of priority, posteriority, and so forth.
When the concealment of entities is admitted, that very state is their non-existence;
once concealment has attained its sequence, it is perceived as "perishing."
Having fallen away from the preceding state and not yet having attained the subsequent stage,
birth is said to occur in the interval between them due to the dependence upon various distinctions.
The substratum of existence is either its own self alone, or entities distinct from it, or its own powers; these are the causes for the perception of differentiation within existence.
In the manifestation [of sound] upon earth and other substrates, it does not depend on a specific configuration;
for the genus (jāti), because its locus is never severed, remains even when that locus is impermanent.
Some declare that every birth has a basis that cannot be cut off;
they maintain that there is no simultaneous dissolution of everything.
When the various distinctions have dissolved into their primordial nature, the universals, which perceive oneness,
attain the state of substantial existence within their own substrata.
The states such as Brahminhood and so forth reside in all living beings;
they are manifested and serve to accomplish their respective functions—so too says the Smṛti.
Some maintain that even in paintings and the like, there is a manifestation of universals;
however, those [universals] residing in living beings serve as the cause for merit and demerit upon their acquisition.
But they know that the knowledge of those superior to us regarding all those [subtle objects] belongs to all the senses,
just as for experts there is [knowledge] regarding the specific qualities of gems, silver, and so forth, due to repeated practice.
In the world, that reality of difference which is based upon the fragrance of the *jāti* lily and so forth is not denoted by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) because it is impermanent.
But in the case of classes such as "Man-Lion" (narasiṃha), which are denoted by words that are not [etymologically] composed of their own parts,
another auditory perception resides in them as if they were composed of similar constituent parts.
In the delimitation of the state of a genus, number—or indeed the very nature of being a number—even when remote, serves as a benefit through its association [with it]. (BVaky_3.1.49)
Indication (lakṣaṇā) is an operation within the grammatical refinement of a word for the sake of accomplishing its function;
it is observed even when the verbal roots are identical, as in the case of the powers of number, object, and so forth.
No entity existing as a sentient being can be expressed without a number; therefore, in the description of every such thing, the number would be unintended [as a primary meaning]. (BVaky_3.1.51)
For some, unity or plurality is not intended to be expressed;
indeed, that [unity] is for the purpose of denoting the genus, whereas duality would be intended to be expressed.
"If these two were diseased, this medicine should be given"—
in such a case, the duality of the object [indicated by the dual ending] would be unintended.

The number expressed by words such as "one" is accepted as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) in verbal actions; for it is dependent [on the action] through its form, as in the cases "he digs with one" or "with two. (Brahma-vākya 3.1.54)

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," just as the genus [of the animal] is understood as the means of accomplishment, so too is its singularity understood as a means of accomplishment, since even a preparatory rite (saṃskāra) is possible here.
However, because of the grammatical gender (liṅga), the singular number and so forth [of the noun] would be intended;
and that gender serves as the indicator for both the genus and the number when they have a single object as their domain.
That [word] is primarily the injunction for the animal sacrifice that has not been prescribed elsewhere;
and its status as a subordinate element (aṅga) in the ritual action is what is intended to be expressed by this [injunction]. (BVaky_3.1.57)
Elsewhere, however, the planets are prescribed with various distinct numbers,
endowed with such distinctions as "nine for Prajāpati" and so forth.

When those understood as subordinate members are again specified with respect to their primary referent (the *aṅgin*) for the purpose of purification (*saṃmārjana*), how could that number [of the subordinates] be intended [as significant]? (BVaky_3.1.59)

There is no rule [for number] other than this: neither grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) nor the status of being the principal element (*aṅgitva*) is the cause for the intention to express number; rather, it is through deliberate effort that number is intended to be expressed.
Furthermore, no specific distinction regarding the act of sweeping is ever based on the cup;
rather, those [sweepings] are prescribed as things to be consecrated (saṃskārya), and therefore they serve as the substratum for all [the cups].

If, when the genus has been completed in each respective substratum, the ritual action could not be accomplished by means of a single animal, then that [provision of multiple animals] would indeed be a valid arrangement.
And when an action has been accomplished by one [agent], if another animal were to be employed because of its possibility, that employment would be purposeless. (BVaky_3.1.63)
Just as the rite of conception is useless for a woman who is already pregnant,
so too is another animal useless once [the sacrifice] has been accomplished by one.

Some maintain that because the purpose is accomplished by that much alone, there should be no deviation from the singular number; however, in this case, the number is not taken as a constituent part of the action.
But as for the gender [of the word] from the second case onwards, it merely restates the previously stated rule;
therefore, number is not understood as a means [of action], just like the universal (jāti).

When number is accepted on the basis of positive and negative concomitance, it is logical that it should function as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); it is not, however, a mere indicator of something else.
When a word-meaning functions as a means [to an action], its capacity is not lost;
therefore, by that indicative mark, the property of the operation of number is understood.
Because that which is not previously established is what is to be enjoined, its primacy is determined;
because that which has been enjoined exists for the sake of another, its status as a subordinate element is understood.
Since the act of sweeping is what is to be enjoined, when the vessel has been prescribed elsewhere,
the number heard in the injunctive sentence is not sublated by the secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
In another injunctive sentence, there is no number that contradicts the animal;
therefore, it is understood as possessing its quality together with oneness.
When a substance has already been ascertained as being connected [to an action],
a quality that is prescribed in relation to that action is understood to be required by it just as much as the substance itself.
Just as a certain quality in a substance is characterized by its capacity (sāmarthya),
so too the substratum of that very quality is established as being characterized by capacity.

When those two are perceived as having distinct referents, the relationship that is understood between them is not subject to sublation; nor can another [relationship] be postulated, for it is not heard in the scripture.

The connection between those two—the substratum and that which rests upon it—with the action is established by direct audition (śruti); however, the restriction [of their specific application] is established by the sentence (vākya).
In that case, in the absence of substance and quality, there would be an option for each [word] individually;
for the connection established by direct audition (śruti) is stronger than that characterized by syntactical context (vākya).
But when a genus or a capacity is taught with reference to an action,
then, by virtue of contextual implication, the substance and the quality are brought into proximity there.
When both the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) are equally auxiliary to the action,
qualities such as those of a goat and so forth may be substituted, but the genera cannot.
Genera are closer to the individual power [of denotation] than qualities are;
substance is directly connected with action, whereas a quality is differentiated from it. (BVaky_3.1.79)
Some maintain that when, due to parity, neither [of two options] is present, there is an option;
therefore, either a goat devoid of those qualities would be [the victim], or a ram possessing those qualities.
The application of a number inherent in a genus is observed;
sometimes that very same [number] occurs even after setting aside a specific number.
A general property that has become subordinate to another is connected with the number of the substance;
however, when it functions toward its own primary meaning, it does not depend upon number.
In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," when the word "animal" is heard as part of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice),
the primary action is accomplished by means of that single animal whose purpose has been fulfilled.
If one were to perform the touching [of the sacrificial animal] with as many qualities as are possible for it,
then by that means the primary object would have been rendered effective through its attributes.
But in a ritual procedure where the scriptural injunction for an action involves a vessel that is being cleansed,
we do not take any account of the mention of a specific number.

The fact that the word "one" (eka) was employed in the rule concerning the remaining part of the sentence (*vākya*), even though the remainder possesses a specific number, is clearly an indication [of this principle]. (BVaky_3.1.86)
Just as the Vedic revelation (śruti) is established in the rules for compound formation and suffixation,
so too is it logically justified through reasoning in the case of subordinate qualities.

Even though it is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), number is not admitted [as a qualifier] for the sake of establishing another primary element (*pradhāna*); likewise, the agent is perceived as being no different from the object.
When there is another [number] already applicable, and a further scriptural mention is for the purpose of restriction—
since its purpose is fulfilled by the exclusion [of others]— the number therein is not intended to be significant.
But when a case-ending is prescribed after a collection [of sounds] that possesses a specific form,
it is established therein that one [element] alone is the expressive unit of the collection and possesses meaning.
Whether in the prescription of a subordinate element, a primary element, or even a compound,
when there is an intention to express number, the quality is in every way subordinated.
Similarity consists in non-difference in form, and the powers are identical with the self;
it is also described that these [powers] possess synonymous designations with the universal (jāti).
Even if one acquires a staff with the desire to take up a staff, one is not understood to be "staff-bearer" solely by virtue of that [act]. (BVaky_3.1.93)
The cognition "one who possesses desire" does not arise from the cause of desire itself;
therefore, even though the capacity exists, the intellect (buddhi) rests upon something other than the object [itself].
Either an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to be designated, or a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) remains;
since this is the case at the end of everything, conventional linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is not tenable.
When, having set aside the differences, [the object] is grasped by the intellect as if it were one,
then the intellect functions as a single unit directed toward that very nature of the individual manifestation.
When the intellect perceives that which is permeated by diverse forms as if it were one,
then that cognition arises from many [individuals] through the grasping of a collective whole.
When, in the desire to express them together, a collection whose constituent parts are bound by a single cognition is denoted as having its division of parts suppressed; (Vākya-kāṇḍa 3.1.98)

Because the counter-action is completed, [the action] is endowed with a single distinction; however, in the case of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), it is understood as possessing distinctions such as duality and so forth.

When there is a single occurrence, unity is attained; when there is repetition, the identity of similarity is reached by individual entities that possess distinct natures, through the exclusion of difference.

"Just as a cognition is perceived as differentiated when it occurs in succession, so too an object, although its nature is exclusion (vyāvṛtti), is grasped as such in its true reality. (Brahma-siddhi-vākya-kāṇḍa 3.1.101)
For all things that possess identical forms, there exist no denotative words that fall upon their distinctions, nor is any distinction apprehended.
Regarding those specific distinctions established as the objects of the words "knowledge" and so forth,
because they are difficult to discern, there is the view of the oneness of knowledge and the rest.
Just as in the case of cognitions that correspond to reality, so too do universals exist in all [objects] when they are perceived in relation; and these are what establish the nature of the object.
The universal (sāmānya) residing in the object of cognition alone is what assists cognitions;
for a cognition is never manifested through the form of another, just as the object of cognition [is not].
Just as light is not illuminated by another light,
so the form of cognition is not grasped by another cognition.
Furthermore, the power of cognition would not be capable of ascertaining a universal inherent in the self, [if it were] based on another object already known. (BVaky_3.1.107)

If cognitions were not simultaneous, there would be no apprehension of "this" [as belonging to the object], nor would there be recollection according to how it was perceived; for recollection arises only regarding what has been perceived. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya-vākyārtha 3.1.108)
The cognition "the cognition of a jar" is distinct from the cognition of the jar itself;
whereas the cognition "jar," which occurs in relation to the object, is that [latter].
Since the form of cognition is not apprehended as having the form of the object,
and its own nature is not determined as distinct from the form of the object.
3.2: The Section on Substance (Dravyasamuddeśa).
Self, entity, intrinsic nature, body, and reality—these are synonyms for "substance" (dravya), and it is traditionally held that this is eternal. (BVaky_3.2.1)
The real entity is determined by means of unreal forms;
the real itself is denoted by words through unreal adjuncts.
Just as Devadatta’s house, though apprehended by means of an unstable indicator,
is expressed by the word "house" as being purely [the house itself], so too is it here.
Just as gold and the like, when conjoined with their own non-permanent forms, become the denotable objects of names such as "necklace" while remaining pure in essence; so it is here.
And because it is delimited by specific modes, its universal capacity is restricted,
just as the capacity of the eyes and other senses is restricted by conditions such as the presence of light.
Whatever word functions with respect to those forms as they truly exist,
because it has that reality as its essence, it too expresses [the object] eternally.
"There is no distinction between reality and unreality"—this is the traditional teaching from the elders.
They consider that which is not investigated to be "unreality," though it is in fact reality itself.
The reality that is itself free from conceptual construction assumes the form of conceptual construction;
yet there is no difference in time here, even though a difference in time is perceived.
Just as the properties of objects are absolutely impossible within cognition, so too that [cognition],
though appearing as if identical to them, is established as being absolutely not of their nature.
Likewise, there is an absolute impossibility of modifications existing within the reality; and that reality, though appearing as if it were their very self, is absolutely not of their nature.
That which remains at the end when the withdrawal of forms has occurred is eternal; it is denotable by words, and it is not distinct from the word.
It is not that it exists, nor is it that it does not exist; it is not one, nor is it separate;
it is neither conjoined nor divided, neither transformed nor otherwise.
That does not exist, yet it exists; it is one, yet it is manifold;
it is conjoined and it is divided; it is modified, and it is otherwise.
Of that [cognition], the nature of the relationship between word and meaning is seen as one;
that which is seen, the seeing, the seer, and the purpose of the seeing [are all perceived therein]. (3.2.14)
Just as gold is the reality when its modifications have ceased,
so they say that the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) is the reality when its modifications have ceased.
That [sphoṭa] is the denotable object of all words, and words are not distinct from it;
yet, if they are not distinct, there can be no relation between the two, as if they were separate entities.
Self and other, the beloved and the hateful, the speaker and the spoken, and the purpose—these opposites appear as forms of a single mind within a dream. (3.2.17)
Likewise, in that reality which is unborn, eternal, and devoid of priority and posteriority, the nature of birth and so forth is perceived as a contradiction. (Brahma-siddhi-vākya 3.2.18)
3.3: In the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*:
When words are uttered, the knowledge of the speaker, the external object, and their own form are perceived; the relationship between these is firmly established. (BVaky_3.3.1)
In some cases, doubt may arise for the cognizer regarding either the object or the cognition;
however, when their own forms are perceived, no deviation [from their nature] exists.
The relationship that "this is the designator of this" or "this is the designated" is understood through the genitive case;
therefore, the reality (tattva) of the connection between word and meaning is also designated by this.
There is no designation by its own property that expresses the relationship;
because it is absolutely dependent, its form is not taught.
Because it provides assistance, that [capacity] is understood to reside wherever a property exists;
it is the capacity of capacities, and it is the quality of qualities.
But the application of those [names] to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) occurs because they possess those properties;
furthermore, the specific conditions (*upādhi*) for these two are fixed for the purpose of mutual assistance.
For indeed, there is a certain specific state, indicated by the production of an effect,
in which a conjunction arises between someone and something.

Since things are devoid of self-nature, the restriction that their arising occurs only in certain instances— and that this very restriction prevents their universal occurrence— is established by that [restriction] itself once difference has been attained.

That by which the self of another is apprehended as if it were one's own self, and because of which neither unity nor plurality is determined as the true reality; [that is the nature of the word]. 3.3.9.
That power called inherence (samavāya), which assists other powers,
transcends both difference and non-difference, and is established in a manner entirely distinct [from them].

The tradition from the predecessors is that *saṃbandha* (relation) is the property (*dharma*) of all things, transcending all individual characteristics, and it bestows its favor [upon them]. *Brahmavidyābharaṇa* 3.3.11.
Others everywhere accept that the relation itself is treated as a distinct category;
therefore, it is impossible to distinguish the relation from the meaning of the word.
Through inherence, one's own substratum and one's own genus are perceived;
however, through inherence in the same object, qualities that reside only in their own substratum [are perceived].
Substantiality, existence, and conjunction are bound to substrates other than themselves;
so too are their spatial divisions and those qualities such as duality and the rest.
Some [words] are connected with their own substratum; some are inherent in that [substratum];
others are inherent in things that are themselves inherent in what is connected [to the substratum]. (3.3.15)
But it is understood that the omnipresent [entity] is conjoined with those things conjoined with its own substratum;
no further relation of inherence is observed there.
Since the relationship [between word and meaning] would be undifferentiated, there could be no restriction here;
therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is not conceived in this manner.
Just as the conjunction of the self with something else occurs through the acquisition of an unseen potency (adṛṣṭa),
even though there is no actual difference [between them], so too is that same process applicable elsewhere in the case of what is called the relation between property and its owner.
But the speaker or the listener does not, by means of words, apprehend that "attainment" (prāpti) called "inherence" (samavāya), which transcends the properties of the objects denoted.
When that which is expressible as "inexpressible" is determined to be expressible by way of its inexpressibility,
then it becomes indeed expressible.
Furthermore, even if one says "this is inexpressible," that which is intended to be expressed is not thereby understood;
for the very state of the object that one wishes to convey remains undetermined.
Even in that case where it is said that something is inexpressible— whether as such, otherwise, or in every respect—
it is not at all that state which is negated by those words.
For when an object in the form of doubt is established as a subordinate element (śeṣa),
another doubt regarding its own nature does not arise so long as that [initial] doubt has not been dispelled.
And when a determination is undertaken as a determination within the cognition of determination,
then that cognition does not abide in its own property.
The statement "I speak everything falsely" is not intended to be expressed [as a literal truth];
for if that itself were spoken falsely, the matter under discussion would not be understood.
And that which functions in the form of a signifier cannot be the signified;
for that by which something else is signified is not itself the object to be signified therein.
It is not merely this that is stated—that the proposition is unestablished;
rather, in the same way, no property whatsoever of this [proposition] is perceived here.
Since there is no other operation whatsoever for an operation, one should therefore never resort to either contradiction or infinite regress in any case. (Brahma-vākya 3.3.28)
Just as the capacity of the sense organs for their respective objects is beginningless,
so too is the relationship between words and their meanings— their capacity— beginningless.
Some maintain that an incorrect word is expressive by means of inference;
or, if there is no distinction in their expressiveness, there is a restriction regarding merit and demerit.
In the case of a word for a relation, the relation [is established] with respect to fitness; fitness arises from convention, as in the connection between mother and son. (BVaky_3.3.31)
The word is the cause of the meaning, for it is produced by that [meaning];
and likewise, the word is cognized from the object which is the domain of cognition.
Even food and such things are considered to exist for the sake of cognition when they are impossible [otherwise];
for once that which exists for the sake of cognition has arisen from cognition itself, even that is perceived.
Even in things that are impermanent, permanence exists by virtue of the nature of the denotable object;
or else, impermanence is its own power (*svaśakti*), and that [power] does not differ from the permanent.
The refinement of meaning by means of a word serves both seen and unseen purposes;
how could that refinement occur without a relationship [between the word and the meaning]?
Such a refinement is not necessarily observed in the objects denoted;
nor is such a relationship as is intended [by the proponent] actually seen to exist.
The relationship [between word and object] is established as a causal condition when it exists;
for it is from this that one understands that the relationship exists there, in the object of the word.

Whether the object be eternal or non-eternal, it is in no way possible for a person to establish a relationship between that object and words whose own relationships have not already been established.
In the designation of word-meanings, there is another, figurative existence which manifests the essential nature of all things in all their states.
Just as a substance such as crystal, through its own inherent power, enters into a connection with various colored substrates as if it were identical in form to them; so too does the word.
In the same way, a word also, having previously been established in this Being (sattā),
enters into relation with properties that are both non-contradictory and contradictory.
And thus, when the objects to be negated are resorted to by way of metaphorical designation for the sake of establishing the negation, the negation proceeds.
The acquisition of self-nature is called "birth," and that which exists is what is acquired.
If it already exists, how can it be born? Or if it does not exist, how can it be born?
For there is movement for one who exists as a mover;
it proceeds when there is something to be moved toward.
If [the mover] were like the [non-existent] mover, the purpose of birth would not exist.
If it does not arise in that manner, then it is not so.
However, for the sake of the application of verbal designation, one metaphorically treats the agent as the object,
and likewise that action which has him as its substratum.
Therefore, in that case, the suffixes *la* and others must be prescribed for a figurative existence (*upacāra-sattā*);
however, because it is contradictory to [actual] birth, primary existence (*mukhyā sattā*) does not exist there.
One is designated as "existing" when one sustains oneself by means of oneself;
and because that [self] is included within it, this [verb] is not transitive with respect to that object.
And prior to its connection with existence, how could there be primary existence?
Furthermore, a non-existent thing cannot be the agent of the verb "to exist"; however, figurative usage may apply as before.
Therefore, among distinct and contradictory phenomena,
