there exists a non-contradictory [universal] which is resorted to by various words solely for the purpose of manifesting contradiction.
[The speaker perceives] that which is non-different in time [and yet] resides in objects that are different in time,
which is the cause of the application of all words, and which is figurative (aupacārikī).
For no entity whatsoever transcends this existence;
and that [existence] has been shown in the Bhāṣya to be distinct from present existence.
Whether it be a portion of a region, or a determination based on another [object],
or its opposite, or its absence— it is linguistic usage that follows these.
Just as a cognition arising from objects appears as if it were superimposing a measure due to a defect in the sense organ, so too does the understanding born of a mere mention [of a word].
Relying upon a cognition in which the object does not appear in its entirety, the word expresses the object through a form other than its own, while it remains unascertained in its own form.
On the worldly path, both the child and the scholar are alike with respect to cognition and verbal expression, owing to their susceptibility to transformation and their capacity for designation.
The purity of cognition consists in its being the form of all objects, independent of any external support;
yet some declare that its supreme purity is even beyond this, being formless.
For the pursuit of external forms is indeed an affliction of knowledge; it is like turbidity produced by contact through the intermingling [of the object] with that [knowledge]. (BVaky_3.3.57)
And just as cognition, due to its representation, remains fixed upon impurity, so too the object, when possessing a substratum, is displaced from its own essential nature.
Thus, when there is a discrepancy regarding the object, the word, and the cognition,
existence and non-existence follow worldly usage without distinction.
Just as the non-existence of something is understood by relying upon its existence,
so too its existence is understood by relying upon its non-existence.
Non-existence does not become existence, nor does existence pass into the state of being indefinable;
for existence and non-existence are conceptual constructs that are not other than the one Self.
Because non-existence is indefinable, a cause cannot establish it;
but as for an existent thing that possesses definition, what could a cause possibly do for it?
Therefore, everything is held to be either non-existence or existence;
there is no other state whatsoever that exists as something distinct from the single reality.
Therefore, those in the world who maintain the doctrine of existence do not accept non-existence,
nor do those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence accept existence as the defining characteristic of reality.
And although everything is non-dual and, by its very nature, possesses a single characteristic,
a manifold variety of boundaries is perceived within conceptual constructions.
For just as four states are imagined in that which is indefinable,
so too this twofold nature is dependent upon existence and non-existence.
Whether non-contradictory or contradictory, existent or even non-existent according to reason,
whether possessing succession or lacking it, non-existence is not logically tenable.
Whether it be non-contradictory or contradictory, existent or even non-existent in reality,
whether possessing succession or lacking succession— in that sense, no entity exists.
In the absence of non-existence, the possibility of difference across the three times does not exist;
that being absent, even existence cannot persist throughout the three times.
The abandonment of the reality of the self is not possible through another;
moreover, the reality of the self is not established either through another or through itself.
In reality, there is no contradiction in multiplicity, nor is there any assistance whatsoever;
when both identity and difference are abandoned, conventional discourse ceases.
Those who know the Upanishads (the end of the three Vedas) rely on the truth of that very reality wherein the seer, the seen, and the seeing are non-conceptualized.
Since words denote either a universal or a particular as something possessing distinctions, they are established precisely within those unreal differences.
For when non-existence exists, the self of an entity is not destroyed;
nor, when non-existence does not exist, is the self of an entity produced. (Brahma-vidyā-vaṭāraka 3.3.74)
The existence of the brindled cow does not sublate the existence of the black cow; nor is it on the grounds that "the brindled cow does not exist" that the black cow is postulated.
If non-existence were a real entity, then this investigation would apply to it;
and even in the case of its absence, this [same] investigation would have to be performed once again.
If that which has passed away were a non-entity (avastu) yet still within the scope of linguistic usage,
then a distinction based on its substantial reality (vastu) would not be capable of being expressed in words.
There is no application of a word to a meaning that lacks a basis, nor does a cause exist;
yet, when a cause is present, the prior non-existence [of the effect] is observed.
"What was its prior state?"—this [question] relies upon a real entity;
however, this "prior state" does not exist, for neither of these two [states] exists in a non-entity.
And there is no basis for stating that "it exists" or "it does not exist" regarding what is beyond;
they declare this to be a state beyond the reach of speech.
But this mode of operation is truly extraordinary: that the essential nature of entities—which previously did not exist, which lacks parts, and which lacks sequence—is manifested.
All worldly linguistic usage is carried out by means of entities produced solely by conceptual construction,
just as it is by primary referents.
Therefore, proponents of eternalism consider this [sequence] to be the power of the entity;
they say that sequence is the entity itself, for there is no sequence other than the entity.
In reality, there is no difference between succession and simultaneity;
just as non-existence is not determined to be anything other than existence itself.
Ordinary people indeed designate one time as another time;
yet, by mere designation, a distinct difference is not established.
Constructing a basis through the intellect, one does not rest in the absence [of such a basis];
for even regarding non-entities, no one's imaginative construction is ever obstructed.
Therefore, by means of the division of its powers, a single entity— which is eternal and consists of both being and non-being—
manifests in many forms when it is denoted by words.

The worldly linguistic usage of people proceeds by means of conceptualized entities; however, in the scientific treatise, a worldly entity is analyzed for the sake of accomplishing a specific purpose.
3,4: The further enumeration of substances:

Having arisen from the form of the composite whole and being extracted from the form of consciousness, they are analyzed in the treatise from the meaning of the sentence, just like the meanings of stems and suffixes [are extracted] from the meaning of a word. (BVaky_3.4.1)
Certain word-meanings, which serve as the indicators for grammatical correctness and whose nature is inferred from the treatise, will be explained in brief according to tradition.
That object where a pronoun is employed for the purpose of indicating a thing is called a "substance" (dravya), when it is intended to be expressed as something divisible.

3.5: Whatever is perceived as associated with [a substance], as a differentiator, and as possessing an operation, its status as a quality (guṇatva) is declared in the treatise because of its dependence on another. (BVaky_3.5.1)
When a quality that serves as a differentiator for the purpose of designation is applied to a substance that is itself not designated, the excellence of that quality is expressed [as a comparative].
For every primary substance, excellence does not exist without a cause of distinction;
nor does it ever become the denotation of a word.
Not all causes of differentiation, though present in the primary substances,
are expressed by specific words that denote excluded objects.
If, in that case, a distinction were active in the perception of the object,
then excellence would be without a cause, as there would be an absence of restriction.
And everything is necessarily and invariably drawn out from every side by a connected cause, whether it be inferior or superior.
If it does not depend on a cause occupied with excellence,
then the material cause of a substance would be useless with respect to that excellence.
Therefore, a quality, being active and based upon its own excellence,
indeed differentiates the substance itself by establishing that excellence within it.
Just as a substance that lacks form is designated by means of another form,
so too is a quality that lacks excellence characterized by means of excellence.
"Direction, means of accomplishment, action, and time"—these [terms] denote entities that are absolutely non-existent in the form of the power (*śakti*) of things. (BVaky_3.6.1)
The cause of exclusion (vyatireka) between the two— the limit and that which is to be conveyed—
is such that, by means of this very "straightness" (ṛju), cognition proceeds without anything else.
That power, which is the basis for the manifestation of the various distinctions of genus arising from action, and which is differentiated by its own limiting adjuncts, is called "Direction" (diś).

The priority and posteriority of material objects, which are based on spatial distinction, are determined from that very [spatial relation]; however, when they take the form of a sequence, they are determined by time.
Through its spatial divisions and other distinct parts,
that [ether] serves as the limiting adjunct for conjunctions and disjunctions.
There is no fixed spatial arrangement of directions for locations;
indeed, the powers of entities are manifested through their mutual assistance.
Direction, which is essentially formless, is designated as "east" with respect to objects;
for it is from that [direction] that the cognition of "east" arises. Otherwise, it would be a mere conventional name.
In the world, the determination of directions based on one's own body parts is not fixed;
for that which is behind a person facing west becomes the front when he turns around.
The restriction of spatial arrangement is not fixed among the directions;
even that which is established as "western" is designated as "eastern."

Therefore, because it has been previously used in the masculine, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) is not established; for in this sense, "procreation" (*prasava*) is nowhere expressed by the word [itself].

But when there is the denotation of the power of direction, the perception of directions such as "east" and so forth is necessarily restricted, just as the determination of a lifespan is restricted to sixty years.
Through shadow and light, a division of parts is conceived for mountains and the like; however, in entities that do not possess those properties, no division of parts can be conceived.
A division of the partless atom is postulated by means of spatial direction; they call that first capacity for the conceptualization of parts "direction."
Entities are indeed without location, without parts, devoid of emergence, and without support;
yet, through their form as associated with others, a differentiation of powers is postulated.
The state of being partless is equal for both the atom and the jar;
the "part" in that case is merely a difference in capacity, as is their respective magnitude.
Since difference is conceptualized from that [unity], and difference is also seen therein,
the wise consider it even more improper to assume a difference whose cessation is not perceived.
Because that effect is observed everywhere, it is held to be all-pervading (vibhu);
they say this alone is its omnipresence, while for others there is a rule [of pervasion] like that of embodied beings.
The conceptualization of space and time exists in the world like consciousness;
for who indeed can establish that nature of living beings otherwise?
There would be a confusion of legal procedures if there were a reversal of the fundamental nature [of things];
therefore, one who abandons these states of being nevertheless clings to them once again.
The distinction of that power as "east" and so forth is based on other entities;
therefore, direction, being distinct through that distinction, serves only to produce further differentiation.
And when there is a connection with the requirement of a limit (*avadhi*), the rule characterized by direction (*diglakṣaṇa*) applies;
however, in the case of "this is prior to that" (*pūrvam asya*), the genitive alone is seen when it refers to another property (*dharmāntara*).
Furthermore, a reversal of the directions such as east and so forth is not observed when there is no confusion regarding the limits [of space];
and this indicative mark—that "this belongs to him" in a straightforward manner—is not intermingled.
Or rather, a property of the internal organ manifests externally in this manner;
however, in this [grammatical] analysis, the distinction between internal and external does not exist.
Having understood that the conceptualization of these powers as either one or many falls into the realm of the unreal, one should not grasp at them as true in reality.
Since linguistic conventions are based on arbitrary designations for entities whose true nature transcends conceptual construction,
worldly practice follows those conventions.
There is no unity without plurality, nor is there the other without unity;
in the ultimate sense, this distinction between the two does not exist at all.
The distinction among powers is not as great as the status of those who possess them; nor does that worldly unity which exists among the possessors exist within the powers themselves.
Unity would not be established if one did not conceive of plurality;
and plurality would be lost if one did not conceive of unity.
3.7: *Sādhanasamuddeśa*.

They know that the capacity for the accomplishment of actions—whether residing in their own substratum or likewise in another substratum—is the *sādhana* (means of accomplishment). *Bhāṣyapradīpa-vyākhyāna on Vākyapadīya 3.7.1*.
Since the universe, which consists of a collection of mere potencies and possesses manifold properties,
exists at all times and in every way, something or other is intended to be expressed in a particular instance.
And the linguistic usage of means [of proof] is based on states of cognition;
whether real or unreal, a distinction among the forms of objects is constructed by the intellect.
When a speaker, having first conceived the unity of the Pañcālas with the Kurus through the intellect,
subsequently divides them again, then their disappearance (apāya) is perceived.

And one regards Kaṃsa and others— who have had their forms superimposed by words and have thus become objects of cognition— as if they were directly perceived, [considering them] as the means of accomplishment.
And by speakers, having superimposed the form of the activity of the intellect upon objects, a conceptualization of distinct powers is constructed.

When the individual (vyakti) is the referent of the word, the status of being a means (sādhanatva) for the action being produced— such as [the utterance] of a sound— is likewise established as being conceptually constructed (prakalpita) by the form of cognition (buddhi-rūpa).
Independence and dependence, as well as the nature of sequence, have been shown to be based on conceptual construction, even though all entities are devoid of activity.
For those who maintain the theory of relation (*saṃsargavādins*), all entities consist of both powers (*śakti*) and power-possessors (*śaktimat*);
it is within these that the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is determined when they are not expressed by their own specific names.
When the jar is the object of the act of seeing, its properties such as magnitude (mahattva) and so forth are the means of accomplishment;
when color (rūpa) is the object of the act of seeing, its properties such as color-ness (rūpatva) and so forth are the means of accomplishment.

In the world, the flavors and other [qualities], being possessed of their own general and particular properties, have fixed perceptions; likewise, their powers are determined by their respective substrata.
In some cases, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the connection between the sense organ, the object, the mind, and the agent;
whatever assists something at a particular time, that is the means of accomplishment for it at that time.
But when it is expressed by its own words, that property is not denoted;
rather, this assistance is understood through the case-endings and so forth alone. (Brahma-vākya 3.7.13)
The state of being a cause (nimittabhāva) of entities is resorted to for the sake of assistance;
thus, "inclination" (nati) and "bending toward" (āvarjana) are established as the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
Whether it is distinct from them or their very self, it is conceived as a means of accomplishment by relying upon its distinction [from them]. (3.7.15)
Manifestation [of the object] occurs in the desire [to act]; however, in the case of determination (*vyavasāya*), it is immediate.
Likewise, determination leads to the commencement [of action], which serves as the means for accomplishment.
That very action which exists in the prior [element] is considered the means in the subsequent one;
however, in the act of perception, they know that consciousness is the specific means.

The status of being an agent exists in every factor of action (kāraka) simply by virtue of its bringing about the accomplishment [of the result]; however, when there is a requirement for a distinction in their specific operations, the status of being an instrument (karaṇa) and so forth becomes possible.
Just as agency is attributed to both parents at the birth of a son,
the distinction— expressed as "he is in her" and "she is from him"— is made according to the speaker's intention.
The agents of qualities and actions have their powers suppressed by the primary agent;
yet even when suppressed, they remain endowed with their own complete operations.
Known as instruments and so forth through their participation in various actions,
they subsequently attain autonomy and reach the status of agents with respect to the primary action.
Just as the status of being a warrior resides in those warriors appointed by a king,
yet it is the king who obtains victory or defeat based on their conduct.
Likewise, when all [factors] are directed by an agent and perform a single purpose,
the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) and so forth is not contradictory with the status of being an agent (kartṛtva).
When the operation does not depend [on another], it is accepted as a cause (*hetu*);
however, when it depends on a state of being delimited, the wise know it as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The cause (hetu) has substance and so forth as its object; the agent (kāraka) is that whose action is restricted.
An agent who depends on another agent is accepted as the cause with respect to the action.
An instrument is seen to exist for the sake of an action, and likewise its substitute;
however, since an action exists for the sake of a cause, it is not substituted.
The cause that establishes an object is characterized by both direct and inverse order;
however, its being for that purpose follows from its conformity with the direct order through its nature as a cause.
The innate power exists everywhere, persisting as long as the substance itself;
however, at the time of action, it assists by being manifested through its substrate.
A wall has the power to obstruct, while swords and the like have the power to cleave;
yet that property, though always existent, is only discerned at the time of action.
Just as the nooses belonging to Varuṇa, when joined with the limbs of the Daityas,
become manifest [as weapons], so too are the powers of substances manifested for those who desire victory.
When the sword, by means of its own sharpness, weight, hardness, and shape,
is engaged toward that which is to be cut, it is then perceived as possessing power.

Some maintain that the means of action (*sādhana*) arises from a cause other than the action itself; others hold it to be innate (*sahaja*); while still others maintain that it exists prior to the action. (Brahma-vākya 3.7.32)
Activity itself, initially independent of anything else,
draws forth the powers residing in a single substratum like a flowing stream.
Some say that this entity characterized in such a way is either an unprecedented potency (*apūrva*), or the power of time, or an action, or time itself; and why should they not? (Brahma-vākya 3.7.34)
For others, six eternal powers, endowed with both difference and non-difference,
are established in objects like a genus (jāti) for the sake of the successful accomplishment of actions.
Due to differences in substance, form, and so forth, these [powers] appear as if they were infinite; however, their reality does not transcend six powers.
Due to the difference in signs (*nimitta*), the single power (*śakti*) is perceived as divided;
they say that agency itself is sixfold, being the basis for its manifestation.
Whether it be identity or difference, that [object] is said to be distinct;
the world has verbal testimony as its authority, and it is followed by the treatise.
But in the ultimate sense, there is no oneness distinct from difference as a separate characteristic;
rather, reality itself manifests in the form of both difference and oneness.
That which is undoubtedly distinct does not differ from unity;
that which is undoubtedly one does not differ from distinction.
The sky, the earth, the wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers,
and the directions are the external manifestations of the reality of the internal organ.
That very same single entity persists in the form of temporal divisions;
for that reality, being without prior or posterior, is perceived in the form of a sequence.

For even when there is no exclusion (vyatireka), an exclusion is observed; and even in the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), there is the positive concomitance of the referents such as "tree. Therefore, the meaning of the case-ending is held to be distinct [from the nominal stem].
The general factor of action (kāraka) has seven primary sources of differentiation;
six are distinguished by the categories beginning with "object" (karman), while the seventh distinction is the "residual" (śeṣa).
[Now begins the section on the object of action (karmādhikāra):
It is considered to be threefold—as that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*).
Among these, the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) is the *karman*; the other is conceived as fourfold.
That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent,
that which is not designated by other technical names, and that which has another as its antecedent [are all included].
Whether it exists or does not exist, that whose changing nature (prakṛti) is not relied upon is declared to be "that which is to be produced" (nirvartya). (Brahmavākyapadīya 3.7.47)
However, when the material cause (*prakṛti*) is intended to be expressed, some maintain that it is the "object to be modified" (*vikārya*);
in the grammatical treatise, the object (*karman*) is shown to be both "that which is produced" (*nirvartya*) and "that which is modified" (*vikārya*).

That which is non-existent and comes into being, or that which, though existent, is manifested through birth—that object is established as twofold: the *nirvartya* (that which is produced) and the *vikārya* (that which is modified).
Some [destruction] arises from the cutting off of the original nature, like the ash of wood and so forth;
some arises from the production of another quality, like the transformation of gold and so forth.
That in which the accomplishment of specific qualities produced by action is not apprehended through either perception or inference is said to be "attainable" (prāpya).
A specific attainment exists everywhere through seeing and other means;
for some, however, there is the accomplishment of its manifestation in cases such as the "poisonous gaze" (dṛṣṭiviṣa).
Appearance, manifestation, and endurance—
these are the specific stages of an action as it is being accomplished, established for the purpose of achieving the result.
Having first experienced independence in the case of things to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth,
it subsequently becomes the object (*karman*) in relation to the operation of other agents.
Even when the operation of that [verbal root] is absent, [the suffix], being established in its own operation,
receives in certain instances those rules prescribed for the object (karman) which are based on the grammatical treatise.
When the instigation has ceased, the object remains within its own action-part;
as its status as an object ceases, it persists in its status as an agent.
The wise understand those other elements to be like the words *pac* (to cook) and *sidh* (to succeed);
although there is a difference [in their specific forms], they are conceived as one because their underlying nature is the same.
Verbal roots such as *pac* and others, endowed with identical forms, function by their very nature to denote both a single constituent action and the collection of actions.

In the case of the root *ruh* in its simple form, "causing to descend" (*nyagbhāvanā*) and "descending" (*nyagbhavana*) are understood; likewise, these are also recognized when the root is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*).
They say that the fifth state occurs when [the root] ends in the causative suffix (ṇic) with the agent as the object;
the causative suffix (ṇic) is said to be applied to the original meaning of the root once the instigation has ceased.
The root *sidh* expresses the meaning of *pac* (to cook) without the suffix *ṇic*;
that [root] ending in *ṇic* is restricted to the primary meaning of *pac*.
The operation belonging to certain agents, such as Devadatta, which [involves] an object in a transitive verb,
is intended to be expressed without [mentioning] Devadatta and so forth when applied to objects such as mats.
When the instigation has ceased, the object becomes the instigator of its own agent;
when it is connected with another instigation, it is expressed by the suffix *ṇic* in the form of the periphrastic future (*liṅ*).
In cases such as "similar" (*sadṛśa*), where the status of both object and agent is attained,
there the two actions— namely, the reaching (*āpatti*) and the causing to reach (*āpādana*)— have [the object] as their respective domains.
If one were to bring in a word from somewhere else and thus construct [the meaning] in this way,
then those words denoting seeing and so forth would possess the status of being bhāvas residing in the object (karmasthabhāvaka).
Where there is a perception of distinction, there action is established;
however, for others, the establishment of action is manifested by words alone.

When time, state, distance, and place are construed with all intransitive verbs through the mediation of other actions that are implicitly contained within them, they acquire the status of an object (*karman*).
Having attained, as it were, the status of a locus (ādhāra) with respect to substances and actions,
time and the other factors subsequently reach the status of an object (karman), though they belong to a different category.
Therefore, the verbal root, though devoid of substance and lacking an object by virtue of those [intransitive] actions,
becomes fit to serve as the cause for the *la*-suffix to express both the object and the state (*bhāva*).

And every unmentioned object (*akathita-karman*) is understood to belong to a different category, because it differs from the objective of the verbal root's meaning; indeed, that is not considered the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*).
That which prompts the action is called the primary object (*pradhānakarman*);
however, another [object] connected with the action for the sake of accomplishing that [primary object] is traditionally known as the "unspoken" (*akathita*).
In verbs such as *nī* ("to lead"), the status of being an object (*karman*)—which is not based on the specific verbal designation (*akathāśraya*)—is similar to that in verbs like *duh* ("to milk").
However, when the verb *ākhyā* ("to tell") is used with *anupayoga* ("lack of purpose"), the remaining [object] is intended by rule.

For verbs such as *duh* (to milk) and others that have an implied causative sense (*antarbhūta-ṇij-artha*), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 1.4.51] just as it is for those with an explicit causative suffix (*ṇijanta*). Likewise, the restriction regarding the causative suffix applies in the same manner.
Just as there is no recourse to excellence within the category of the instrument itself,
so too there would be no preeminence within the category of the object itself.
But since one relies on the fact that an action is desired to be attained, a distinction is thereby resorted to;
therefore, there is an absolute difference from the previous [category of] action.
Just as in the case of a causative verb (*ṇijanta*), the agent, being active, is employed [as the subject],
so too in roots such as *duh* (to milk), the agent is employed even though he is inactive.
But as for the sentence expressing the separation (*bhedavākya*) which occurs in the causative (*ṇyanta*), and that which occurs in the base forms of *nī* and *duh*,
because they are different words, there is no contact whatsoever between them and the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Just as a single *apādāna* is shown in the treatise through its divisions,
so too a single *karman* is presented through its divisions.

Whether it be something to be produced (*nirvartya*), something to be modified (*vikārya*), or something to be attained (*prāpya*), that which is the locus of the means of accomplishment is designated as having a "perfected" (*siddha*) form, because it is the actions themselves that are to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Just as a desire arises in an agent toward things that are harmful due to greed,
so too does that [desire] proceed toward [harmful things] such as poison out of fear and other such motives.

Where there are two distinct capacities for a substance belonging to the primary and the subordinate actions, and where the quality depends upon [the capacity of] the subordinate, there the primary action is followed.
When the power whose primary object is the principal meaning is expressed by a suffix,
then that [power], although not explicitly stated when it pertains to a subordinate element, is nevertheless manifested.
When an action not previously mentioned is expressed by a suffix ending in *ktvā* denoting a state (*bhāva*),
that [action] manifests as possessing the properties of that [state], even when it is stated to have a different capacity in the case of the root *bhuj*.
And because of the contact between the root *iṣ* ("to desire") and the root *gam* ("to go"), the suffix *lo* which is prescribed [after *iṣ*] when it means "village" is employed;
therein, the object of the action of going is experienced by the desirer alone.
In the expression "it is eaten after being cooked," for some [grammarians], the verb *pacati* does not require [an object];
that [object], namely *odanam*, is understood through inference.

Likewise, that action which is expressed by an affix ending in *-anta* (denoting the agent) is also expressed by an affix ending in *-ktvā*; yet, even when it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), they do not accept the locative case (*saptamī*) there.
Furthermore, that action which has its substratum already ceased and has not yet been accumulated through acquisition is intended [as the object],
being differentiated by the occurrence of objects such as food and so forth.

An action is considered intransitive when the verbal root functions in a sense other than its primary meaning, when the object is included within the meaning of the root itself, when it is conventional usage, or when the object is not intended to be expressed. (Brahma-vākya 3.7.88)
These four divisions which have been shown in general are further divided in many ways according to the distinction of causes (*nimitta*) and so forth.
[Thus ends the section on action.
[Now begins the section on the instrument:
That whose operation immediately precedes the completion of an action [is the instrument].
When, however, instrumentality (karaṇatva) is intended to be expressed in that context, then it is traditionally held [to be so].
In reality, that [agenthood] is indefinable, for no entity is fixed [in its role];
since we observe the intended meaning expressed as "the pot cooks" (*sthālyā pacyate*).
But with regard to the instruments, they repeatedly initiate refinement and specific applications for the sake of accomplishing the primary purpose.
Furthermore, there is no excellence of the instruments within their own respective spheres;
rather, the characteristic of superiority in that case is the possession of an excellence derived from something else.
Even when [the agent] possesses independence, the users [of instruments] assist only from a distance;
for the operation of all [agents] is mediated by the instrument.

This excellence belongs to the action, while the agent remains subordinate; for when the accomplishment is achieved, the general property of being the "means of accomplishment" (sādhakatva) is intensified.
When the sword and so forth are the agent, they know sharpness and the like to be the instrument;
when sharpness and the like possess independence, the self (ātman) is established in two ways.
Even though there is a difference in the individual selves, that single object remains as it is;
because the agency resides in that [object], agency persists despite the difference, and therefore there is no contradiction.
Just as instrumentality is understood through proximity,
so too is it understood even in the absence of proximity, because the accomplishment of the action occurs.

They declare that the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) belongs to "a little" (*stoka*) and so forth, either because of the accomplishment of a small amount or because of its non-accomplishment.
In the same way, [the cognition] is distinguished by the difference and non-difference of the properties and their possessors;
it is differentiated according to the specific delimitation of the limit of the action, just as in the case of [the cognition of] an action.
[Thus ends the section on the instrument.
[Now begins the section on the agent:
Prior to obtaining power from another, and even before being brought into a state of subordination, [the self is the agent].
Because the activity of those who have engaged [in action] proceeds dependent upon that [knowledge], and because it brings about their cessation.
Because no substitute is observed [for the agent], and because [the agent] is seen even in isolation,
the independence of the agent is asserted despite the fact that [the action] is assisted from afar.
Restriction applies to the word through the properties that have arisen [in it], but not to the object itself;
when there is a desire to express a property of the agent, the agent is understood from the word.
When a distinction is imagined for a single entity through its various cognitive states,
the status of agent, instrument, and object arises.
The non-existence prior to origination is based on a state of the intellect;
it is indistinguishable from other existing things, yet it becomes the agent of birth.
When the cause does not remain distinct from the state of being the effect,
it then acquires the designation "effect" and arises as an effect.
Just as the coiling of a snake or the coming together of those who were scattered,
so do some declare that the nature of birth belongs to existent things.
Whatever effect proceeds from its causes with distinct origins,
its own genus also remains established in the form of that individual manifestation.
The placement of words occurs only with respect to existing entities, whether they be objects of cognition or speech;
even the statement "it does not exist" does not apply to that which is non-existent, nor is the existent differentiated from it.
The intellect and words function with respect to things as they truly are;
no linguistic usage exists apart from their actual reality.
Just as there is a division of space and just as there is the movement of a shadow,
so too have birth and destruction been conceptualized by some, even though there is no actual differentiation [in the underlying reality].
Just as the non-existence of space is unreal when defined by a material form,
so too the non-existence of a material form is unreal when dependent upon space.
Just as the essence of action is designated by means of those purposes and operations,
this sequence of cause and effect arises from the apprehension of non-difference.
Regarding the doubt as to whether the agent of birth is a modification (*vikāra*) or primordial nature (*prakṛti*),
the views of those who understand [the matter] differ according to the observations of the indicative marks (*liṅga*).

The dative case used in the sense of "becoming" (*saṃpadyamāna*) expresses a transformation; for example, the statement regarding a gold lump as the material cause (*prakṛti*) refers to its state as an earring (*kuṇḍala*). (Vākya-kāṇḍa 3.7.115)

In the sentence, the agent of the verb *saṃpad* is said to be the "group" (*saṅgha*) when it ends in the suffix *cvi*; in the derivative form (*vṛtti*), as in "the Brāhmaṇas are becoming a group," the independence belongs to the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
That which has attained the state of "you" (tvam) is no longer "you";
in that [state], the activity based on the word *yuṣmad* does not apply to the person, for he is then designated as belonging to primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Not abandoning its prior state while touching upon a subsequent property,
the essence of an object is said to be "being born," as if it were swooning.
In some cases, a certain property is perceived as being more actively engaged;
moreover, the powers of entities, though distinct, may become conjoined.
In the case of error, the activity of the person would be understood as directed toward a contrary object;
for here, the means of accomplishment is perceived as being accompanied by an operation.
The conceptual construction that "you are someone else" would apply there, just as it would be the case when a king has fallen into the state of a servant; such would be the transition.
Based on the expectation that the action will be accomplished, one is assumed to be the agent;
thus, with respect to an action to be achieved by oneself, one is the prompter of the means of accomplishment.
Relying solely on its own sovereignty, it remains subordinate even when merely engaged in application;
thus, it becomes indistinguishable from other independent [factors] that are free from doubt.
All [actions] proceed from signs for the sake of one's own being;
even the compliance with an intention is for the accomplishment of one's own purpose alone.
[Thus ends the section on the agent. Now begins the section on the causal agent (*hetu*):

"While performing instigation (*preṣaṇa*) or entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇa*), or while performing actions conducive to those, the agent itself acquires the designation 'causal agent' (*hetu*) as prescribed in the grammatical treatise. (Vākyapadīya 3.7.125)

When there is an injunction regarding the mere substance of an action such as "asking" and so forth, the imperative suffix (loṭ) is prescribed; however, when that same action is employed as being accompanied by an agentive operation, that is the domain of the causative suffix (ṇic).
Having attained the status of an object (*karman*) through the act of commanding due to its independence regarding the action of a quality,
it is expressed by its own grammatical property because of the restrictive rule concerning the technical designation of "object."
The object (karman) is the cause that impels the action; it is the instigator of the agent.
And the action arises for the sake of the object through [the processes of] production, refinement, and attainment.
[Thus ends the section on the cause.
Now begins the section on the recipient (saṃpradāna):
"That which is desired by the object of the action is the recipient, because it is not rejected by the agent and is a factor in the act of relinquishing."
And through instigation and consent, it attains the status of a recipient (saṃpradāna).

Whether it is designated as the cause (*hetu*), the object of the action (*karman*), or the residual factor (*śeṣa*), that which is a *kāraka* is called the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) by the grammatical treatise in the case of verbs meaning "to please" (*rucy-artha*) and others.

And when a distinction is intended, because each subsequent subordinate element (anga) functions as the object (karman) with respect to each preceding action, the term "action" was not included [in the definition]. (Brahmavidyābharaṇa on Vākyapadīya 3.7.131)
But when unity is intended with respect to a collection of actions, then the object (karman), by virtue of its connection with the action, is figuratively designated by its own name [as "action"].
The intention to express either difference or non-difference is established by its own inherent nature;
therefore, no deviation is observed regarding the status of the object of a verb meaning "to go."
If both designations were to apply everywhere solely by virtue of conceptual construction,
then the rejection of the undertaking of yoga would be equivalent [to its acceptance].
Regarding that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be attained, there is the perception of association;
the action established therein assumes a twofold form. (Brahma-vākya 3.7.135)
[Thus ends the section on the recipient (saṃpradāna).
Now begins the section on the point of departure (apādāna):
Some [grammatical operations] have their scope explicitly indicated, while others have their scope implied.
And that which involves an expected action; thus, the *apādāna* (ablative) is said to be of three kinds.
Just as the act of going (*gati*) itself becomes "revolving" (*bhrami*) due to a difference in conjunction,
so too does "separation" (*apāya*), though it has a fixed limit (*dhruva*), reside likewise in that which is not fixed (*adhruva*).
In the Sūtra it is understood that the intrinsic nature of a substance is not permanence; rather, what is intended to be expressed is permanence as the object of non-departure.
In the case of Devadatta’s refuge, there is permanence; however, in the case of a horse’s fall, that which is entered by misfortune is declared to be impermanent.
Although both rams are unstable even when [the action] arises from the effort of both,
the two actions are nevertheless intended to be distinguished there in the case of a division.
With respect to their respective actions, the two rams each possess a distinct status as the limit (avadhi),
and with respect to their own actions, each possesses a distinct status as the agent (kartṛ).
If, however, a single action is intended to be expressed as being accomplished by two [agents] without distinction,
then both rams are the agents in the act of moving away, provided that another limit (avadhi) exists.
Without a limit (avadhi), it is not understood that there is a departure;
this is illustrated in the Bhāṣya by the example: "the leaf of a tree falls. (Brahma-vākya 3.7.143)
Difference and non-difference, distinctness and persistence— these contradictory properties are not intended to be predicated of a cloud simultaneously.

In the expression "he pierces with a bow," since there is no intention to express separation (*apāya*), the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) does not exist; therefore, those two [the object and the instrument] are mentioned together.
Or rather, being one and the same, the power exists in two forms;
therein, the secondary [power] is sublated by the primary in the case of the two designations.

The rule concerning the ablative case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), as well as the rule for words such as *bhī* ("fear") and *trā* ("protection"), involves an implied departure (*apāya*) that is not explicitly mentioned; this is intended for the comprehension of the unlearned.
[Thus ends the section on the ablative case. [Now begins the section on the locative case:
That which, being separated from the agent or the object, holds the action not directly, [is called the locus].
In the accomplishment of an action, that which assists is traditionally recorded in the treatise as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the cases of sesame seeds, space, mats, and so forth, there is no difference in their contact;
however, the benefits conferred by those things that are conjoined or inherent do differ.
The non-destruction of gravity, independence upon obstruction,
delimitation by a specific direction, and so forth, are the causes of differentiation.
For some, space itself is considered the primary supporting power (*ādhāra-śakti*) of all things that possess conjunction, due to the conceptualization of spatial distinctions.
Since there is no existence of entities such that "this is here," designation [of location] is not possible; they declare that to have space as its cause.
From time actions are differentiated; from space all material forms [are differentiated].
This difference is precisely of such a nature that it is based upon non-difference.
Although the act of fasting depends upon a specific location,
it nevertheless relies solely upon time, because that is the nature of the operation of the word.
Even when the verb *vasati* ("he dwells") is not employed, the location is then the locus (*adhikaraṇa*);
furthermore, the ritual acts such as the three-night fast (*trirātra*) are traditionally held to be included in the term "fasting" (*upavāsa*).
[Thus ends the section on the locus (adhikaraṇa).
Now begins the section on the residual relations (śeṣa):
A relation (saṃbandha) is distinct from the kārakas; it is preceded by action and kārakas.
Whether the action has been heard or not heard, he is designated as such.
Although this [word] resides in two [places], it is distinguished by its subservience to another;
being expressed therein, it serves the primary element as well.
The restriction of the specific occasion for a word's application is not grasped from the word itself;
rather, that particularity is delimited by the *karmapravacanīyas*.
Furthermore, when an action is heard [implied] even though it is designated by its instruments,
the genitive case is prescribed for every word in order to prevent compounding.
In the case of a completed action (*niṣṭhā*), the genitive case governed by the object (*karma*) is also prohibited;
there, a compound with a genitive case characterized as "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is not desired.
When that which is designated by one [word] undergoes exclusion (*vyatireka*) in another [context],
it acquires two properties in that different domain.
Having attained primacy through its own quality, it becomes subordinate to the principal element;
therefore, in the case of the *saha-yoga* (conjunction with "together"), its status as a principal element is not lost.
[Thus ends the section on the remainder.
Scholars understand *saṃbodhana* (addressing) to be merely the manifestation of that which is already established toward the speaker;
for it is the essence of the object, having attained such orientation, that is employed in actions. (BVaky_3.7.163)
It is the traditional teaching of the predecessors that the vocative case is not the meaning of the sentence;
rather, the meanings of the case-endings are extracted from the sentence-meaning by means of mere indication (uddeśa).
Let it be understood from the rule regarding *avyayībhāva* compounds that they occur in the sense of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*);
that which is distinct from a substance (*dravya*) and constitutes the meaning of a case-ending is expressed by an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
But whatever substance exists in a certain way, it remains exactly so in its ultimate state;
even when engaged in action, its essential nature as a substance is not lost.
Therefore, that substance which is an instrument could not again become an object;
otherwise, there would be a change of state for that very essence of the substance.
3.8: *Kriyāsamuddeśa*.

Whatever is designated as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whether it be already established (*siddha*) or not yet established (*asiddha*), is understood as "action" (*kriyā*) because it possesses a nature that depends upon a temporal sequence. (BVaky_3.8.1)
Because it resounds through the relationship of cause and effect, sound (dhvani) is said to possess a sequence;
however, when that sequence has ceased, it is simply called "sound."
"In 'the white [thing] is white,' this [object] shines forth as whiteness; the verbal expression proceeds because it possesses a nature that depends upon a temporal sequence."
A collection of parts that arise in succession,
whose difference is mentally constructed by the intellect and which function as subordinate factors, is designated as "action" (kriyā).
That collection, having become that [single entity], is completed within each of the members of the collection;
therefore, when there is a distinction [between them], the possibility of a difference in time arises.
In due order, the natures of those [objects], whether existent or non-existent, do not— being aggregates—
enter into a relationship with the eyes and other senses whose objects are real entities.
Just as the entire aggregate [of a cow] denoted by the word "cow" is not within the range of the senses,
yet the form of that which is perceived part by part is determined by the intellect.
When the sense-faculties, falling upon the constituent parts [of an object], apprehend it otherwise than it actually exists,
the form of actions is conceptualized as being like a whirling firebrand.
Just as the pouring of water and so forth are parts of the act of cooking,
so too should other constituent parts, such as the pouring of water, be understood [as parts of those acts].
And that which is perceived as having reached the limit of reduction—
there, a word denoting an action is not employed in isolation for that single [element].
Established in its sequence by preceding and succeeding parts,
that single [entity] is nevertheless designated by various names due to the superimposition of what is unreal.
That form which conforms to time is understood as "it exists";
but when it is delimited on all sides, it is simply called an "entity" (bhāva).
Since worldly usage is already established, this is not a postulation of a quality; for a metaphorical designation persists only when the primary sense is possible.
Because they possess an enhanced capacity either individually or as a collective, the constituents of a group,
though non-sequential, appear to have multiple forms as if they were sequential.
They know that action to be the primary one from which the immediate fruit arises; because it exists for the sake of those others, the others receive their designation [from it]. (3.8.15)

Whatever effort is made for the sake of that which is the cause for the engagement in an action, one should employ it while determining "he goes," regardless of [any other] consideration. (BVaky_3.8.16)
As long as this entity, which consists of the conditions [of cognition], has not yet arisen,
it is designated as "existent" by means of the form of other [entities] while being that which is to be established.
Once the goal is accomplished, the requirement for a means ceases because its purpose has been fulfilled;
therefore, there is no application of words denoting action in that context.
And that [word-meaning], being unitary, is devoid of sequence and not subject to prior or posterior states;
it is nevertheless followed by the properties of the preceding and succeeding [sounds] for the sake of that [meaning].
Therefore, that which exists is perceived;
and this [perceiver] is grasped as if it were a single self of both existence and non-existence.
Others say that *jāti* (the universal) is the action (*kriyā*) residing in multiple individuals;
it is unachievable in its own form, yet it is perceived as if it were achievable.
That very genus which exists in the constituent part of the action is traditionally held to be the action itself;
it is understood as if being born when its manifestation is produced in accordance with it.
Alternatively, action (*kriyā*) is the existence (*sattā*) of the agent and the object as qualified by their own respective operations;
or it is the existence inherent in the various specific operations.

Some maintain that the existence (sattā) which resides in the ultimate self is itself action; for the traditional teaching is unbroken: "The meaning of a verbal root is indeed being (bhāva). (Brahma-vākya-kārikā 3.8.24)

Others, however, maintain that it is the intellect (*buddhi*); still others, its genus; and yet others, the existence of the intellect (*buddhisattā*) as it is projected onto entities—that they call "action" (*kriyā*).
Manifestation and disappearance, as well as birth and destruction, are conceived by others among the six modifications of being as conventional [distinctions].
By these two, all active processes are subsumed without distinction;
birth itself, when its similarity [to the preceding state] is relied upon, is designated as "stability" (sthiti).
There is nothing other than Being for that which is being born, nor is there the status of being a non-entity in its destruction;
therefore, among the modifications of existence, Being alone remains constant.
But that which has arisen from a preceding part is designated as "its birth," when one intends to express its causality by means of a form that relies upon a temporal sequence.
By means of verbal forms (ākhyāta-śabda), that very object is denoted as being thus constituted;
meanwhile, the nominal words (nāma-śabda) function as if withdrawing their sequential order.
Whether it be the fruit, or what is designated as the fruit, or whatever object is opposed to those [preceding states],
that which is entirely different from them is designated by the ancients as *nāga*.
Without grasping an entity as "neither existent nor non-existent," another entity is conceptualized through the form of something else and is thus apprehended.
Even without touching with his hand the existence or non-existence of jars and other things, someone may perceive them either in the absence of light or even in its presence.
Pervasive and subtle, it sometimes undergoes expansion and sometimes undergoes contraction;
or else, performing no action whatsoever, it manifests itself through its own power alone.
Others understand that action to be the gradual perception of the reality of all forms, as well as its construction, as it were, through parts.
Existence, through its connection with its own powers, is established in all forms:
as both the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment, as well as the fruit and the enjoyer of that fruit.
Others, however, consider action (kriyā) to be an unfailing activity that does not depend on anything else, which brings about a single purposeful result through its means.
Having first existed as a universal, it is divided into its constituent parts; thereafter, it is established as if being accomplished through the form of its various functions.
That [inherent nature] is the primary means among all instruments, and it is the first causal factor (*kāraka*);
others, however, describe its difference from the various operations (*vyāpāra*).
When many meanings are possible, only some are contributive; however, in their combination, one among them is perceived as predominant.
Because it is that which is to be accomplished, there the operations— being the means of accomplishment—
are expressed by verbal suffixes as the primary element, even though they are set in motion by the result.
In the synthesis of difference and non-difference through the presence or absence of the state of oneness,
numbers are perceived therein as the operations of the numerable parts.
How can an accomplished object, such as cooking and the like, be connected with a means of accomplishment?
Or, if it were something yet to be accomplished, there would be no difference whatsoever between [the meaning of] a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and that of a primary suffix (*kṛt*).

In that regard, if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the basis for the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*), then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is excluded by that [suffix] when there is a relation between the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). (3.8.44)
A single entity denoted by a single term cannot simultaneously possess two properties if it is already established; how then could it be something yet to be proven?
The conceptual construction that "this much is the means" and "this much is the goal" exists only within the treatise;
in reality, there is no such distinction in the sentence itself.

Just as in the case of a verb, the status of being the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is attributed to its two parts according to the treatise, that same sequence applies to words ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes as well.
In that context, action, as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is based on the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*);
however, its state of being an existent entity (*sattvabhāva*) is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*.
In the word "bandhu," [the meaning] is established in the form of a non-differentiation from kinship;
however, the collective state of being kin is expressed by the suffix.
In that regard, action is unestablished with respect to that [agent] for whom it is yet to be accomplished;
but it is not established with respect to that very same [agent] for whom it has already been accomplished.
In the expression "the grandson of the king's son," [the term] does not deviate from [denoting] the king;
nor is the status of being the primary referent of the word "son" revoked for it.
"Just as one says, 'Look, the deer runs,' [indicating] the nature of the goal and the means,
so too does the occurrence of running [of the mind] arise through the distinction of objects."

In the case of [words] formed with *kṛt* suffixes other than those having the sense of *la*, *kta*, or *khal*, as well as indeclinables (*avyaya*) and *kṛt* suffixes, and also in the case of conventional terms (*rūḍhi*), past participles (*niṣṭhā*), and [suffixes] such as *ghañ*, the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Because the object to be established is not yet fully accomplished, there is no apprehension [of identity] such as "this is that"; therefore, since this [identity] is absent without verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), comparison is not effected by them.

Since the status of being a means (sādhanatva) is well-established for those things connected with verbal suffixes (tiṅ), there can only be a superimposition (adhyāropa); however, no comparison (upamā) exists.
And when [the parts] are deficient, a comparison is prescribed for the sake of completing the sense;
for every action is completed within its respective substratum here and there.
By the very same reason for which it is said that "the swan flies," because that [action] is completed in the act of striking, no sense of comparison exists.
Similarity is not perceived among actions that differ in their genus;
furthermore, since the goal is already established at the outset, it cannot be compared by means of analogy.

Just as one says "the forest consists of trees" based on the relation between difference and non-difference, so too the essence of an object is differentiated within its existence; this is the sequence [of analysis] regarding both the external and the internal.
Whatever gender is perceived in the expression "existence in the universal" (sāmānye bhāvaḥ), that is not intended to apply to the particulars, because those particulars are what are to be inferred.
In the case of verbal suffixes (*liṅga*) used in the sense of an action (*bhāva*), the gender is not intended to be expressed because their purpose is fulfilled by the explanation [of the action].
Furthermore, in the case of roots such as *pac* and others, because they function as rules for comparison, the suffix occurs in a sense other than that of the action itself.
That which is taught here for the roots *pac* and so forth by means of the suffixes *bhū* and *tu*,
the gender of the roots *pac* and so forth is not inherent in those suffixes.
And that single object called "Being" (sattā) is described in some way by certain [theorists];
yet its indicative marks (liṅga) differ, just as there are differences in the forms of verbs such as *pacati*.

Just as a single person is designated as both "teacher" and "maternal uncle" due to a difference in relationship, so too is that same essential nature [of the object] the basis for the two states of being "cooked" and "cooking."
3.9: Exposition of Time (Kālasamuddeśa).
Some declare that time exists apart from activity;
it is eternal, one, all-pervading, a substance, and the measure of those things possessing action. (BVaky_3.9.1)
Measurements such as *diṣṭi*, *prastha*, and *suvarṇa* serve to differentiate material forms;
time serves to differentiate actions; but number is the differentiator of everything. (Vākyapadīya 3.9.2)
Regarding the origination, the persistence, and likewise the destruction of things that possess those [qualities],
they say that time alone is the cause, existing with its nature divided [into distinct parts].
Him they call the stage-manager of this world-machine;
by means of prohibition and permission, the universe is divided by him.
If [the sequence] were not to obstruct [it], nor would it relinquish its obstruction;
then the states [of cognition] would become intermingled, devoid of priority and posteriority.
Its self is divided in many ways through distinctions that serve as the substrata for other properties;
for indeed, no entity whatsoever exists that is either distinct or non-distinct.
It is neither one nor many; it is neither white nor black.
That substantial self, however, appears in such a form only through association.
The various distinctions among those things that are associated with it are considered its specific qualities;
differentiated by them, time serves as the basis for the differentiation of temporal states.
The acquisition of activity is conceived through connection with a specific time;
it remains as the cause for the conjunction of the powers.
The rules governing birth and manifestation are dependent upon application;
and because its existence is contingent upon the eternal, its persistence is preceded by those very rules.
Then, for that which persists, there occurs through those various associated factors [of speech] its favoring, its obstruction, its disappearance, and its abandonment. (Brahma-sūtra-vārttika 3.9.11)
However, it is the operation of time that is established here for each distinct state;
for Time itself, the soul of the universe, is called "operation."
Therefore, through transformation associated with differentiation, the individual accumulations and depletions of all distinct forms are perceived separately.
Through activities resembling the continuous revolution of a water-wheel,
the all-pervading Lord, fashioning all the constituent parts (kalās), receives the name "Time" (kāla).
And those diverse activities of the universe that have arisen from Him,
He alone brings them about, just as a spider [produces] its threads.
When the powers have attained their maturation through connection with specific times,
the eternal action is manifested by the operation known as "usage."
In that [capacity], however, the manifestation of the fruit arises as connected with the genus;
it is regulated by powers through some wondrous mode of operation.
Then, however, the power called "inherence" (samavāya), which sublates difference,
brings about a state of oneness in those individuals through its causal factors.
Then,
after this restriction, all those classes that serve as the motivators manifest themselves within it, like reflections in clear water.
Since they conform to their causes, the qualities (guṇas) arise there preceded by their causes, serving as the means for the manifestation of their own respective classes.
The substrata are eternal, and that which is supported by them is also eternal; stability (sthiti) is thus postulated because it favors those individual manifestations.
Just as there is dependence on others for the arising of what is impermanent, so too is there for its duration;
it is created solely for destruction, and the wise know its existence to be not under its own control.
Abiding together with associated entities, it is assisted in its own functions;
for the activity of those things that possess birth is not held to occur without grasping their existence.
That power of time known as decay, which is antagonistic to other powers, obstructs those powers; and thus, things that are mutually opposed come into being.
But those causal factors which are the causes for the stage of persistence all disappear, because of which the self is relinquished.
Just as everything arises without support, without foundation, and through a marvelous process, so too is this self abandoned.
How could there be a determination of two actions that have reached completion and are inherent in different objects, without a single related entity?
Just as weight, established through various substances on a scale or in the hand, is measured precisely by means of time, so too is the course of action.
He abandons the activities that accompany him as they remain established;
like rice [losing its husk], he thereby attains the designation "year."
Through its eternal functioning by way of both obstruction and permission,
that [Speech] being divided thereby assumes the form of succession.
Due to the difference in agents, that single [Word] undergoes increase or decrease in its various meanings, or attains a state of equality or inequality.
Just as the designation "carpenter" and so forth applies to a single person due to the difference in his activities,
so too the designation "sacrificial priest" and so forth arises for a single person due to the difference in his activities.

It is designated as "commencement," "action," and "completion" due to the distinction of superimposing other properties upon that which consists of both being and non-being. (Brahma-sūtra-vṛtti 3.9.33)
Whatever size belongs to the dyads and so forth, that same size belongs even to the Himavat;
for the self of anything cannot be broken or even measured.
However, the accumulation of other entities [in relation] to others is postulated;
by means of that, it is perceived as "this slowly" or "this quickly."
And for that which is non-existent, there is no sequence, for it cannot be divided;
and even for that which is existent, its essential nature remains exactly as it is.
And being conditioned by action, it is understood as divided into the states of past, future, and present through eleven modes.
In that regard, there are five types of past [time], four types of future, and two types of present declared; thus, there are eleven conceptual constructions.
When one's own form is deposited in time and restrained by wisdom,
then all entities turn back from it, their powers having been transferred into that [wisdom].
And the form of things yet to come, as well as its reflection,
appears in time itself, as if in a perfectly polished mirror.
Just as a current carries away grass, leaves, creepers, and the like,
so too does time set in motion the measures of those who possess measure.
Just as the wind, having entered, coordinates the movements of those who possess motion, so too does the self of time (kālātman) assume the form of sequence within that very [speech].
The division of the solstices, the fixed courses of the luminaries,
and the origins and cessations of living beings are all dependent upon that [time].

Those transformations of the constituent elements (mātrās) which follow the course of time are designated as "constellations" (nakṣatras); among them, the stars (tārakās) are merely the visible marks.
The Lord of the Seasons is discerned through the cries of beasts and birds, the activities of stationary beings, and the transformations of shadows and other phenomena.
This appearance that seems to occur in a sequence for the universe, though it is actually without sequence— that is the activity of Time.
Just as the determination of "far" and "near" is based on space,
so too the determination of "slow" and "quick" is based on time.
In worldly convention, three divisions— as if produced by action— are established within that undivided time, which the world does not transcend.
The three powers of Time are established as one;
it is through connection with these that existing things undergo appearance and disappearance.
It is said that through two powers it is of the nature of obscuring entities;
however, the power called "present" is that which reveals the form of the entity.
The power of that which has not yet come into being does not obstruct the capacity for birth;
however, that power which is designated as "past" is incompatible with birth.
These three paths are established like darkness and light;
although they are without sequence, a sequence of entities is perceived within them.
But among those two, one consists of darkness (tamas) while the other exists like light;
moreover, for some, even that which has passed away recurs again.
The property of that [word] simultaneously acquires the state of being present;
and because some [of its properties] are present, it likewise [acquires] the state of being past.
Drawn forth by the assistance of its cause, it has come into the present state;
yet, once the assistance of the cause has ceased, it does not come into view again.
According to some, the omnipresent Time possesses only two paths of power,
by means of which it effects the manifestation and the concealment of all entities.
Some describe that [word], which is by its very nature divided into parts with distinct meanings, as being characterized by the synthesis of cognitions.
Whether it be a power following from cognition or something existing externally as a reality,
it is impossible to engage in linguistic usage without relying upon time as the soul of all things.
Every entity possesses three powers of being;
by means of these inherent powers, everything both exists and does not exist at all times.
Since they are not distinct from Being (*sattva*), all three are established as such;
their sequence follows from that non-difference, and thus existence and non-existence do not differ [from it].
Through being seen and not being seen, that very same thing is both seen and unseen; yet there is no unity of the temporal paths (adhvan), nor does anything whatsoever cease to exist.
The first view of time is that which is divided according to the positions of power (śakti), self (ātman), and deity; it exists within ignorance (avidyā) and is not found in knowledge (vidyā).
If time were non-different [in itself], then the appearance of difference seen in short, long, and protracted [vowels] would be like the cognition of "long" and "quick."
How could there be an accumulation [of sound] in cases such as water in a tube through the repetition of short, long, and protracted [vowels],
if it were caused by mere conceptual construction?
The essence of the word, though undivided and not consisting of accumulation, appears to increase through the accumulation of the causes of its manifestation.
Thus, for that which consists of a quarter-measure or for that which consists of ten verses,
no distinction exists within the nature of the word itself due to the variation in its magnitude.
Those words which, as it were, exist in the interval by way of being co-produced, serve as means for the cognizers to achieve comprehension.
Depending upon various specific limits,
time— the single entity among those things that possess time— comes to be conceived as divided into moments, months, and seasons.
And due to the distinctions in the apprehension by the intellect,
time— whether it be a mere moment or even eons and intermediate kalpas— is established as existing within the nature of conventional usage.
The flow of water into the cavity of a water-clock, resulting from both obstruction and permission,
is the very activity of Time itself.
Whether the gap be small or large, the operation of time is not divided by its connection with it; the self (ātman) likewise follows that very [operation] of his.
That which appears as the playground of Time through its own powers is divided in many ways among the various states of the multiform [Brahman].
Whether it be the growth of the bamboo or that of the palmyra palm,
the reality of time is conceptualized through the application of such growth.
Even when there is a transgression of the constituent parts, there is no transgression of that [word];
there is no distinction in the path whatsoever due to the difference between the goer and the act of going.
Due to the established worldly perception of the rising and setting of the luminaries,
even though there is no actual transgression of time, it appears as if it possesses that property [of transgression].
Furthermore, others who know time understand time as the movement of the sun, planets,
and constellations, which is differentiated according to the various types of its revolutions.
That activity which, having set out to delimit another action, has its own measure fully determined with respect to that [other] action, is designated as "time" (*kāla*). (Brahma-vākya-kārikā 3.9.77)
The transfer of form into cognition and its withdrawal by means of cognition itself—
since there is no other intervening action, that very [process] is accepted as the action of time.

The expression "the jar has come into being" (bhūto ghaṭaḥ) refers to the very state of existence (sattā) as having become manifest; and when one says "existence has come into being" (bhūtā sattā), the existence of existence itself is designated as having become manifest.
Everything is differentiated by means of another, but the self is not conceptualized as such;
therefore, the stability of mountains and so forth is differentiated by means of other forms.
Actions whose distinctions are well-known differ through their dissimilar constituent actions;
those whose constituent actions are similar are distinguished by their association [with other factors].
A collection of actions such as eating appears as if it were interrupted, or as if it had ceased, because of the activities occurring in the intervals between them. (Bhāṣya on Vākya III.9.82)
And even though it appears in a discrete form, that [action] does not cease because there is no interruption;
for every action whatsoever is perceived as intermingled with another.
Or rather, every action of the parts perceived during that interval is grasped as being subordinate to that [whole] because of its similarity, even though there is a distinction between them.
A thing may be either existent or non-existent; there is nothing whatsoever that is a third.
Therefore, apart from the past and the future, no middle exists.
The form of manifestation is not possible for a single entity because of the absence of differentiation;
therefore, whether it be existent or non-existent, how could a single thing possess a sequential form?
And because many [phonemes] do not persist [simultaneously], only one is perceived;
and in that case, recollection occurs in accordance with that perception. (3.9.87)
If one were to postulate the unity of everything, then that which has both existent and non-existent forms would be a single entity;
or else, the universal might be the form of cessation [itself], because of its cessation.
Or rather, that [entity] which is capable of producing an effect by its own nature would be grasped as such through its own essence; and that is what constitutes its "presentness" in this context.
That which consists of a continuous stream of activity, when internally restrained and concentrated in a single form, they call that "presentness."
The non-occurrence of an action is characterized by the absolute non-arising of that action;
and what has already occurred is not unarisen, nor will what is yet to be so.
Prior to the production of a contradictory action, or when the contradictory operation has ceased,
the object there is differentiated by the distinction of its limit.
When there is deviation [from the rule], the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the cause is not established;
by the sūtra "bhāvya āsīt," that [correctness] is taught for another time [the past].
If correctness belongs only to its own [proper] time, how can there be an application when the time differs?
Since they do not have that meaning, the state of being qualified [as correct] is not established on the basis of the sentence-meaning.
If a constituent part [of a word] were to signify that object, then there would be no perception of the future state [of what is currently present];
rather, only absolute pastness would be possible there.
Although the qualification of time was mentioned previously, nevertheless,
because it is more internal (antaraṅga) than the substratum, that [time] will be valid there as a qualifier.
That entity under discussion is indeed mixed;
for a purely eternal object, the state of being mixed is not possible.
When the time is pure, the explanation is successful; it does not succeed when mixed. That correctness [attained] at the wrong time is taught by the Sūtra.
Since the meaning expressed by the verbal form is that which is to be brought into being, it possesses primacy;
as a qualifier, it is established at that time through its implication by that [action].
Either it is an imitation of conviction, or it is simply the operation of the word itself;
this is superimposed upon a contradictory object, yet it is not contradicted by that [object].
The two notions of "past" and "future," without relinquishing their status as present, arrive at a state characterized by contradictory substrata.
In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that for the sake of grammatical operation (*kāryārtha*), a present time-period is designated as "future" with respect to a future object. *Vākyapadīya* 3.9.103.
In the case of "icchā cikīrṣati" (desire desires to act), [the desire] conforms to its own time;
however, when it occurs in the sense of the root-meaning, it does not conform to that time.
Because the expression of hope is dependent upon that which is being hoped for, there is a reversal [of the grammatical subject] in the case of hope;
the property of the speaker is attributed by words themselves to the meaning of the word.
