When the term "niṣpadi" (non-arising) occurs in reference to the combination of rice and water seeds,
it serves as a negation of future arising because it functions with respect to the constituent parts.
But when the form consists in the production of a fruit, the two [words] are in the past tense;
that form is conceptually constructed by superimposing it upon other properties.
When the operation of the signs has been employed for the sake of accomplishing the result,
that form which was superimposed there is perceived at that very time.
In the case of accomplishment, there is a certain limit, and a certain [limit] is intended to be expressed;
it is said that "the arising of the fruit" occurs due to the dependence upon the cause and its birth.
When a proof is intended that does not depend on external means of accomplishment,
it is designated as "established" because of the absence of any other means of accomplishment.
Therefore, through the distinction of limits (avadhi), the primary state of being past is established; likewise, the state of being future and existence depend upon the relation to causal properties.
For those who possess [the means of knowledge], that very existence is distinguished through the connection with the sense faculties;
for linguistic usage based on difference is indeed dependent upon another entity.
The existence of the mere object is grasped by the intellect;
however, the distinction arising from its specific determination is not intended to be expressed therein.

Or rather, through its connection with femininity and masculinity, nothing at all remains established in its own self; in that regard, another [quality] is spoken of as having been past or being future.
3.10: In the *Puruṣasamuddeśa*, the state of being the self (*pratyaktā*) and the state of being the other (*parabhāva*) are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the agent and the object respectively;
by virtue of a specific scriptural rule (*śruti*), the middle and the highest [voices] denote these two.
Whether real or unreal, consciousness is understood through these two;
however, the first person (the Puruṣa) does not exist within the portion of consciousness itself.
When the primary person (puruṣa) exists as consciousness through the functions of intellect (buddhi),
ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas), the utility of consciousness (caitanya) is not manifested by means of the objects of cognition.
Some maintain that the vocative is everywhere included within the middle [person];
likewise, they know that when used for addressing, the entire first person belongs to *yuṣmad*.
In the world, there is no such thing as an address [to someone] by means of an object that is to be enjoined, such as "O Indra-śatru, may you prosper" or "Become a king. (3.10.5)
Because the referent of *yuṣmad* is already established, its initial udātta accent is fixed;
however, this [accent] does not apply to a nominative-form *yuṣmad* if it follows another word that is not a *pada*.
The distinction between the subordinate and the primary, the reversal of [the status of] *puruṣa* and so forth,
and the different explanations in the treatise are not contradictory because of its eternality.
The meanings [of words] would correspond to their definitions provided that the treatise were prescriptive;
however, the exposition proceeds by relying upon some commonality [among them]. (3.10.8)
Just as in the case of the words "yo 'śve" and "yaḥ pīṭhe," where the two entities— the horse and the seat—
serve as mere indicators (upalakṣaṇa), so too is the grammatical instruction (anuśāsana) applied to meanings.
3.11: *Saṃkhyāsamuddeśa*.
A thing possessing number (*saṃkhyāvan*) is an entity that exists as a real being (*sattvabhūta*), and it is all such things that are denoted [by words].
For in the world, the distinction between difference and non-difference is based upon number.
That property is either distinct from them or is their very self;
it is designated as "number" by relying on its status as the cause of differentiation.
Inhering in the objects to be delimited, it resides elsewhere;
it brings about the distinction of number for entities as well as for itself.
Just as the same word applies equally to priority and posteriority despite their difference,
so too does the status of being denotable by a numeral apply to a quality, which is the cause of differentiation.
Just as the state of independence in that which is dependent is a property of another [category],
so too the state of being divisible in that which is indivisible is a property of substance [imposed] upon a quality.
Having extracted that [meaning] by means of his own intellect, the world also, relying upon tradition (āgama),
explains it through one property for the sake of comprehension, even when it differs from its own property.
A word that denotes the reality of the assistance rendered by others independently is, from its own nature, remote from all other word-meanings. (Brahma-vākya 3.11.7)
Just as no object whatsoever appears to a cognition that lacks an objective domain,
so too no entity whatsoever is perceived when it is not associated [with a cognition].
But that which is declared according to specific distinctions is followed even by the world;
such linguistic usage, resembling the sacred scriptures, is described as being based on tradition.
When these [words] are thus established in the intellect, the superimposition [of one upon another] is not difficult to achieve;
for in this case, the existence or non-existence of the property of another is not the determining factor.
Generality is postulated in generalities, particularity in particulars, number in numbers, and gender in genders; thus it is conceived.
Therefore, the proponents of inherence (saṃsargavādins) maintain that number is a quality residing in a substance,
which effects both distinction and non-distinction among things that are themselves beyond distinction and non-distinction.

That by which the self of other selves appears as if it were of that same form, despite being of a different form due to association—that is "conformity with the cause" (*nimittasarūpatā*). (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 3.11.13)
Just as causal efficiency (arthakriyā) occurs even when elements are combined yet remain indivisible,
so too is it perceived in all the constituent measures (mātrās), such as the *sattva* and the others.
Unity is the source of duality and the rest, for all distinctions are preceded by it;
without that, there is no possibility of other numbers.
When there is oneness accompanied by cognition, that [oneness] is the cause for the production of duality;
or rather, it is perceived as having been produced from two unities.
Whether it be a collection of unities, or two things considered separately while being mutually dependent,
if there is duality within that unity, then the dual number would apply to those two.
Even a single entity may be conceived as having a division due to the distinction of its qualities;
for the distinction between the substratum and the superstratum is based upon that very [distinction of qualities].
The collection (*saṅgha*) that consists of the enumeration of countable things is called "number" (*saṃkhyā*).
Among twenty and so forth, it is the differentiator of another collection of substances.
The number twenty-one, which consists of two similar numbers,
arises through the non-repetition of a single cognition,
just as there is a conceptual construction of two parts.
Because it is a collection of innumerable [parts], the function of number is prescribed;
however, if it were merely a "mass" (*samūha*), that function would not exist, as in the case of a collection of one's own limbs and so forth.
That number which operates within numbers that depend on intervening calculable units—
such as the number of repetitions in a group— they know to be a number of that kind.
There is no possibility of "two" or "ten" existing either in the number itself or in the thing numbered;
because there is no differentiation in the number, and because of contradiction, it cannot reside in its substratum.
The two groups of ten are counted by the number "twenty" (dvidaśa),
or rather, when the object to be counted has that form, the repetition [of the unit] is reckoned.
Just as it is said that "number" is not a number but merely a designation, so too form is not form; for that is merely a designation applied to white and other such qualities.
But because of its connection with the universal *saṃkhyāna*, it is called "number" (*saṃkhyā*);
and because of its connection with the universal *rūpatva*, it is traditionally known as "form" (*rūpa*) in the case of color.
In the expression "the single cause" (*nimittam ekam*), the case-ending does not denote the [cause] itself;
rather, the case-ending functions with respect to the oneness that belongs to that [cause].
Accumulation is observed in a single thing, and likewise a collection in two;
therefore, number is a distinct differentiator that exists apart from [other] causes.
Moreover, even that single unity is not expressed by that word without the hearing of a case-ending;
rather, it is expressed by that word together with the case-ending.
If positive and negative concomitance were to exist through another word,
then in the absence of that [other word], the meaning of the base would not be postulated.
In the expression "one-ness" (*ekatva*) and "one" (*eka*), [the former] is a qualifier of the pure substance (*śuddhadravya*);
however, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), which possesses qualities, is differentiated by the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*).
Because of the instruction "in the case of two and one," it is possible [for the word *eka*] even in the sense of mere number;
however, its status as having a numerable object (*saṃkhyeya*) is stated on account of the well-known usage of "one" and so forth.

3.12: On the Designation of Voice (Upagraha). Wherever a distinction of meaning is perceived between the middle voice (ātmanepada) and other substitutes for the L-suffixes, they consider that to be "voice" (upagraha).
In some cases this [word] is the means of accomplishment itself; in other cases it is a qualifier of that [means].
In those instances, the object (*karman*) and so forth are the means of accomplishment, while the explicit word is the qualifier.
Action varies according to the distinction of its objects, such as livelihood and so forth;
that differentiation of action is also regulated within sentences by means of the substitutes for *l* (the verbal suffixes).
The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) and its specific qualification have been stated; in some cases, the voice (upagraha) [is also significant].
The meaning of the root may consist of "hinting" (gandhana) and so forth, while the reciprocal action (vyatihāra) serves as a further qualification.

Regarding the engagement in action, some have stated that the status of being for one's own sake or for the sake of another in verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) is based solely on the speaker’s intention, whether such [self-interest or other-interest] actually exists or not.

For some [grammarians], the ātmanepada ending is optionally used along with the causative suffix (ṇic) when the intention refers to the agent; for others, the base form itself has that meaning. (BVaky_3.12.6)
One buys (*krīṇīṣva*), one sows (*vapate*), one wears (*dhatte*), one piles up (*cinoti*) and also one piles up (*cinute*);
in these cases, the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) is expressed through the employment of a competent agent (*āptaprayoga*).
In some cases, the meaning of cooking and so forth is understood as the preparation [of food];
likewise, other actions such as placing [the pot on the fire] are also caused by that [preparation].
In the Sūtra, the state of being for the benefit of the agent (*kartṛabhiprāyatā*) is an indicator of a specific type of action;
for that action which is of such a nature is one by which the agent thereof partakes of the fruit.
Just as time is perceived through the non-appearance of stars and other such signs,
so too is the distinction between actions indicated by the specific results they produce.
In the case of words expressing specific actions, the expressive power [of the suffix] is obstructed;
however, for some others, the *ñit* suffixes are likewise marked with the *svarita* accent.
Furthermore, once the meaning has been established, the suffix is attached for the sake of recollection;
moreover, even among words with identical meanings, it is not necessarily the case that they all possess the same grammatical property.
Even though the objects of the roots *dṛś* (to see) and *īkṣ* (to look) are similar, there is no identity between them when preceded by *pra*;
because they take on the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*), they do not have the same meaning as *pac* and other such roots.

Since the root *kṛ*, when functioning in the sense of "protecting" (*umbhi*), possesses a distinct property, it necessarily adopts the meaning of the causative (*ṇyartha*); therefore, the powers of words are restricted.
For thus, when the *ātmanepada* affix follows the verb *kṛ* used in the sense of "employing" (*anuprayoga*),
the rule for the *svarita* accent presents itself upon the application of the term "as before" (*pūrvavat*).

Even though the action expressed by a verb is a single entity, it is differentiated by the number residing in its substratum— the means of accomplishment (sādhana)— but the distinction known as gender, which depends upon that [substratum], is not differentiated there.
Therefore, even though the object exists, the expressive power of a certain word is obstructed; however, this very rule is explained in the grammatical treatise.
That purpose for the sake of whose accomplishment actions such as cooking are undertaken is their primary fruit; acquisition and the like are not the motive.
But where both master and servant undertake an action together,
there the verbal root does not function with respect to two simultaneous distinct properties.
Where the root *pac* has the sense of "counteracting" (*pratividhāna*), there the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs;
elsewhere, when it denotes "preparation" (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used.
And due to the proximity of the agent who performs the arrangement, the property [of being a servant] is attached to the servant,
just as the state of being a *plakṣa* tree is attributed to a *nyagrodha* tree due to its proximity to the word *plakṣa*.
And just as the designation "sacrificial cake" (puroḍāśa) applies to parched grains and so forth by virtue of their established connection with it, so too,
through association with those who possess umbrellas, the term "umbrella-bearer" (chattrin) becomes a designation for [the entire group].
That is to say, the mutual subservience that is understood [from the context] is not intended to be expressed;
thus, this is described by some here as the domain of the *śeṣa* (the residual relation).
Now, as for the opponent who says that the [agent] who ploughs with five ploughs is not cited in the Bhāṣya, why is the ātmanepada ending applicable there?
If the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) were to be assumed for that meaning because it is already well-known,
then that [rule] which allows for an option regarding what has been obtained would not exist as a sublater of the *svarita* accentuation.
However, when the purpose is already established as pure, some maintain that agriculture is intended here;
in that case, since the sacrifice would possess those [agricultural] properties, the middle voice (ātmanepada) would not occur.

But here, this distinction of meaning is understood through the secondary word (*upapada*); since an option (*vibhāṣā*) is prescribed for what is already established, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not apply here.
3.13: In the section on gender (liṅgasamuddeśa): Gender is either the connection with breasts, hair, and so forth, or it is specific breasts and such;
it is a genus characterized by those secondary marks, as well as the states of qualities and the qualities themselves. (Brahmanavākyapadīya 3.13.1)

"The essence of the object produced by the word," "the refinement of the word," and so forth—seven such conceptual constructions have been shown by those who know the true nature of logical marks (*liṅga*) regarding logical marks. (BhV 3.13.2)
And seven types of conceptualization based on grasping have been described for the gender markers—
those which are established in words through both conceptual construction and formal application.
These three types of birth exist for some beings as mutually compatible,
being unopposed by other incompatible species such as those of cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
The cognition "this is a female" occurs with respect to both a female elephant and a mare;
therefore, they maintain that this [cognition] refers to a genus (*jāti*) which inheres in substances and other categories.
When the extraction of the dependent nature is intended,
that grammatical refinement of words is based solely upon words themselves.

The establishment of femininity and so forth also occurs even in grammatical markers (liṅga) whose forms are constructed by the intellect; for that [establishment] is designated by means of those markers.
Just as an appearance of water arises in mirages due to a seed that conforms to the perception of water, even though no water exists there.

In the same way, in the world, distinctions among stars and other such objects are established on the basis of reasons that cannot be verbally designated, just as they are established through primary indicative marks.

Since breasts and other such features are seen in manifest forms among manifest individuals, a genus (*jāti*) is not postulated for that which is unmanifest due to the non-manifestation of its gender-markers (*liṅga*).
For one who asserts existence and yet desires that it be always unperceived,
there can be no certainty regarding its non-existence when it is absolutely unperceived.
And a word that has not been preceded by perception is not sufficient for inference;
for once perception is established, what would be the purpose of employing inference?
Manifestation, disappearance, and persistence—
these imperishable attributes are observed as the defining characteristics (liṅga) in all embodied forms.
In each and every quality, such as sound and the rest, which constitute the essence of all forms,
those three attributes— sattva and the others— are present everywhere in a state of inherence.
And of form and its constituent parts, such as white and so forth, some portion perishes at every moment while some other portion somehow increases.
And their instability, like that of boiling water,
has been described repeatedly in the Bhāṣya itself regarding all entities.
The uniformity or the equilibrium of the process of manifestation is called "stability" (sthiti);
it persists through the process of appearance and disappearance.
Or rather, it is considered that the state of being a basis for the cognition "these are qualities" (guṇāḥ) constitutes their stability;
and because of this stability, all gendered forms are said to possess the status of pronouns (sarvanāman).
When all possible genders are present, the operation of grammatical refinement (saṃskāra) is desired in some cases to depend upon a restriction based on the speaker's intention.
When several causes are present, only one among them functions as the motivator;
just as there is a restriction regarding genders for words such as *takṣan* and others.
The learned ones, who perceive the true nature of reality, are established in the meanings of words;
whatever serves as an indicator (liṅga) that leads toward dharma, they declare that to be [the meaning].
Just as words are correct in different senses due to a difference in accent,
so too is correctness understood from a perfected word through a difference in gender.
A treatise is undertaken where both application and non-application are observed in the world; it is not undertaken where there is no such application or its opposite.

Due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi), a certain quality-attribute (guṇadharma) serves as the cause for correctness (sādhutva) among objects; thus, both the intention to speak (vivakṣā) and the established rule are determined.
In the Himalayan forest, which is characterized by its vastness, the state of being female is established;
likewise, there is the capacity for procreation in a hut distinguished by the limiting condition of its small size.
For other words whose meanings are distinct, [grammatical devices] have been presented as means for comprehension by determining them as if they were one, for the sake of brevity.
The arising of others is "production" (prasava), and their destruction is "dissolution" (saṃstyāna);
however, the very nature of entities is designated as "stability" (sthiti).
For some, the perceived sign (nimitta) remains constant like caste and so forth;
however, for others, it is merely a mental construction based on the phonetic refinement of the word, just as it is perceived.
Just as even when unity is well-established,
words used by those who are intent upon multiplicity seem to produce multiplicity, such is the case with gender as well.

"This is that," or "This is this"— such [cognition] is described by some as occurring everywhere with respect to an object, being merely a mental construction (*saṃskāra*) based on words, arising from the perception of a sign (*nimitta*).
A cause does not necessarily function as an object;
rather, the sense organs and so forth are accepted as the causes of differentiation according to how they are observed.

3.14: Vṛttisamuddeśa. However, a word whose meaning is already complete is joined with [terms expressing] contempt, praise, or intensity, because all [meanings] such as its own primary sense (svārtha) and so forth are causes for contempt and the like. (BVaky_3.14.1)
The word *kutsita* (despised) functions to express the contempt directed toward Devadatta and others;
but what [additional] meaning is prescribed for that contempt which itself resides in the despised object?
The word *prakṛṣṭa* denotes the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of [qualities] such as white;
however, when there is an excellence of that which is already excellent, suffixes such as *tarap* are prescribed.

Or, [if it were] contemptible by virtue of being contemptible, or even if it were not properly contemptible—by what could the meaning be understood as qualified when it is already expressed by its own word? (3.14.4)
And no contemporary contempt is perceived, because there is no distinction [between the two states];
that which is honored is treated as contemptible, and that which is praised is treated as contemptible.
The relationship of qualifier and qualified arises between two words;
it is not the case that the meaning of the nominal stem itself is differentiated therein.

That which is not yet known is the qualificand (viśeṣya), while that which is already known is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). All auxiliary elements are subordinate because they exist for the sake of another.
Due to the rule regarding the difference in case endings between words denoting a quality and its possessor,
the well-known grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) occurs only between two words denoting substances.
The word "black" is applied to a substance whose genus is not yet known;
likewise, the word "sesame" is employed for that whose quality is not yet known.
Because universals have no connection [with one another], those two [universals] reside in the particular;
yet, because their forms are undifferentiated, they are unable to manifest that particular.
When those two very same [words] are presented separately,
they remove doubt by effecting, as it were, a delimitation.
The substance-soul is apprehended separately due to the distinction of its association with qualities;
and due to the distinction of its connection with universals, it is perceived as if it were a second entity.

Due to its connection with various causes (nimitta), that which possesses a form similar to those causes allows even a single entity to be conceived as manifold through the differentiation of its forms.
The third state, however, is that of the substance, in which the two [aspects] are conjoined;
due to the distinction between those two states, it is assigned the status of being their substratum.
By means of the intellect, the one is divided, and the divided attains unity;
through the intellect, the states [of objects] are distinguished, for it is the intellect that determines the object.

In a single entity, a conceptualization of multiplicity occurs through the process of designation, as if it possessed distinct designations; by means of that [conceptualization], the nature of the object, though existing as a unity, is designated as if it were divided.
When stones and other such objects, which have been perceived through a particular action, are perceived again and again,
one perception is designated by means of another perception.
Having conceived the manifold nature of verbal roots through the diversity of their applications,
the state of having a single vowel (ekāctva) is sometimes predicated by resorting to both difference and non-difference.
Through positive and negative concomitance, it is postulated as being meaningful;
though it is one, it is metaphorically designated as a "phoneme" (varṇa) due to its departure from the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu).

Therefore, these three, which are substantial in nature, are established as distinct within the intellect by way of the relationship between substratum and superstratum; this is the tradition handed down from our predecessors.

And some maintain that there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between two words, as well as the relation of qualifier and qualified, and even the relation of name and named. (Brahma-vākya 3.14.21)
For some, the application of a word denoting a substance is held to occur when both genus and quality are inherent in the same object, as in the case of "black sesame seeds. (Vākya-kāṇḍa 3.14.22)
But the substratum of color, taste, and so forth is not denoted [by the word];
for, without the denotation of the substance, those [qualities] would exist only in a state of mutual conjunction (dvandva).
A word denoting a substance, such as "black" (*kṛṣṇa*), proceeds [to apply] when there is expectancy;
because it conforms to its cause, that [expectancy] does not exist in the case of sesame seeds and the like.
Thus, when a substance possessing birth is proximate to an action, the substance—
characterized by the property of a quality and permeated by that quality— is capable of differentiation.
Some maintain that in verbal derivations (vṛtti), words denote only the quality [of the action],
because of their connection with [the agent] in cases such as "ajā" and "aśva," just as conventional meanings [denote only the quality] in the case of conventional terms.
Or rather, when the word *tila* has already been taken [as the prior member], the possessive suffix *matup* is desired in that very context;
and since that property (*dharma*) is a quality (*guṇa*) within compounds, it is therefore the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

"In a compound consisting of 'sharp' (*paṭu*) and 'soft' (*mṛdu*), although there is a single unified meaning, the substrata prior to the formation of the compound are distinct, and that distinction is what is apprehended."
When a single cognition arises as if woven together by two distinct [parts],
and there is a desire to express them simultaneously, that is what is called the co-occurrence (*dvandva*) and the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*).
Mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga), however, denotes a collection of distinct things;
this collection is completed in each of the members of the collection.
Just as a collection of activities, such as placing [the pot] on the stove and so forth,
applies to each individual action like a genus, so too does it apply to the words in a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
In this regard, *śauṇḍa*, *ardharca*, *puroḍāśa*, and *chattrin* are examples;
as are [the names] "those Viṣṇumitras" when applied to distinct companions. (32)
Likewise, there is the denotation of a different meaning for those [words] that reside in different meanings;
and by means of those two [criteria], another word is likewise one that has multiple meanings.
Furthermore, because it belongs to a different aggregate [of sounds], such a meaning is not worldly;
nor is it seen to be the meaning of the treatise, according to the methods of positive and negative concomitance.
It is difficult and hard to establish; therefore, it has been cited even in the Bhāṣya.
However, that simultaneous denotation is resorted to for the sake of linguistic usage.
Having approached the aggregate, a word is applied to it;
when explained through its divisions, that [word] is then said to have two meanings.
Certain properties are restricted to the sentence, and likewise some to the two [constituents] in a compound;
however, these are described without distinction as belonging solely to the capacity (*sāmarthya*) itself.

Because they function as qualifiers in a compound, words such as *śyāma* (dark) are cited as expressing a general property (*sāmānya*) when used in comparisons, compounds, and the like, even though they denote a particular (*viśeṣa*). 38. *Brahmanavākya*, 3.14.38.
The function [of a compound] that occurs when another word is the referent is impossible in sentences;
furthermore, for words in a copulative (dvandva) compound, there is no function when there is a distinction in meaning.
If there were a difference [between the word and its meaning], it would be impossible for words such as *nir* to have meanings such as "transcending" (*krānta*);
furthermore, [words] like *gaura-khara* could not denote a genus (*jāti*) prior to their application [to individuals]. (3.14.40)
Since there is no mention of [the suffix yaṅ] in the context of play or livelihood,
it is not appropriate to include the word "nitya" (constant), just as in the case of the rule for the formation of the intensive (yaṅ) after the root *kuṭil* (to be crooked).
Since dependence alone persists in cases such as selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) and the like,
there is therefore no purpose for the prohibitions against compound formation.
The demonstration of difference and non-difference is effected through injunctions and prohibitions,
just as in the case of a dual compound functioning as a singular, or in the teaching on the collective function of a group.
Although capacity is stated without distinction, it is differentiated by competent speakers according to worldly convention regarding the occurrence or non-occurrence [of a word's application].
Because the meaning has ceased [to be expressed separately], elision (*luk*) and the like are not contradicted;
therefore, the designation "compound" (*samāsa*) is prescribed only when there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).
And some maintain that the optionality [of the rule] is restricted to the general case;
likewise, a sentence is taught for the state of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), while a compound is taught for other cases.
Even when the identity [of the king and others] is accepted because their phonetic form is identical,
the requirement for a qualifier in the usage [of the word] ceases, because it is already expressive [of that meaning].
Every relative term is always employed with dependence [on its correlate];
that dependence, as if it were its own meaning, is not lost even when the term is used in a compound (vṛtti).
Those things which have a connection with a whole, such as a teacher’s family and so forth,
are also joined with that [whole] by means of their parts being touched.
And for the sake of practice, there are various means for those who are ignorant;
because they are different words, there is an absolute difference between sentences and compounds.

Since [the term] *yukta* and others are not observed in compounds such as *goratha* (ox-cart) both when they are uncompounded and when they are compounded, the treatise has not effected their exclusion or inclusion by means of a formal rule.

Because it is a distinct word, *yukta* and so forth are employed in certain sentences; likewise, the word *gata* is used in compounds such as *praparṇa* and *prapalāśa*. (Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 3.14.52)

Some maintain that the relationship of qualifier and qualified, as well as a single substratum, is accepted for both the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*), because of the vision of reality regarding the means [of expression]. (BVaky_3.14.53)
Just as a word such as "tree" is established in reference to a qualified object,
so too a term like "blue lotus" functions even without [the presence of] its two constituent parts.

Furthermore, for those such as the *śrotriya* and the *kṣatriya*, there is no cognition of difference in the world as there is for the Vāsiṣṭhas and Gārgyas, because they lack a common connection with an identical form.

Just as in the case of the *saptaparṇa* tree and others, no distinction exists anywhere within a compound; yet, the division between conventional and non-conventional usage is made for the sake of comprehension.
That designation which has a general substratum and that which has a specific object—
due to the inclusion of the term "mostly" (bahula), there is no application of both of these.
If a compound were to occur within a part, such as in *susūkṣma-jaṭa-keśa-* and the like,
then the accent of the member would be the sublater there, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*).
Furthermore, when a whole is functioning [as a single unit], its parts are not expressed as distinct;
for the scope of analytical distinction (*vibhāṣā*) is necessarily restricted to differentiation alone.
And since that [ultimate reality] is not an object for this [speech], there is no lack of fulfillment of its purpose;
for, in the process of non-differentiation, all distinctions are entirely eliminated.
In this way, there would be no distinction between the three words [in the compound] such as *mahā-kaṣṭa-śrita*;
for in a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), the substitution of *āt* for the final vowel of a constituent member is not prohibited.
But once the *mahāraṇya* [pause] has passed, the accent becomes distinct from the three-pada [rule];
for in that case, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the accent of the constituent part (*avayavasvara*) acts as a sublater.
Because that which remains after [the application of] *sati* is stronger, there is indeed the accentuation of the *thā-thādi* group;
therefore, in a two-word compound, the triad is not compounded simultaneously.
For those [words] whose non-qualification arises from their consisting in the pursuit of another's meaning,
even the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not possible for them.

Even when a distinction is heard, whether in the primary elements or the subordinate qualities, it exists because of the difference in words; however, in a sentence, such a distinction never exists in its operation.
Even when the connection with a specific action has been exhausted by means of the past tense suffixes (*kṛt*) and so forth,
another word formed with *kṛta* is employed that is independent of such specificity.
Only when it is intransitive does that form ending in *kta* denote the abstract state (*bhāva*);
from that, there occurs a connection with objects through an agent who possesses the action.

Just as an action, though devoid of physical form and existing in its prior state, becomes connected with objects such as villages through verbal operations like "going," so too does it abide in expressions such as *kṛtapūrvī* ("one who has previously done").
Roots such as *muṇḍi* and *sūtri*, though they appear as if followed by unreal parts,
are divided and conceived as having distinct natures, like the words *kuṭṭi* and *carci*.
In those who desire a son, no son actually exists; rather, there is such a specific desire that, even without following from the existence of a son, it is fixed upon the son.

Just as the act of supporting (dhāri) exists without the vital breaths (prāṇa), yet when one is alive, it has the function of the vital breaths; so too, in this case, there is neither the act of supporting nor the vital breaths, but rather "living" (jīvati) is a distinct action.
Likewise, in the *Putrīyā* [section], there is a different procedure by the two sons of Vineśin;
however, the various alternative explanations (*anvākhyāna*) present similar means of demonstration.

And because it is implied by the verbal suffix (*ākṣepāt*), even though the object of the desiderative suffix (*icchāka*) exists as something present in another context, it is employed only within the sentence itself. (3.14.73)

A word that is already established as expressing contempt for an action is not used with the *yaṅ* affix when there is repetition, because its form remains identical [to the base]. (Bhāṣyavākya 3.14.74)
Just as words are analyzed as if divided into conceptual parts, so too should they be explained; the grammatical treatise stands at a great distance from this [ultimate reality].
Having perceived some semblance of meaning, one merely imagines a word within a sentence,
a verbal root within a word, and a stem-portion within a root, just as one might imagine a "shaven-headed" person (muṇḍin) [where there is only hair].
One should not consider as real the non-separation from correctness, the unstable proficiency [in it], or the means for the various modes of understanding. (3.14.77)
Just as one says "Devadatta throws" (*ḍitthe davati*) or "the cook cooks" (*pācake pacati*), so too both *ḍayati* ("he flies") and *pacati* ("he cooks") are non-ordinary (alaukika) expressions.
The base and the suffix are to be inferred from the word, and likewise the word from them;
however, the authoritative scripture (śāstra) does not concern itself with those [elements] such as the indicatory letters (anubandha) and accents, which are taught by the learned.
But the perspective of the scripture is applicable even when the attainment of the scripture is merely uncertain; for those who do not see the scripture as their eye, there is transgression.
Furthermore, because it expresses a different meaning, the sequence [of words] does not differ in any way in cases such as *rājadanta*, *āhitāgni*, and *rājāśva*. (3.14.81)

Even without the application of suffixes, those [names] such as *Garga* and others which denote a distinct meaning [of a lineage] are understood to be grammatically correct through the elision (*luk*) [of the patronymic suffix].

If words such as *bhṛgu* were employed [to denote a descendant] without a suffix, on the basis of a connection expressed as "this is he," there would be no restriction regarding the offspring. (Pāṇini-vākya 3.1.14.83)
In the connection expressed as "this is that," unless there are gender markers or secondary characteristics,
the specific class [of the object]— such as a *praṣṭha* (a draft-ox)— is not necessarily perceived.

When a specific relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge is thus accepted, then measures such as the *prastha* would likewise be incorrect in the absence of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

Depending on the distinction of connection, that [word] may be either a derivative (taddhita) or a sentence, as it is optionally prescribed; furthermore, in that case, when there is an excess of measure, the nominative case is taught.
If it is argued that [the suffix] is correct as something distinct [from the base], then that very same example holds;
for that which has accepted an addition is logically consistent with all case-endings.
In words such as *śukla* ("white"), there is the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, because a distinction [between the quality and the qualified] is observed;
they are considered correct forms for the purpose of excluding what is incorrect, just like the *bidādi* group.

Some maintain that when a qualifier [is applied] to the qualified object, and there is an intensification of its state, and then [that qualifier] is withdrawn again, [the word] functions [in this manner].
The prior cognition of the signifier (nimitta) has not yet reached the signified (nimittin);
nor does the intellect possess the same form as the signifier when directed toward the signified.
There is no contact with memory even from cognition accompanied by mental impressions;
nor would there be a graspable object remaining in that state during the operation of its causes.
And since [the object] exists within the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), the postulation of an external object is futile;
therefore, either it does not assist [the cognition], or the object of apprehension does not exist in that manner.
The intellect functions as if woven together with objects that are intermingled;
commentators, however, explain those objects by dividing them according to their distinctions.
And although the self is undivided, those who rely on another cognition imagine,
as it were, a division between the qualifier and the qualified.

And those who maintain a conduct devised for the sake of the ignorant say that the nature of dharma consists in the renunciation [of one's own interest] and the excellence [of another's] when speaking for the sake of others.
That meaning is understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or its opposite is excluded;
they say that in such cases, the word has two meanings or even another meaning, and it is subordinate (*upasarjana*).
The diversity [of means] is merely a matter of expedient; the aggregate, however, is truly one.
Or rather, the conceptualization of distinction and conjunction arises through the intensification of mental constructions.

Thus, for the sake of the instruction of the ignorant, various means of awakening have been formulated; these methods are not fixed among persons, as they proceed according to their specific circumstances.
Whether expressed verbally or indicated by the case-endings of numerals,
when a word functions with reference to a constituent part possessing that form, the distinction of number ceases.
Or rather, another number, namely non-dual unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*), arises there;
that which consists of the nature of their conjunction is called "undivided" (*avibhakta*). (Brahma-vākya 3.14.100)
Just as all the potencies of medicinal herbs, when placed in honey,
exist without distinction, they know that state to be such a number.
Alternatively, by abandoning the particulars, that [universal] which consists of number is of such a nature;
it functions through the exclusion of particulars by means of the operation of the generic element.

Just as one is perceived as "possessing form" by means of a form whose specific qualities have not been grasped, yet the distinct forms such as white and so forth are not apprehended; [so it is with the universal]. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttika 3.14.103)
When the immersion into the form of differentiation is likewise not intended to be expressed,
some particular aspect is manifested and is grasped as a constituent part (*aṅga*) in the treatise.
At that time, that part [of the object] is perceived in the form of a general number;
for while an object possesses multiple powers, it is apprehended by words whose powers are restricted.
That which constitutes the nature of indeclinables and that which is the sequence of those possessing distinctions—
the intermediate state between these two is worthy of being designated as non-distinct.
And there is the formation of a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) with *aluk*; when that [formation] exists, the elision (*śiṣyate*) does not occur.
Furthermore, that property belongs to words such as *goṣucara* and others in other grammatical rules.
Because the dual number does not exist in the genus (*jāti*), it is not found in its derivatives; however, when the rule is rejected, words such as *goṣucara* apply to the substance (*dravya*).
Because difference exists by virtue of its substratum, there is a concomitance with all differences;
thus, even the position that [a word] denotes a substance does not hold when referring to a genus.
In this way, the movement of all substances [is explained], and the "single remainder" (ekaśeṣa) is not stated;
otherwise, if the Sūtra were rejected, there would be a movement of distinct substances.
In the *vṛtti*, the treatment as if [the compound] were a single word (*yuktavadbhāva*) is prescribed for [words like] *varaṇa* and so on;
however, in the case of the number one denoting non-difference, the form *godau* is not established therein.
Prior to the formation of a compound, when there is the treatment as a single unit (*yuktavadbhāva*), the genitive case would be based on a distinction [between the members];
however, in the compound, because specific numbers are abandoned, that distinction ceases to exist.
While numbers already exist, some recognize another number called "non-difference" (abhedākhya), which is inclusive; and that [number] arises in the case of a compound (vṛtti).

In some cases, the Self undergoes activity through its own parts known as "divisions" (bhedas); in other cases, it becomes the instrumental cause for these divisions while remaining independent of them.

The distinction in the function of number is clearly established from this very fact: that [the word] *godau* is seen to mean "the husband of a slave-girl" (*dāsyāḥ patiḥ*) as well as "two cows. (Vākya-kāṇḍa 3.14.115)

And in cases such as "two sons," the external distinction expressed by the dual case-ending ceases because it refers to its own [grammatical] meaning; however, the cause [of that distinction] remains.
In a collective [referent] where duality is subordinate, the word *dvi* occurs there;
because of the connection "this is that," such is not the case for the word *ubha*.
In that context, both [terms] are used in their technical application (*vṛtti*) with the same meaning; for that very purpose, the word "always" (*nitya*) is also stated in the *sūtra*.
Furthermore, because they do not have another as their purpose, no differentiation arises;
therefore, the term "both" (ubhe) is employed in its own sense to function with respect to the distinction.
Even in the view that [the word] denotes the state of being female (*strītva*), there is a reversal of the subordinate status;
because it is not for the sake of another by its very nature, the distinction therein is not lost.

Therefore, other than in the case of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, [the elision] is observed elsewhere; however, setting aside the suffix *tayap*, it does not occur again when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
The designation *pragṛhya* would not apply to the suffix *prāpti* due to the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*;
for there is no compound [of *kumārī*] with *agāra* in any other grammatical form.
The optional application of *luṅ* (the aorist suffix) for the two words beginning with *yañ* is not possible;
furthermore, the forms *yauṣmākaḥ* and *tāvakaḥ* are not established because there is no distinction [between them].
A distinction is observed between "Gārgyatarā" and "Gargatarā";
likewise, the designations "your father" and "my father" are established according to their respective locations.

The number that exists as an inherent attribute (upādhi) residing in the primordial material cause (prakṛti) is manifested either by substitutes (ādeśa), by technical names (saṃjñā), or even without case-endings (vibhakti).
In the case of [weights like] *śaurpika* and [measures like] *māsaja*, the measurement exists by its own nature;
it functions through differentiation by relying upon a number that serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
Even when [a cow] has been purchased, no determination of age is perceived;
since that [determination] is desired only through non-difference [from the object], the measure of the owner in that case is useless.
Because a word denoting what is divided expresses non-difference, the suffix *śas* is prescribed after words such as *prastha*;
however, because they possess that same property [of being a measure] and thus imply non-difference, it is not seen after words such as *ghaṭa*.
Where a word is heard, there its referent is distinguished;
when a word ceases [to apply], its referent does not exist.

An effect is that which rests upon existence; according to the treatise, its non-occurrence is non-perception. That which is seen absolutely not to exist in a sentence [is understood to have] its absence in the individual words.

The non-perception of what is expected is traditionally held to be for the purpose of distinguishing the object of the notion; however, the word that is actually being heard is perceived as qualified.

Where either the absence of a suffix (*luk*) or a suffix possessing a specific phonetic form (*rūpavān*) is prescribed, an ungrammatical form (*asādhu*) results there due to the deviation of the cause (*nimitta*). (Bṛhad-vākya 3.14.132)
The difference between the sentence and its constituent parts has been explained as either a distinction in form or a distinction in number;
however, such a distinction does not necessarily exist in every single case.

And because it is the cause of differentiation, the primary element [the universal] is not qualified by the gender, as is the case with "deer's milk" and the like; that same sequence does not apply in the case of "Gārgīputra."
Since non-difference [of the universal] would entail the application of gender and number— as in "the white cloths" (*śuklaṃ paṭāḥ*)—
this treatise has been commenced for the sake of establishing [the correct usage of] gender and number.
That quality which assumes a subordinate status for the sake of another within its various functions is designated as a *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier) in the Sūtra.
Even though specific distinctions are heard in sentences because they consist of different words,
the function [of the sentence] does not exist in those [words], because the form of the function is non-different.
Since the refinement of sound (*śabda-saṃskāra*) has as its object the universal (*sāmānya*) that is derived from form (*rūpa*),
it follows that the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the verbal expression (*vacana*) must likewise have that [universal] as their basis.
Then, that word which denotes the substance is connected with both the gender and the number; in that case, there would be a distinct auditory perception for those two.
By the statement that the external [word] is to be understood as the future tense, the gender and number of the substrata of the qualities are established by the rule.
Moreover, because the specific property (*viśeṣa*) is not perceived due to the non-difference of form even when there is a specific function,
no differentiating effect is postulated here on that account.
The universal is indeed the particular, since it is distinguished from the particular;
for non-difference among particulars, when relied upon, brings about exclusion.
Whatever is relied upon serves to exclude its opposite;
however, the distinction between difference and non-difference cannot be determined with respect to a universal.
And since the abstraction (*apoddhāra*) is a universal (*sāmānya*), that [universal], being the benefactor,
is therefore grasped by its own property as existing solely in the state of the cause (*nimitta*).
Because their true nature has not been determined, it is only the particularities that are conceptualized;
they are designated by means of signs, though they are not distinguished by names denoting universals.
But when gender and number are designated by their own inherent nature,
then grammatical correctness is established only in the actual usage within the sentence.
In that regard, the application of qualities with their substrata is indefinite;
whereas that which is a universal is absolutely established in that very [substratum].
The cowness of a *śābaleya* cow is not designated as "cow";
rather, the whiteness of a *bāhuleya* cow is designated as "white."
And if there were indeed a distinction [between the quality and the possessor], then the suffix *matup* would be heard;
therefore, its elision is prescribed, and that suffix does not exist after words such as *rasa*.
Because it functions through the non-difference of form due to the relation "this is that," its elision does not occur in the case of taste and so forth, as it does with [qualities] such as white.
In some cases, such as with the word *mañca*, the imposition [of a property] occurs through gender and number;
however, this [imposition] does not exist in the case of a *prastha* and the like when there is the relation of identity expressed as "this is that."

The gender-mark (liṅga) is abandoned when the gender is set aside; the rule (sūtra) teaches the suffix (pratyaya). This occurs because of the connection "this is that" in the case of a masculine word denoting a female.
According to the established rule of the grammatical treatise, that which is supported [the qualified] is designated by the gender and number of its substratum (āśraya),
because qualifiers do not possess their own genus.

Because they conform to their respective signs, those properties that exist in the causes of differentiation are understood not to exist even in the substratum; thus, the notion [of their presence there] is set aside.
And it is stated in the treatise that, in accordance with worldly convention and by its very nature,
the application of gender and number in the case of [words like] *godā* and others is based on similarity to the underlying cause (*nimitta*).
In words such as *harītaky-ādi*, the individual entity (*vyakti*) [is the denoted meaning]; in words such as *khalatikādi*, number (*saṃkhyā*) [is the denoted meaning].
For the specific types of humans formed with the suffix *lup*, both [the individual entity and the number] depend upon the denoted object itself.
If, in the application of a genus (jāti), it enters into a relationship with the genus itself,
then that qualifier [the word] conveys the properties (dharma) belonging to that genus.
When a word ending in a *luP* suffix is joined with another qualifier distinct from its genus (*jāti*),
it is designated by the properties of that [qualifier], because the word ending in *luP* is the primary element.

The various distinctions regarding gender and number that occur in negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*), *bahuvrīhi*, *dvandva*, and words expressing excellence, should be stated in accordance with the *Bhāṣya*.
If the suffixes *tamap* and so forth were to apply to a base ending in the genitive or accusative case when it denotes something inferior,
while the resulting word denotes something superior, there would be a discrepancy in gender between the base and the derived form.
From the word *kālya* ending in the second case, when it denotes time, the suffix *tarap* occurs after *kālya*;
likewise, in the sense of "one who humbles," the suffix occurs after *gārgya* as well as after *garga*.
Furthermore, if [the suffix] were derived from Gārgya in the sense of "one who treats with contempt," that would not be desired;
for in the case of a feminine suffix like *ṅīp* used in its own right (*svārthika*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is not augmented. (Vākyapadīya 3.14.162)
From that [word] ending in the sixth case, when there is a sense of "in excess of," it is prescribed [to express] either a quality residing in its own locus,
or an action inherent in something superior.
The meaning of the base is that which is appropriated, and substance alone is the substratum of those two;
through the relation "this is that," it is perceived as non-different [from the quality].
And because its form is non-different, that substance is perceived as possessing expectancy;
it is joined with particularities of distinct forms as if they were its own substrata.
That gender which is established among particularities of diverse forms,
as well as number— by means of these two, the substance-nature is designated as non-different from them.
The substratum is both the inherent cause (samavāyin) and the efficient cause (nimitta) of the gender and number;
therefore, the root *śī* (to lie down), which has its state of being located in the agent (kartṛsthabhāvaka), is cited as an example in the Bhāṣya.
If the indicator were apprehended as the substratum [of the operation],
then there would be the application of gender and number in that case, just as in the instance of the two [suffixes] prescribed after an object (*karman*).

In the grammatical treatise, the meaning of "female" (stryartha) is extracted from the aggregate [of phonemes] as a formal cause (nimittabhāva); its connection with either the base (prakṛti) or the suffix (pratyaya) occurs according to the will [of the grammarian].
The word "strī" (female), being a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*), shares the same properties as [words] such as "white" (*sita*);
it would be employed either for the mere quality itself or for a substratum possessing the quality of contraction (*saṃstyāna*).
If the meaning of the feminine suffix were a substance (*dravya*), like "contraction" (*saṃstyāna*), and if it were the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then in that case,
"contraction" would serve merely as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the substance.
If a substance is observed in some cases through its condensation (saṃstyāna), then there would be a cognition [of it] as occurring in that [condensed state],
even from that which has not admitted such condensation.

When the six designations beginning with *bhūta*—namely, *bhūta*, *jāti*, *dravya*, *guṇa*, *kriyā*, and *saṃstyāna*—apply to [the qualities] such as Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) which are characterized by contraction (*saṃstyāna*), then suffixes should arise from them. (BVaky_3.14.173)
For those who possess [the gender] are the instigators of the suffixes because they are primary;
therefore, even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the occurrence of feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and so forth is possible.
When it is described that the feminine suffix denotes merely a quality (guṇa),
then the meaning of the base is "concretion" (saṃstyāna), and the suffixes are *svārthika* (denoting their own inherent meaning).
The primary elements (prakṛti) do not function when in a state of mere dissolution;
rather, they are perceived as abiding together within the substance that has been permeated by them.

The feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and others are applied to those words for which a concretion (*saṃstyāna*) that serves as a benefactor is required; however, in words such as *bhūta*, that [concretion] is not intended to be expressed.
When the meaning of the suffix is understood as "conglomeration" (saṃstyāna) and is relied upon in its pure form,
then the status of having two suffixes or multiple suffixes is not established.
If it is a genus, then this [genus] is simply femininity, while the distinction in other cases is not intended to be expressed;
for that single existent is qualified by various distinct substances.
For when the constituent parts (*mātrā*) have disappeared, no dimension exists;
therefore, the term "maidens" (*kumāryaḥ*) would apply even to a single maiden, because the possibility of differentiation [among them] still exists.
Just as actions operate upon a substance that coexists with genus, number, and aggregate when its unity is required, so too [do they operate] in this case.
Because the non-difference of the properties of the forms from the forms themselves is thus observed,
both grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and connection with action (*kriyāyoga*) are possible.

But when grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is required through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, the rule "there is elision (*luk*) when there is elision of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)" would apply; and in that case as well, [the term] *luk* is to be understood as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
In the case of certain substances where the distinction [between quality and substance] has been abandoned,
the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and others are prescribed for those possessing contraction (*saṃstyāna*), because they are connected with it through non-difference.
The substance-nature, being universal and characterized by a delimited grasp,
is joined with various actions and persists as distinct parts.
In words such as *śukla* ("white"), the substance that serves as the substratum is expressed primarily;
however, since femininity is the meaning of the suffix, it is the object of expression [only] because of that.
Through the connection expressed as "this is that," one apprehends the substratum;
[the cognition] is either femininity established by its own nature, or a reversal of the state of being a subordinate quality.
Because it requires a complement, it is taught as a quality or as a universal;
this is a property of individual entities, serving as the basis for their appearance as one.
And such is that state when,
through the intellect alone, the partitioning of parts has been performed and the status of being the substratum for those distinctions has been conceived.
Therefore, even when the distinctions are abstracted, based on the form of the individual (vyakti),
one arrives at gender and number through the reflective awareness of the mark (liṅga).

And even without the employment of the word "ca" (and), it is understood that those things which constitute a *dvandva* compound function with an undifferentiated meaning, because there is no difference in their form.
Alternatively, when there is an operation involving conceptual construction, whether [the action] is to be excluded or combined,
it is restricted by that which indicates the power of those [words] whose capacities were previously unknown.
And because it possesses a distinct form within the grammatical operation (*vṛtti*), the word "and" (*ca*) is excluded;
even though there is a difference in meaning, due to their similarity of form, that [operation] is designated by means of the object.

If that very meaning which has become non-existent [in the compound] is what is relied upon, then it follows that the state of being its property (taddharmatva) exists; for in the case of a dvandva compound, that [distinction] is indeed determined by the meaning, as in the case of the *cādi* group.
In some cases, the meaning is established in the word through a certain distinction;
particles such as *ca* and so on are its indicators, while a copulative compound (*dvandva*), however, expresses those [meanings] themselves.

Furthermore, if the object denoted by [words] such as "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) were the referent of another word, it could not be considered a qualifier because it would merely be indicative; therefore, it is perceived as being existent.
In that regard, when the inherent characteristic is dependent upon the property of the word,
a certain word brings about the understanding of that very object in a particular manner.
Meanings are understood from words, and that [word] is the establisher of distinctions;
there exists no means of inference for the speaker's intention other than the word.

The meaning of a *dvandva* compound may be a collection in which the elements are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), or it may be a collection in which the act of collecting itself is subordinate. (Bhāṣyavivaraṇa 3.14.199)
When the aggregate is primary, gender and number [of the word] follow its own nature;
when the aggregate itself is primary, the grammatical rule would be the means of expressing it.
Others, however, maintain that even when the meaning possessed of the collective aggregate is primary,
there is a lack of establishment regarding gender and number, because [the word] conforms to its cause (nimitta).
If there were a collection [of meanings], it would follow the cause;
and by means of positive and negative concomitance, the meaning is dependent upon the *dvandva* compound.

Furthermore, whether the meaning consists of a collection of causes or whether it has disappeared, the gender and number of the *dvandva* compound remain fixed, established by its own nature. (Brahma-vākya 3.14.203)
Because it merely indicates a meaning residing in another word, it is not appropriate for a particle [to denote gender and number];
however, a *dvandva* compound is expressive of its own meaning through both gender and number.
And because, when conforming to a formal cause (*nimitta*), there is no regard for the properties of the substance (*dravyadharma*),
the connection with action (*kriyāyoga*) cannot be established by way of the relation of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*).
For that which lacks the application of action, independence does not exist;
in that case, the referent of a copulative compound would be such that its mention would be purposeless.
The word denoting an object that possesses a collection [of qualities] does not follow [the individual qualities];
therefore, its meaning is also connected with its own properties.
In a copulative compound there is no external substratum; for two distinct entities are heard there. Their collection is the substratum, and it is designated by means of their properties.
That single aggregate which is associated with two distinct parts— as if it were itself possessed of distinctions— partakes of the properties belonging to those two parts.
And this single object, which possesses a dual nature, is endowed with both difference and non-difference;
it assumes the gender and number residing in those two differences upon which it depends.
Just as the word "Caitra" is not employed when the referent Caitra has already been expressed by its own name,
so too there would be no employment of the word "Caitra" within a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Just as there is no denotation of "white" and so forth by the word "cow," so too, first of all, that which is related to cows is what is cognized.
A fixed and conventional relationship does not exist for various [words],
as is the case with "Vajrapāṇi" being restricted to cows or "the three-eyed one" being established [as a name] for Śiva.
Even though specific distinctions are heard in sentences because they are different words,
this word "vṛtti" is indeed distinct and denotes the general [meaning].
The term *agoh* (non-cow) excludes both the cow and the brindled cow because of the difference in their forms;
however, *citraguḥ* (the owner of brindled cows) does not exclude particulars, because there is no difference in its own form.
Just as when one says "the owner of the painting," [the word "painting"] is not used again;
likewise, if the universal were [already expressed], its specific verbal expression would not occur.
But particular [words] such as *sarva* and others set aside the general rules; just as specific rules set aside other general rules.
Alternatively, the genitive case is not employed because the meaning of the case-ending has already been expressed;
however, that word (the noun) is employed [as a separate term] because the substance itself has not been expressed.

If grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is postulated through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, then because that suffix itself would have the same meaning [as the base], an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.
Furthermore, for a relation, another related entity and yet another relation would follow [ad infinitum].
Moreover, when the meaning of the case-ending is primary, connection with an action is not possible.
Because the meaning of the case-ending is predominant, there is no verbal action [implied] by the words "from that" (tataḥ) and "therein" (tatra);
rather, [the word] "visible" (dṛśya) and so forth serves as the cause for [grammatical relations such as] the object (karman) and the agent (kartṛ). 3.14.221.
And how could the relation, which is expressed as primary, be included within [the meaning of the stem]?
And how could that [relation], being of such a nature, become the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)?
But since a direct relation is impossible, there occurs— within that which accompanies the relation—
the possibility of grammatical operations such as those pertaining to genus, number, and collective aggregation.

Because of the connection expressed as "this is that," words denoting a qualified substratum will possess gender and number, just like [words] such as *śukla* ("white"), due to the commencement of the grammatical treatise.
But when there is a desire to express a distinction, or when a universal is intended to be expressed, there would be no comprehension of the word-meaning as possessing gender and number.
Grammatical correctness is not observed in a word that functions merely as a case-ending;
since correctness belongs to that which functions with its full meaning, the term "meaning" (artha) has been included [in the definition].
When this [word] functions as a substance (dravyavṛtti) through its connection with "this is that" (so 'yam),
then it is said to be grammatically correct (sādhutva) when accompanied by gender and number.

Just as the genitive case is not heard when its meaning is already included within the word itself, so too would there be a lack of hearing [of the endings] for those items that express gender and number.

In that case, there would be agreement in gender and number with the indeclinable [in a compound], because the grammatical refinement (saṃskāra) caused by gender and number would be set aside in a bahuvrīhi.
And because of its connection with that which is employed [in speech], there would be the hearing of "Caitra" and so forth even without a case-ending;
for a connection exists even without a case-ending.
Even when number is denoted, its nature as a number does not cease;
however, when the meaning of the genitive case is denoted, it would constitute the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha).
Some declare that no postulation of a case-meaning is made for the sake of establishing the secondary application (*anuprayoga*); rather, it is a distinct entity that has been introduced.
Either relations qualified by their relata serve as the cause [of cognition], or else the relata themselves, as qualified by their relations, serve as the cause. (3.14.233)

Some say that the cognitions regarding that which possesses [a quality] arise from a staff through conjunction and from horns through inherence; and they explain the *bahuvrīhi* compound in exactly the same way.

Others understand the relation to be distinct according to the difference in the related entities; that [relation], which is the cause [of the case-ending], is expressed by the compound as the meaning of the case-ending.
The primary element, being distinct from its own subordinate elements due to its subservience to another purpose,
is expected last of all— whether as the cause or as the expressed meaning.
Even though a distinction from the possessor (*svāmin*) is observed in the sentence,
it is intended only for the sake of its predominance when a *bahuvrīhi* compound is desired.
When that which possesses them (tadvān) functions by virtue of being a qualifier of cows,
such that [the meaning] is "these belong to him," the *bahuvrīhi* compound does not apply in that sense.
But when there is a reflective cognition such as "the owner of these cows," then the connection with the cows serves as the basis for that [cognition].

If one were to assume a relationship [of the word] for the sake of avoiding its being conventional (*rūḍhi*), it would follow that the meaning [of the word] would possess the properties of that [cause], because it conforms to its cause. (3.14.240)
Just as one conforms to a sign, thinking "it is various and manifold," so too would a *bahuvrīhi* compound apply even when [the referents] have become diverse.
When the cause is a related entity, the property of the substance is not lost;
for the absence of a gender-marker exists as the opposite of the gender-marker itself.
An object possessing number and gender, having undifferentiated properties,
is [designated] by way of its cause;
being closely related due to its substantiality, it is not contradicted by those properties.
Substance exists in two ways: as that which is permeated by the meaning of a case-ending and as that which is pure.
A property belonging to a pure substance could not belong to one that possesses other properties.
In the description of substance alone, this distinction is not intended;
however, in the preceding treatise, the distinction was presented in the second [section].
And here, the apprehension of a substance is qualified by gender and number;
for since those two [gender and number] reside in a substance, they are not established for anything else.
The compound operates upon a substance-universal that follows a specific meaning, which is delimited by a relation distinct from its relata. (Brahmanandin’s Vākyapadīyavṛtti 3.14.247)
Not transcending its status as a substance, yet abiding in its various differentiated states,
it assumes gender and number in accordance with the substratum that is yet to come into being.

Even though there is a difference in the application of the grammatical treatises, the worldly meaning does not differ; for it is in that regard—namely, in the negative compound—that three positions have been examined.
Moreover, this investigation is conducted by relying on the unity [of the word] even when another word is present;
for indeed, the use of the negative particle *nañ* is not found in words such as *abrāhmaṇa*.
Prior to the formation of a compound, the negation (*nañ*) indicates the exclusion of word-meanings;
however, because those meanings are naturally excluded and their forms are indistinguishable [from the positive], this exclusion remains unperceived.
For that which has a connection with an action denoted by a verbal form within sentences belonging to Brahmins and others, no [independent] function exists.

If the action residing in words such as "cook" is connected with the negative particle *nañ*, then because existence (*sattā*) is not being predicated there, the threefold alternative (*tripakṣī*) is not tenable.
If it is assumed that the connection with existence itself applies everywhere,
then in this compound "asat" (non-existent), another existence must be postulated.
In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) ending in either a *ktvā* suffix or a *tumun* suffix,
the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not observed with the negative particle (*nañ*), because it denotes non-existence.
The negative particle (nañ) is established in reference to the general substratum that accomplishes the action;
it is then connected with specific substrata such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth.

Just as in the case of a verbal derivative (*vṛtti*), prefixes such as *nir-* and others are joined with means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and loci (*ādhāra*) by taking on meanings such as "gone" (*gata*); that same sequence applies even in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).

In that case, since the operation of the negative particle is impossible [if it were applied directly], the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, and so forth is postulated, like that between a hunchback and a lame man.

And if there were such arbitrary usage (kāmacāra), then that which is non-existent would possess the status of the primary (pradhāna), while the others would have the status of qualities (guṇa); or else, those [non-existent things] themselves would possess the status of the primary.

Previously, those such as Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas were based primarily on their general functions as heard in the Veda; now, however, they have proceeded specifically [according to their individual capacities].
Just as their delimitation is effected by [qualifiers] such as "white" and so forth,
so too is that identity— which, though non-existent and unmanifested, [is present]— made manifest.
Just as an object is postulated as "existent" for the purpose of denoting existence,
so too is that which is indefinable postulated for the purpose of denoting non-existence.
Having established its footing in [the word] *kṣatriya* and so forth, the cognition— which rests upon a distinct existence (*sattā*)—
thereby excludes that existence which is differentiated by genus (*jāti*).
When the negation of an entity is intended by the term "non-existence," that negation is not possible without relying upon its having a defining characteristic.
Words that express multiple properties and denote a collection function with identical forms by their very nature when they refer to individual parts.
Just as a collection [of letters] is called "done" when even one part is completed, and "not done" otherwise, that same principle applies to the term *abrāhmaṇa*.
Consequently, from that very proposition, it follows that a Brahmin would be a non-Brahmin;
or else, because of the attachment to what is uncreated as being created, he would be indistinguishable from one who has both acted and not acted.
When the primary sense is possible there, the negative particle (*nañ*) employed at the time of explaining the scripture serves as a specifier for the purpose of excluding that primary sense.
Without destroying the nature of the object, another qualification is perceived; or rather, some property of the object possessing the universal is excluded.
It is not necessarily the case that some dharma does not exist in a Brahmin;
since no specific [dharma] is mentioned there, the hearing of the negative particle would be purposeless.
In the case of an unqualified [word], it follows that its negative-qualified synonym is also [unqualified];
for through grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), correctness is understood to belong to such a form.
Even though there is no qualification here that does not impair the meaning of the word,
it is the state of an object existing as a metaphorical reality that is illuminated by the negative particle (*nañ*).
Just as an object exists in its specific substrates,
so too is its existence perceived in that state by means of the causes of differentiation.
When that constituent part has ceased, how can it subsist in the word-meaning? For the application of a word is not possible without a cause.
If the word *nañ* functions by its very nature to denote a contrary meaning at a distance from [the object] like a sound,
then the actual hearing of the word would be purposeless.

Now, if it is argued that an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) deserves to be explained through verbal expression, then that [nature] must be stated; however, because it is not established, the meaning of the negative particle (nañ) is excluded.
Even though the occurrence in both is primary, it is perceived as the departure [of the suffix]; for even when that meaning is pure, the suffix *tiṣṭhati* is not understood as "departure."

For what purpose is the application of the word "brāhmaṇa" accepted in a figurative sense toward one who is not such [a person], when that [primary object] exists and the primary meaning is possible? (BVaky_3.14.278)
