"A certain word-meaning does not exist in this [referent], such as a Kṣatriya, etc."; it is for the sake of such a cognition that a word denoting that [absence] is employed.
When an object has become the domain of the intellect, activity or cessation is understood from the word; for it is through verbal testimony that the object is connected [to action].
The application of the word [“cow”] occurs either due to incorrect instruction or due to doubt regarding the [actual] cause;
however, it does not apply to clods of earth and the like because of the contrary nature [of those objects].
The expression "it is not [the case] from many" is established when there is predominance;
thus, dependence is appropriate for predominant factors alone in the application of the suffixes -tva and -tal.
And because one [of the two] is primary, when it is in proximity with its qualifier, the property of the primary does not cease; therefore, there is no need for another statement.
In this context, because it is that which is to be differentiated, the modified single referent [of "one"] is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*).
Even numbers such as two and so forth, having abandoned their own properties, function [as one] when they have attained oneness.

Just as Kṣatriyas and others, when joined with the negative particle *nañ*, come to be designated as "Brāhmaṇas," so too is singularity figuratively attributed to duality and the rest through their connection with *nañ*.
Having attained the state of oneness, that property is negated;
yet the word for it applies to those [entities] starting from duality, just as the term "Brāhmaṇa" and others do.
Just as this [number], when included in the sentence, is employed in the sense of "two" and so forth,
that number does not cease in the compound because it remains the primary element there.
Just as that which is to be negated exists in its true state, so too does it persist when joined with another statement; for that object is not thereby negated.
Just as the term "non-white" is understood to have its meaning as "black" and so forth,
so too the term "many" is here designated as denoting a different number.
When there is an engagement with action and all ritual acts have been accepted,
even if one is prohibited, another [act] is understood to be obtained.
And when the verb is heard in the context of a prasajya-pratiṣedha (absolute negation), it applies;
but in the case of a paryudāsa (relative negation/exclusion), another object of enumeration is necessarily expressed.
The meaning of the verbal root, having as its object the action, is designated by its own instruments;
it remains there, having by implication already projected all the various actions.
When a verb is employed where the substratum of the means [of action] is already known,
the word "aneka" (many) follows it, and the word "tiṣṭhati" (remains/stays) is subsequently supplied.
Because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), action there is characterized by a substance already established;
since the substance is accepted as prior [to the action], it is therefore distinguished from the former [category].
A number itself, by its negation, requires another number;
therefore, even in a sentence, it is not mere oneness alone that is negated.
In the same way, the exclusion [of other fats] from non-existence is understood through another fat;
for when oil is used for a meal, no other condiment is required.
When a word denoting a non-existent [quality] and the word "brāhmaṇa" denote the same object,
it refers to an external person of a different caste, such as a kṣatriya or the like.
Just as a dark-colored knife is designated by another term as "the maiden," so too,
by these two [terms] "non-existent" and "Brāhmaṇa," others such as the Kṣatriyas and so forth are designated.
Just as in the expression "the hornless ox," the gavaya is designated;
it is understood not as a different genus from the cow, but rather as the absence of horns in the cow itself.

Just as one recognizes a *khadira* tree from a date palm by its specific genus, even though it appears identical in form and is indistinguishable from thorns that cause piercing; so too [is the word recognized]. *Brahma-siddhi-vākya*, 3.14.300.
Just as a person who does not possess Brahminhood might be described as a "Brahmin" by means of an accepted metaphor,
so too is another object expressed in that manner.
Just as non-rainy seasons appear like rainy seasons when shrouded by mist and clouds,
because they possess that same form, the winter season is perceived as undifferentiated from them.
Others maintain that for all words denoting castes, such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth,
when a substance is the external referent (anyapadārtha), there is a connection with the negative particle *nañ*.
Furthermore, no such bahuvrīhi compound can be postulated as having such a referent [as "non-existence"],
for which there is no pervasion by the negative (nañ) compound, such as *agauḥ* or *anaśvaḥ*.
Since it has been stated that for a *dvandva* and for a single member [of a compound], the gender of the final member prevails,
there follows a failure [to apply] the desired gender and number in the case of *avarṣāsu*.
When a qualifier such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth is distinct from its object—that which is connected to the action—then its non-existence [at that time] is perceived. (BVaky_3.14.306)
Because [a thing] does not exist as a Brahmin, it is said to be "existent" in another way;
likewise, by means of existence, the existence of that which is existent is negated when it is called "non-existent."
Because it resides in a common substance and conforms to its causes, there would be no connection with gender and number; or else, it would possess the nature of a universal property.
Previously, it was stated that a compound denotes non-existence, yet it expresses a substance;
furthermore, conformity to the cause does not occur everywhere by its very nature.
And if [the word] conforms to the external sign (nimitta), the connection with action (kriyāyoga) is not possible;
likewise, because it would be indefinable (avyapadeśyatva), its employment (upādāna) would be purposeless.

Alternatively, the universal residing in non-existent [particulars] becomes identical with the number and gender of those particulars— such as the Kṣatriyas and so forth— which are employed as its substrata, even though it is distinct from them.
For previously the substratum, having been internalized within the primary [meaning], was [not distinct];
yet, through subsequent reflective awareness, it appears as if divided once again.
In a compound, that which possesses its own meaning and serves as its substratum is heard;
however, the substance (dravya), though accompanied by gender and number, is internalized within it as if non-existent.
Two words that have the same referent [denote] that [single entity], even though they function with respect to different meanings;
yet, all distinctions [between them] are subsumed as if they were non-existent.
They may be expressed by "kṣatriya" and so forth, or by all [other] nouns;
they do not attain the status of being the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), because there is no conceptualization of a form for the negative particle (*nañ*).
If, however, the qualifier (viśeṣa) is not employed, gender and number are not established;
furthermore, there is a fault in cases such as *avarṣā*, because [in that case] "winter" (*hemanta*) would have something else as its substratum.
When the form (ākṛti) is understood as the denotable meaning of all words, it is logical that there is only one word for it, because that form is one; this is what is described.
In that [aggregate], there would be the assumption of both genders, like a group of village dogs;
moreover, because of its oneness despite the plurality of substances, the singular number would apply there.
For that [gender] is indeed restricted to being joined with the specific gender-marks of the substrata;
and thus, the prohibition regarding the occurrence of the gender of the substantive would be purposeless.

If one were to adopt the gender [of a word] as it appears in common worldly usage, it would follow that [the grammatical rule] would apply to all genders indiscriminately; however, that worldly usage is not what is relied upon here, because it is contradictory [to the intended meaning].
In the case of the terms *sāmānya*, *ākṛti*, *bhāva*, and *jāti*, the gender used in common worldly usage is not possible; therefore, another [gender] is adopted.
"Manifestation" (pravṛtti) is stated to be its general characteristic;
it is then divided into appearance, disappearance, and persistence.
All objects of meaning, being possessed of activity, are never permanently separated from the three types of activity; and it is within this context that speech itself comes into existence.
And that entity whose nature is inactive and which is perceived as pure consciousness seems to follow the activities of others, which are based upon the manifold world.
Therefore, its form as cognition and the time of cognition are distinct;
however, no difference whatsoever exists in its own essential nature.
In insentient objects, consciousness appears as if it has been transferred;
that which occurs through the principle of reflection is the basis for the use of the word [“consciousness”].
There is no such state that is not connected with a grammatical indicator (liṅga);
however, in some cases, when there is no basis for the indicator, there occurs a refinement of the word-form (śabda-saṃskāra).

In the grammatical treatise, the gender of entities denoted by primary (kṛt) and secondary (taddhita) suffixes is not considered contradictory; likewise, it is accepted as being based on their state of quality (guṇāvasthā) and their form (ākṛti).
There is no distinction regarding gender even in the case where [the word] refers to a substance;
therefore, those seven alternatives constitute here what is called "inherent gender" (aviṣṭaliṅgatā).
The restriction regarding the utterance of a substance is accepted from the treatise;
for otherwise, that treatise is shown to apply to the form (ākṛti).
When a meaning that exists in many [individuals] is intended to be expressed without distinction,
its verbal expression in the treatise is said to be designated by means of its own substrata.
But when a difference is perceived solely through a difference in substrata,
then no difference exists for the form (ākṛti) on the view that it is a substance (dravya).

But if there were no distinction [between the individual and the universal], since there would be a single word and because of the authority of the treatise, when the expression occurs, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) need not be stated; for the plurality of words is possible.
But surely, if substance is inexpressible,
then this benefit which belongs to the configuration (ākṛti) by depending upon it cannot be conceived, because of the absence of substance.
In the treatise, no designation whatsoever is based on a denoted object;
the category called "substance" (dravya) is not what is being refuted here.
The state of being a quality (guṇabhāva) with respect to that which is to be denoted is not dependent upon the substance;
rather, the conceptualization is that a quality is auxiliary, subordinate, and exists for the sake of another.

There is no status as a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva) with respect to a substance (dravya) without the denotation of a substance; nor is there primacy (pradhānatva) with respect to a form (ākṛti). Therefore, it is established in this manner.
Some maintain that there is a relationship of primary and subordinate status between them, as in the case of nouns and verbs;
however, this subordination is not described as being for the sake of another, as it is in the case of a *vṛtti*.
Because the various qualities are subordinate, the form (ākṛti) possesses a single designation;
and the difference in number is established through its connection with the difference in substance.
Just as a means of accomplishment (sādhana) is a differentiator of an action by virtue of being a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva),
so too, in verbal forms (ākhyāta), the substance (dravya) is said to be the differentiator of the genus (jāti) expressed by a single word.
Since words possess an identical nature in their denotation,
when there is a specific apprehension of the object possessing that [word] as its cause, [the distinction arises].
Through the connection "this is that," when the form (ākṛti) operates together with its substrates (āśraya) by means of distinct words, gender and number are established.
And prior to the connection with a specific genus, there is the state of being denotable by all pronouns;
words such as *tyad* and so forth are employed toward an entity (*sattva*) as a mere indicator of the thing (*vastūpalakṣaṇa*).
Just as the word "pāka" (cooking) is accepted by some as a differentiator based on its substratum,
so too is that property of words denoting qualities held to be without a material cause (*anupādāna*).
If one were to acquire only the properties of the substratum when the substratum itself is not grasped,
that general principle was examined previously.
When words denoting a genus have previously been applied to that genus,
the individual also arises [as the object of cognition] through a relationship with that which is not directly expressed by the word.

Through the connection expressed as "this is that," the properties of the universal are metaphorically attributed [to the individual]; the substance is accepted as its substratum, and the distinction from the universal is also admitted.
Just as the word "bed" (mañca), though established only in reference to the beds themselves, denotes that which is placed upon them;
in that same way, the word for a genus (jāti) functions with respect to individual substances (dravya) according to their true nature.

In that regard, the fact that the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning is accepted in exactly that way; however, the universal, having relinquished its number, is attached to the essence of the substance (*dravya*).
Wherever the Vedic revelation functions by means of another's property, either through the expression "this belongs to that" or even "this is that," that [object] is designated as "other."
That which is the primary [cause] has no intrinsic nature (svarūpa) because it cannot be defined;
and a substance is characterized by its quality through its own essence as being that [quality].
But at the time when a quality is differentiated, its predominance arises;
the scriptural mention of association does not apply directly to the objects themselves.
When that word, which had previously functioned with respect to a genus, functions again with respect to a substance,
then the status of the genus alone as the meaning of the word is no longer accepted.
Furthermore, the recurrence of those [words] that have already occurred is described as being one;
however, the ultimate reality is not apprehended in the means of comprehension.
When the universal is resorted to for a substance that is denoted by a non-distinct word, provided there is contact [between them], then the universal constitutes the meaning of the word.
When a substance is perceived through contact and is then resorted to as a substance, it must be expressed by that very word; at that time, the substance constitutes the meaning of the word.

Even though it is expressed by a word that does not denote difference, when the universal (jāti) functions with respect to mere difference— just like a relation— it also constitutes the referent of a substance-word (dravyapadārtha).
If it is maintained that even two [words] which denote a universal and a substance, though absolutely distinct,
possess the capacity to assist that which is inexpressible, then they would have both meanings.
However, by one who accepts a distinction based on the substratum in the case of that which is supported,
the fact that the word for the universal is a single word is further described.
That by which there is the cognition of what has not yet been produced is called a measure (*māna*);
by means of it, such as a *prastha* and so forth, the nature of the object of measurement is determined in its entirety.
When an object whose property is not fully ascertained is understood through that which is well-known because its entirety is not comprehended, that is called analogy (*upamāna*).
When there is a common property between two equal things— the object of comparison and the standard of comparison—
there is a compound of the standards of comparison with words that denote them.
The difference [in the quality] of blackness that arises from the difference in its substrata is not intended to be expressed;
this quality, while residing in a single entity, is perceived as having distinct substrata.
The distinction between two qualities is fixed, as is their identity within the universal of that quality;
whether they are identical or absolutely distinct,
the possibility of comparison does not exist.
If there were dependence on the mere genus, there would be no sense of comparison at all;
for the quality of "darkness" exists in both [the subject and the object] as qualities. (BVaky_3.14.365)
By the very same cause by which the dark woman is perceived as a "knife-wielder," that same cause does not differ in producing the cognition of Devadattā.
The distinction among qualities based on their substrata, as well as the non-distinction of the universal—
through both of these, the substance-soul is perceived as being endowed with activity.
Thus, this linguistic usage based on unity and plurality proceeds by means of an intermingled investigation into difference and non-difference.
If only the genus is intended to be expressed, it should simply be called "śyāmā" (the dark-complexioned one);
there is no purpose in employing names such as "śastrī" (knife) and so forth in that context.
That distinction which is not expressible by words and does not reside in mere "darkness" generally,
but whose occurrence resides in some specific dark things— this is what is intended here.
In some dark things, a certain [quality] exists in part; in others, it exists everywhere as a universal (sāmānya). A certain particularity (bheda), however, is established in one specific dark thing.
For if there were fragrance in jasmine, blue lotus, and so forth, there would be a difference [among them];
however, when there is a difference among odors, a similarity is perceived.
The distinction [of substances] is understood either from their being the substrata of qualities, or by themselves,
or from an indefinable particularity (*viśeṣa*), or from a commixture with other qualities.
Because it is well-known, the standard of comparison (upamāna) is distinguished in every respect;
however, its status as the object of comparison (upameyatva) does not cease when there is either superiority or equality.
Others, however, describe measurement (*māna*) as [the means by which] the object to be divided—such as caste and so forth—is characterized;
for an object to be known, whose own nature is not yet ascertained, is measured by that [means].
But that which is established by its own measure as the locus of qualities functions,
by means of its own property, toward the measurement of another locus.
The contact of things possessing distinct forms with another distinct form,
by which there is a comparison of those things to be divided, is called *upamāna*.
When the common property, such as being dark-complexioned and so forth, belongs equally to both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison,
it is differentiated by another property which is treated as predominant.
When it is accepted that "the sword and the boy are similar" in the sense that "he is dark," the ground for designation—
that by which something is designated— resides in the two qualities.
When things possessing certain characteristics appear, through those very characteristics, as if they were identical with them,
then that description of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is based upon their difference.
When there is a desire to express the non-attachment to reality, those [similes] in which difference ceases are called "elliptical similes" (luptopamā), because they rely upon that common property.
The blackness well-known in the case of a knife is the means of measurement; by it, that [knife] is measured.
But another woman who is black and possesses that same form is not measured by it at all.

Therefore, they declare that comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing [an object] by measuring it through its own quality against another substratum whose qualities are not yet fully realized.
A property residing in the object of comparison is inferred elsewhere upon being heard;
or else, a property residing in the standard of comparison is inferred in the object of comparison upon being heard.
It is observed that "the Kṣatriyas study like Brāhmaṇas";
because the object of comparison is distinct, the statement is based on the Kṣatriyas.
In the Sūtra it is taught that "a word denoting a universal is one which expresses a property (dharma) that is common [to many] and established in only a certain [locus]. (BVaky_3.14.386)
A quality residing in two [entities] is not denoted as being either non-different or different;
of two distinct properties, one is heard [directly], while the other is understood [by implication].
That which, being established in a universal (sāmānya), does not measure [the object] absolutely,
is conceived as being near the meaning of the object of comparison (upameya) due to its similarity.
Or, proximity with respect to measurement is perceived through similarity;
for in this context, similarity between measurement and comparison arises from the act of delimitation.
When there is a dependence on a single birth, it is determined as "that very same thing";
when there is a dependence on difference itself, it is understood as "something else entirely."

Since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) are based on distinctness alone, there can be no scope for absolute identity; therefore, in this case, doubt arises.

Even when there is a difference [between individuals], because they possess an identical form, one perceives "those rice-grains"; and because there is no difference in the universal (jāti), a distinct object is designated as "this is that very same thing."
For how can a part belong to another, and yet be called "other"?
Where there is absolute difference, there is plurality, and in that case, no true essence (tattva) exists.
When non-difference is intended to be expressed, there is oneness of the collection and the possessor of the collection;
however, there is no non-difference between two possessors of collections, and thus their distinctness has been illustrated.
In that case, when there is no expectation of distinction, the sense of comparison does not exist;
for whatever is the cause for the cognition "this is a cow" exists likewise in another cow.
But when the operation of distinct particulars is intended to be expressed,
there is no assistance whatsoever rendered by one cognition toward another cognition.
If there exists some generality in something and there are also some particulars,
then "cowness" is the generality existing in cows, and the brindled cow and others are the particulars.
Darkness itself is indeed the commonality, for that is shared by both;
yet, through its establishment and non-establishment, it is designated as a distinction.
The quality of blackness alone is the commonality established for both [the individual and the universal];
because it is complete, it is understood as a particularity in relation to other things.
Alternatively, those particularities which are determined in respect of a certain general form or universal, such as "darkness" and so forth, are what are relied upon here.

Whether there is non-difference or difference of the universal (jāti), they declare that to be similarity; some essence of an object is thus designated as being of such a nature at some time or another.
When there is no differentiation in the cognition regarding an object at any time,
that object is understood to be one, because its differentiation is non-existent.

That object which possesses a diversity based on its substrates is designated as being "that very same thing"; even in that case, they maintain that there is an operation belonging to the generic aspect.
The manifestation based on the universal aspect proceeds there as undifferentiated;
the cognition based on the individual aspect arises there with differentiation.
An existent cause, while residing in one place as endowed with both difference and non-difference,
is nevertheless perceived in another place as if it were manifold.
Having placed its steps upon the substrata, it then approaches that which is their support;
it is designated by others as the object of similarity.
Just as the designation "cause" is applied to an entity that depends on something else,
so too they declare that analogy (upamāna) depends upon the comprehension of another [object].
Just as the relationships between teacher and disciple or father and son, as well as actions, time, and so forth,
are conventional usages, so too is comparison based upon dependence.
If the quality of blackness resides in the object of comparison (upamāna), yet is employed in relation to the action (vṛtti),
then the object of comparison (upameya) is expressed there as external to the compound.
In that case, the word *śyāmā* would have to end in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* when applied to Caitra and others;
furthermore, because there is no nominative case in the sūtra, *śyāmā* and the like cannot function as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).
Now, if it were considered a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) because it has a single case-ending or because it is a quality (*guṇa*),
then the feminine suffix would not be desired in the word *tittirikalmāṣī*.

Because that which remains after the application of rules is stronger, even though the external suffix *ṅiṣ* is present, the accent of the comparative (*upamāna*) would not apply; therefore, a feminine-stem ending is compounded.

Nor can dependence be attributed to the principal [word] when the standard of comparison resides in a subordinate quality; likewise, there would be no observation of such a grammatical gender [conflict] in cases like "vyāghra" (tiger).
Therefore, even though it possesses the status of a quality (*guṇa*), its predominance (*prādhānya*) occurs in another grammatical analysis (*vigraha*);
for a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) of such a kind does not occur in the technical treatise (*śāstra*).
The word *śyāma* (dark) is explicitly stated as residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*),
yet it is understood through the force of context even when not explicitly mentioned in the standards of comparison (*upamāna*).
Even when only the substance is mentioned, as in the case of "moon-faced," it is understood to be a specific quality residing in the moon,
and not [qualities such as] eclipses and the like.
And this [process] is described even in the case of a compound through the cultivation of differentiation:
a distinct word is employed for an object that is differentiated by its specific qualities. (Vākyapadīya 3.14.417)
If [the application of] the suffix is understood from the statement as having a different locus,
then in the case of *mṛgīva capalā* ("fickle like a doe"), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not be established.
But because the preceding word is not feminine, the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) will occur,
just as in the case of "mṛgadugdha" and so forth, provided that the feminine meaning is not intended to be expressed.
Just as Devadatta is described as "the sword-like one" because he is dark like a sword,
so too both [qualities] are said to reside in that very [entity] when there is a grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) according to the treatise.

Because much must be considered for the sake of establishing the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and, optionally, the feminine suffix, both [the masculine and feminine forms] are demonstrated in that [section].

Just as a dark woman is called "like a dark sword," so too is she said to be "a dark sword"; in that case, the word "dark" (śyāmā) is required with respect to both the object of comparison and the other [the standard of comparison].
Now, when one says "this knife is dark" (*śyāmā iyaṃ śastrī*), it is understood only to this extent: "just as this [other] knife is dark. (Bhāṣyavākya 3.14.423)
If the verbal expression of this quality serves merely as an indicator,
then even though it is heard separately from the two [relata], it is not desired to be the denoter of its own meaning.
But when the object of comparison (upameya), which is to be expressed, is being conveyed,
if the qualities (guṇas) are active therein, then there is the expression of everything [simultaneously] upon a single hearing.
Since it is established as a particular through the distinction between the qualifier and the substratum,
how can it be expressive of a universal when it is connected with another word?
Some maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely similarity residing in two things;
or it is intended as a quality (*guṇa*) that, despite the difference [between the two], functions non-differently or occurs in both.
Either the operation of the generic portion, or that of the two substances, is intended to be expressed;
or else, its denotation of a universal is illustrated on the basis of its form prior to its application [to a specific instance].
When the word "tiger" (vyāghra) is established in the sense of human effort through its association with valor, then,
due to the non-difference of the locus [of the quality], the formation of a compound is possible.
But when the word *śūra* (hero) is employed, the word *vyāghra* (tiger) resides in the animal;
since their substrata are distinct, there is no possibility of such a function [of identity] occurring there.
Even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), since a distinction between qualities is possible,
the application of the word "hero" (*śūra*) persists even within a compound.
Furthermore, since the conditions for honor that are observed and the conditions for contempt are based on different causes, the scriptural statement is repeated for the purpose of restriction.
Or rather, even in the absence of actual occurrence, this observation of a grammatical indicator (liṅga) may exist,
just as the indicator "a-cveḥ" occurs in the case of words like *bhṛśa* and others, even when [the condition] is absent.
When a comparison is perceived within a sentence whose constituent parts are complete,
this present rule is deliberated upon in the sūtra that prescribes the formation of that cognition.
Although action is the primary adjunct of the meaning of the verbal root, it is not tenable that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) therein expresses action. (Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 3.14.435)

Whether it be at the conclusion of a word denoting a substance (*sattva*), or even when it serves as an instrument (*sādhana*), that third case [the instrumental] does not apply; for since verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) do not denote substances, neither of those two conditions exists.

Terms such as *pāka* (cooking) ending in the third case are not designated as "action" (*kriyā*) because they are associated with the properties of sentient beings, just as in the case of suffixes expressing the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*).
And whatever indeclinables there are that are endowed with the property of action, their denoting non-substance is no different from that of finite verb forms.
Even in cases such as "śayitavya" and the like, where there is an action governed by the suffixes *kṛt*, *vasu*, or *su*,
the relationship of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is absolutely impossible.
Neither the substance alone nor the quality alone, nor that which possesses them, is compared;
for in cases such as "one who is to lie down" (śayitavya), there is no purpose whatsoever for comparison among them.

In the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared, when the substance has its property unexpressed, actions and qualities—whether based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or etymological derivation (*yoga*)—are understood as the grounds [for that relationship]. (BVaky_3.14.441)
In the case of "the sacrificer is like the oblation," no such meaning exists;
because of the contradiction with the action, that which possesses the action cannot be compared [to the object of the action].
An action is not compared to itself because it is identical to that [action];
even when there is a difference in genus, actions such as cooking are distinct from one another due to their specific modes of cooking.
When there is a distinction based on a difference of substratum, a comparison is possible:
"The study of the Vaiśyas is equal to the study of the Brahmins, which is to be studied. (Bhāṣyavākya 3.14.444)
That is to say, where something is understood as being required either from the context or from the sense,
it follows that the operation of that [word] would occur without requiring it.
And when the cooking of ghee is intended to be equivalent to the cooking of oil,
there would arise a cognition [of similarity] even from the observation of the actions involved in the effects.
However, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* serves as an exclusion of such a compound;
thus, in the case of "the going of the agent" (*kārakasya gamanam*), it would not be possible for a *ṇvul* suffix to occur with any other [word].
The status of being a "collection" (samudāyatva) is resorted to for the sake of excluding everything [else];
otherwise, because a pure [action] is possible among Brāhmaṇas and others, it would not be [an action] belonging to the [caste] class.
When there is an intention to express a comparison, the property of the subject itself is excluded;
for the comparison is not completed by the action [of the verb] as it is heard in the text.
The third type of difference, which is a property residing [in both], is common to the two;
however, there is no equality of the whole with the whole, as one possesses activity while the other does not.
Whether in the case of a substance or an action, that [denotation] is determined by means of a cause;
for since actions are already present, there would be no function [of the word] in the case of cows and the like.
But because the bare [action] does not exist, the object possessing it is understood;
when the primary [action] is impossible, the mention of the action is logically understood as having a secondary (lakṣaṇā) sense.
Just as Brāhmaṇas and others are accepted for the sake of assistance in other rites, so too verbal roots denoting actions are accepted in other actions when they are dependent upon them.
Just as excellence everywhere has another cause as its basis, so too,
even in the case of a word denoting a quality, it requires a basis, just like a substance.
Whatever word is uttered is based on its own form;
just as it is so, even in cases of comparison, the requirement [of the word's own form] does not cease.
When such [an application] is impossible for a word ending in the third case denoting the occurrence of an action,
the root *yuj* is cited in the Bhāṣya as an illustration, employing a well-known logical principle.
But when the instrument is already included [within the meaning of the verb], there should be no further employment [of a separate word for the instrument];
this is logically incorrect, as in the case of the term *jīvati* (‘he lives’) where the action of breathing is [already] implied.
And through the study of the treatises, this distinction is described as "improper," "unattractive," and "incoherent"; thus the conventional usage is established.

How could a case-ending (vibhakti) be a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the base (prakṛti)? Furthermore, if there were a transformation of the case-ending, a different object [of denotation] would have to be postulated.
For when something is connected with one case-ending in relation to a particular object,
its connection with another case-ending in relation to a different object is inferred through the force of logical necessity.
However, due to their similarity of form, it is metaphorically designated as "this is that very same thing";
yet in the grammatical treatise, another word joined with a case-ending is not heard there.
If *prakṛti* (the material cause) ends in the third case, it is understood from the word *tena* (by that);
how then could it be the *kriyā* (action), which must end in the first case?
And when [the word] *kriyayā* is used in the instrumental case, for what could it be postulated?
For its connection with the word *tena* found in the Sūtra does not exist.
In the case of elliptical sūtras, the remainder of the sentence is supplied;
by that means, it is understood that whatever ends in the third case is the action (kriyā).
In a sentence, the employment of some specific limiting adjunct (upādhi) is observed;
however, another [adjunct] that is merely implied is never employed.

In the expression "a blue lotus," there is no word employed in the sentence that denotes either the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) or the qualifier (*bhedaka*), nor any word expressing their common property (*taddharma*).
Because it follows [the meaning] absolutely, there is no need for any modification of case-endings there, whether in the *sūtra* or in its analysis (*vigraha*). (3,14.467)

The term "action" (*kriyā*) ending in the third case is not employed in a *vigraha* (analytical expansion), as is seen in the example: "the stick is the instrument (*praharaṇa*) in the game. (Bhāṣya on Vākyapadīya 3.14.468)
Furthermore, that which was cited in the rule *ghañi ca saṃjñāyām* as an example of usage is never found at all in actual applications [of the term].
Those [factors] by which, even when not explicitly employed, a grammatical operation is understood to apply to the primary elements,
are designated as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), despite the distinctness of the case-endings.

Words denoting things that coexist function with respect to collections; however, when there is no intention to express that [collection], they function in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or alternative (*vikalpa*).
But a collective aggregate (samuccaya) is formed in the case of those [words] whose functions pertain to individual objects;
their connection with number occurs through the basis of differentiation.
Cognitions of perceivers are produced by all those distinguished objects acting as concomitants; therefore, they know those [objects] to be the meanings of words.
All objects, being interconnected within their causal conditions, are indeed contributive;
therefore, all of them, by virtue of their nature as conditions, are denotable by words.
But the form of isolated entities is not apprehended;
and since their forms are not determined, no word applies to them.
And because of the employment of the word "prior" (pūrva), it does not turn away from the aggregate;
nor does it apply to the individual part, nor does it ever abandon what has been grasped.
And if that which denotes the whole were to qualify the particular,
then there would be a lack of grammatical coordination (atulyavibhaktitva), as in the case of "the front part of the body" and so forth.
The term "Pañcālas" is observed to refer both to a collection and to a region;
likewise, the qualification "all" (sarva) is thus rendered appropriate.
Likewise, in the expression "half-pippalī" (*ardhapippalī*), the word is understood as a compound consisting of "half" and "pippalī," in order to exclude other types [of compounds]. (BVaky_3.14.479)
Even a region of the Pañcālas is distinct from other countries;
yet, when a word is used there to exclude something else, no difference [in the word itself] is perceived.

But those [words] which are well-known as being established specifically for a collection [of meanings], their application to a single part [of that collection] occurs through the context of the meaning and other factors.
That which is a secondary mark of a genus, which co-occurs with it in actions,
or that whose connection is conventionally established therein— this is generally observed as a characteristic indicator.
When that [word] does not depend on such [distinctions] as whether it is a whole (samudāya) or a part (pradeśa),
the terms "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth apply without distinction to the nature of the object itself.

And since a word of identical phonetic form is observed to be established as denoting a collection, it is perceived— even when referring to a single constituent part— that its unity is merely figurative.

In the case of oil and the like, which have been processed or damaged so that their [original] measure has changed, it is determined by implication that the word here denotes the genus (*jāti*). (Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 3.14.485)
In words denoting universals (jāti) and qualities (guṇa), a difference in form is not intended;
they are based solely on the difference in the relation to a universal or a quality.

And the designation "black" and so forth [is applied] by means of qualities that reside in all parts; even though those [qualities] occupy only one part, they serve as the differentiators of cloth and other objects.
But when cloth and other such things reside in the constituent parts of the cloth,
then, like oil and so forth, they are said to be class-terms (jātiśabda).
For those for whom the Vedic revelation has the purpose of exclusion, differentiation among them is not required;
in either a specific location or as a whole, the quality serves to exclude others.
In that context, the Vedic revelation concerning the Brāhmaṇa applies to the study of the Brāhmaṇas;
for similarity is indeed observed there with respect to the study and other activities of the Kṣatriyas.
If the application [of the term *brāhmaṇa*] were based on the study of the Veda, then it would follow from the Vedic revelation that it refers to a Brāhmaṇa;
one must therefore state by what property the two actions are identical.
When the livelihood of a Brahmin is said to depend on the student,
the action itself, residing in the student, becomes the cause for that livelihood.
If there were a connection with the word "lion" (simha), which denotes only the lion itself,
then the genitive case would result after "Caitra," just as it does when used in conjunction with words such as "teacher" (śāstrin) and the like.
In cases such as "it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa" or "to a Vaiśya," the connection with the recipient and so forth is not possible in the case of a mere action.
Since the suffix *vat* denotes only the action itself, it should never be included among the indeclinables (*avyaya*);
for both positions are equal. (Bṛhadāraṇyakavākya 3.14.495)
It abandons either its birth or its substance; therefore, it does not reside in a part [of the object].
Since there is a scriptural mention of action, however, it resides in the object possessing that [action].
It is for the purpose of excluding non-actions,
since there is here an explicit mention of action;
therefore, the word for action is understood as referring to that which is characterized by action.
And because, in cases such as "to be sacrificed," another action must be expected— just as in the case of [castes like] Brāhmaṇas—
with respect to a pure meaning, therefore no [verbal root] has a [denotative] function [in that sense].
Whether it be the whole or a single part that is relied upon in some instance,
they call that which functions as a particularization "the whole" when it is established within a distinction.
Whether they be a collection, an alternative, all the individual modes, or specific particulars, they are described as such; or else, the undifferentiated universal is what is meant.
For in the word "brāhmaṇa," no distinction whatsoever is either relied upon or excluded; therefore, this term is established as referring to the entire collection [of qualities].
That distinction upon which an action is based is determined as being "thus," "otherwise," or "in every way"; it does not exist when there is no application [of such a term].
In the case of a comparison, the mention of the action in the object of comparison (upameya) causes the occurrence of the action in the standard of comparison (upamāna) to be understood,
as if it were making the distinction itself a constituent part of the word-meaning.
When similarity is intended through the very operation [of the word], a suffix is conveyed by the word "kriyāvat" (possessing action). (BhV 3.14.504)
Even when similarity is intended to be expressed by means of something possessing action, the cognition [of identity] does not cease, as in the case of "the student is like a Brāhmaṇa."
In the expression "he studies similarly" (*adhīte tulyaḥ*), the word *tulya* functions as a masculine adjective qualifying the agent of the action;
however, when referring to the action itself, the word *tulya* takes the neuter gender.

Even if the meaning of the base word (*prakṛti*) were qualified, since it does not qualify the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the application [of the rule] would result in the sentence "Kapila is equal to the son" (*putreṇa tulyaḥ kapilaḥ*). (BVaky_3.14.507)

Whatever actions in the world are intended to express a relationship established with respect to a son, the suffix *vat* occurs after that son— who possesses those actions— to denote someone who is equal to him in those qualities.
Although the causal factor (*nimitta*) is inherent within conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*),
the actions that accompany them are themselves conventional, just like the referents (*padārtha*).
But if, setting aside the sequence, it is taken as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix,
it remains so because it favors the principal element, due to its equality with the case-ending.
Because the material cause is not distinct [in both cases], it would follow that the action is identical;
this applies to sons and the like, as well as to qualities derived from words, in contrast to what was stated previously.
The external usage of the suffix *vati* is seen in "he goes as one equal to a bull" (*sthūlena tulyo yāti*),
whereas in "he goes as one equal [to himself]" (*animittaṃ tulyaṃ yāti*), the suffix *vati* is accepted [by some].
By that [word], two things are qualified, since the qualifier in one instance refers to that property which resides in both,
for the word "equal" depends upon that attribute present in both.
If there is a single common property between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison,
then it is appropriate to say that they are "equal," being measured by a scale.
And when heard in a sentence, this [action] is understood as residing in two [entities] without distinction;
nor is the action understood from the word alone because it is a general term when it is not explicitly heard.
Furthermore, qualities such as obedience to instructions and so forth, which are understood even when not explicitly heard, are properties that are constant [in the father];
these are not found in the sons and others.
Therefore, that which is devoid of action is not equal to that which possesses action;
for when an action is heard [in speech], its possession of action is also understood.
And because it provides a remedy for two [objections], its superiority is stated:
since it expresses eternal non-existence, it serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix.

Since in a suffix there exists only an operation that has not become a real entity, it possesses the status of being a defining characteristic; therefore, no action is found upon hearing [the word for] that operation.
But because [the suffix] is prescribed after a word denoting an action, when it qualifies the meaning of the base,
its status as denoting an established non-substance is established by its equality with the mere action.
But when similarity is based on action between two things possessing action,
then, because that which possesses action is what is denoted, there is the denotation of a substance.
The word *vati* should be included among the indeclinables (*avyaya*), just like *svarādi* and others;
otherwise, the suffix would not occur in such cases as "one who studies equally with a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena samo 'dhyetā*).
And grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indicated by means of the sense of the suffix *-vat*;
otherwise, the unstated remainder of the sentence would have to be imagined as "equal" (*tulyam*).
And when there is a similarity between two agents of action, with the meaning of the suffix serving as a qualifier,
the rule for *vati* does not apply in cases such as "one who studies similarly to one who studies" (*adhyetrā sadṛśo 'dhyetā*).
The meaning of that third case ending does not differ from [the meaning] of those [other endings] which have the same referent;
even when there is a difference, its meaning remains identical to all the other case endings.
He is fed like a Brāhmaṇa, and what is eaten by one of the twice-born is regarded as equal;
he looks upon him like a Brāhmaṇa, and he is looked upon by a learned sage (vipra) as equal.
It is understood by the Brahmin as equal, and known by the twice-born as equal;
let it be given to the Brahmin as equal, let it be given by the learned man as equal.
"Study much learning from a Vaiśya just as you would from a Brāhmaṇa"— in such expressions, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the third case ending.
I study with Madhurā as if with my own mother; I remember her as equal to my mother.
How can there be a conceptualization of similarity between Madhurā and one's own mother?
The recitation whose object is Madhurā, and the memory whose object is the mother,
are denoted without distinction by the words "Madhurā" and "mother" respectively.
Just as the word "camel" applies to faces resembling parts of a camel,
and the word "palace" applies to a house resembling a palace, so too does the term "sweet sound" apply [to that which resembles it].
Just as the similarity between two acts of recitation is predicated of the two reciters,
so too are the properties belonging to the action stated with reference to their substrates.
Whether it be a word used in the sense of "as if" (iva) or a rule found in a preceding sūtra,
no difference whatsoever exists between those two when a verbal action is heard.
Even if a qualifier restricted elsewhere is not employed here, nevertheless,
because there is no difference in form, an action that was previously unascertained is heard again in this context.

Just as in the case of *vyutparayaḥ pucchau*, where words such as *su* and *dur* are cited with the suffix *kyaṅ*, even though the meaning of the suffix is present, they are so illustrated because there is no difference [in their application]. (BVaky_3.14.535)
And this being the case, the rule for the suffix *vati* established by the preceding [sūtra] applies here as well;
whether it functions as a restriction (*niyama*) or as a designation (*abhidhāna*), the verbal root (*kriyāśruti*) does not differ.
Furthermore, it is stated that the cognition whose objects are substance and so forth is prescribed by the previous rule only when the actions themselves are similar.

In the examples "like houses in Madhurā" and "white like those of a Brāhmaṇa," the suffix *vat* would not occur by virtue of the preceding rule [which applies to similarity of action] because [the comparison here concerns] substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*).
If the initial undertaking were not for the sake of action, there would be no purpose served by the application [of grammatical rules];
since it is grasped apart from action, it is established by the preceding application.
The occurrence [of the term] in its constituent parts has been explained for the word *madhura* due to its being heard as such;
the hearing of the word *brāhmaṇa* will likewise denote the teeth as the constituent parts of a Brāhmaṇa.
In the case of the particle *iva*, however, no genitive is prescribed for an external correlate;
in that instance, the suffix [denoting comparison] would occur by virtue of the preceding rule.
An excess [of meaning] arises through its connection with the word "equal" (tulya);
in that case, the genitive and instrumental cases occur, for the word "equal" is indeed the expressive term.
But when the word *iva* is employed, there is no excess in the object of comparison even without an external correlate; it is used merely as an indicator.
The distinction that exists here is caused by [the presence of] a palace and so forth;
when [the object] is equal, a superiority arises in dependence upon its specific locus.
In that case, the usage would be "the ox is similar to the gavaya";
however, in the expression "it is like a cow," there is no basis for the particle *iva* as a marker of difference (*vyatireka*). (Bhāṣya on Vākya III.14.545)
Because it is connected with the object of comparison (*upameya*), the suffix *vati* occurs first in cases where the distinction (*vyatireka*) is based on causes such as a palace;
it does not occur when the meaning is based on similarity.
When connected with the word *iva*, the third case ending is not prescribed; therefore, having abandoned that [third case] under discussion, another case ending has been resorted to.
Even the seventh case-ending does not exist there; rather, it is employed for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
It is intended as restricted to the remaining scope (*śeṣa-viṣaya*) among the fixed case-endings.
If, however, case-endings were to apply to this object as something distinct [from the action],
then only the instrumental case would demonstrate the deviation [of the rule].
When deviation has thus been established even without the mention of the locative case, every instance is stated using the locative alone; there are no other case-endings [in such contexts].
In this context, the genitive case is absolutely superseded by the locative case used in the sense of a "jñāpaka" (indicator);
however, that genitive is taken up [again] for application.

Since the suffix *vati* is established even in the sense of "worthiness" (*arha*) through the formation of a different compound by means of the two preceding grammatical operations, it is nevertheless illustrated here by means of a single example.
When it is understood that "it is equal to that," the limiting condition (upādhi) of action is established;
as in the expression "he acts like a king" (*rājavad vartate rājā*), where a distinction [between the subject and the standard of comparison] is intended.
Those kings renowned for their sovereignty, beginning with Pṛthu and ending with Yudhiṣṭhira, serve as the standard of comparison for other rulers of the earth.
The distinction between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is created by success and failure;
for in all cases, that which is unestablished is compared with that which is well-established.
When it is intended to express that the king himself possesses a form like that of a king,
it will be expressed by means of a second [case] through its connection with something other than an action.
This is stated as a restrictive rule when there is no intention to express a comparison;
furthermore, the word "dharma" denotes the agent of the action of "arhat," and the statement is made for that purpose.

The expression "like one with a trained hand" (kṛtahastavat) is seen only in reference to those who are already well-known [for their skill]; likewise, "like a king" (rājavad) is used only when the person is already established as being a king.
Those properties whose absolute impossibility is observed in the absence of a king are regulated by the king; those that deviate from this are abandoned.
And when there is an action belonging to one who is worthy (arhat), the suffix *vat* is desired in that case;
for example, "the umbrella is worthy of the king," but not in instances such as these [where the relationship is otherwise].
For when words are employed by the virtuous, they are followed by the authority of the grammatical treatise;
however, regarding the statement concerning the meaning of "umbrella" (chattrādi) and so forth, a rejection [of the rule] would not be possible.
Thinking "it does not deserve that," the Sūtra was not commenced in another grammatical treatise;
for even a mere resemblance is possible, since a distinction [between them] is merely imagined.

When a single entity has been established through the cognition of its function, a conceptual distinction is mentally constructed when one wishes to express its status as a property in relation to another object.
On account of the commencement of the Sūtra, the usage of the word *iva* does not exist here;
furthermore, that [usage] exists in its domain for the suffix *vati*.
The phrase "like Indra, the Dasyu" is employed in a mantra dedicated to Indra;
whereas in other cases, it is used when one intends to express that Indra’s actions are observed elsewhere, as in the example "just as [Indra]."
When a state is designated by relying upon a previous state,
it is expressed in that very context as "you are like yourself."
Where another object of comparison with a well-known distinction does not exist,
there the nature of the subject of comparison is mentally distinguished by one's own intellect.
Even that distinction which is intrinsic is based upon cognition;
therefore, in this domain, neither difference nor non-difference exists.
By pointing out the grounds for distinction— such as "wearing armlets" and "wearing earrings"—
one says of Caitra, "He is such," by means of grasping the particular states of his cognition.
By means of these words, the self of cognition arises according to reality;
and in accordance with those conditions, the object also comes into being.
Through the differentiation of the states of the intellect, the effect of distinction is perceived;
indeed, all meanings of words appear as if they were produced by the speaker's intention.
Even when an external object exists in such a manner that cognitions differ with respect to it,
no one perceives any similarity there, even though it exists.
As long as the manifestation does not differ even when the object is entirely distinct,
so long does the recognition of anything not cease.
This very distinction has been shown by the Sūtra through its differentiation;
for even that which is well-known is understood with difficulty by the unwise.
A non-grammarian does not always speak like a grammarian;
however, because one says to him, "Speak like a grammarian," he too is designated as such.
Some men speak like women, and women like men;
even one's own duty (*svadharma*) is taught by them again when there is transgression.
When it is said in the world, "You are like yourself," any other possible object of comparison is thereby excluded.

In the illustration of the meaning "proper" or "suitable for a king," the term *tadarham* ("fit for that") is prescribed when the intention is not to express a formal comparison (*upamāna*). (Bhāṣāvṛtti 3.1.14.578)

Now, the remaining cases involving the suffix *vat*, which follow from what has been discussed and what follows from that, are being described. This *vat* is cited here because of its connection with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Since the word for a quality (*guṇa-śabda*) is observed even in the absence of the postulation of a primary substance (*pradhāna*), the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is established by means of a prefix (*upasarga*) when the suffix *vatu* is applied. (Vākyapadīya 3.14.580)
In this rule "svaṃ rūpam," there is also the inclusion of the meaning;
since it is indicated as being like the form itself, the meaning which is proximate will be understood.

In this sūtra, it is understood that the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is produced by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) as a means of accomplishment; thus, it is expressed as "that which is brought about by the root."
When a word, having fulfilled its purpose,
is no longer employed because it is not observed in its [specific] object-domain, the elision of that word is designated there.

The suffix *vati* is prescribed in its own sense after those prefixes such as *pra* which are established in relation to action (*kriyā*), means (*sādhana*), or substance (*dravya*), provided they denote a substantive entity (*sattva*).
Without a suffix (*pratyaya*), a prefix (*prādi*) is not employed in that sense;
however, when there is a designation based on distinction, the division is conceptually constructed.
If, however, a means of proof were apprehended as not possessing the status of a real entity,
then there would be a mandatory injunction by means of case-endings, just as in the case of suffixes such as *tasil*.
For those who follow the reading according to which the absence of case-endings is understood even in words ending in the suffix *vat*,
they must explain how the presence of case-endings occurs in the word *udvataḥ*.
Because of the observation that [the rule] *puṃvat* does not apply to the sense of the suffix *-vat*,
that irregular derivation (*nipātana*) sublates the exception consisting of the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ*.

"Since the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* certainly have the sense of 'departing' (*utkrāmatas*), when those two are applied, the general rule [for the suffix *khañ*] is not applicable because it is set aside by them. (BVaky_3.14.589)
That grammatical rule by which *nañ* and *snañ* are prescribed does not apply here;
for that section concerning *vati* is justified as being merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The occurrence of a non-different object of comparison within a distinct meaning is a modification;
likewise, the modification of comparisons is not perceived as being like that of the [grammatical] members.
In the case of the *gāvedhuka* porridge, [the word "paśu"] is seen in reference to the cow-slaughterer and the gambler;
for these two are like Rudra, and thus there is the scriptural usage of the singular number.
And due to the various types of comparison (*upamāna*), the rule for *añ* would apply to many [words];
thus, there would be elision in the case of "Kāśyapās" and likewise even in the case of images (*pratikṛti*).

In this way, however, because it possesses the status of that which is endowed with [the property], the singular number would occur here; likewise, the elision (*lup*) in the case of "human" (*manuṣya*) would be stated for the sake of establishing a single gender.
When the objects of comparison are distinct, yet a single [grammatical] operation applies to them,
that [operation] is always desired to be treated like the [word] to which it is joined (yuktavat) in the application of the suffix.
But when each individual object of comparison is established separately,
then, through the distinction of external objects, that which ends in the suffix -taddhita is accumulated.
Just as there is a difference in number for the members of a *dvigu* compound when they are gathered into a collection—
as in "five bundles" (*pañcapūlī*) and so on— so too would there be a gathering of items ending in the *luP* suffix.
When accumulation is differentiated, the number varies among the heaps;
however, no such difference in meaning is observed in the case of words ending in the suffix *luP*.
In cases where no other word expressive of the object of comparison (upameya) is employed,
a distinction in number is desired for the standard of comparison (upamāna) by others.
Just as molasses, sesame seeds, and so forth, when processed together, are designated by a single number,
but when the processing such as cooking is not applied, they are said to have distinct numbers.
The distinction residing in the related entities is perceived in the actual usage;
therefore, the distinction among the related entities is not understood in the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Therefore, in order to avoid the undesirable consequence [of the word] being a general term,
a distinction residing in the object of comparison (upameya) is observed in the objects of comparison (upamāna).
In some cases, a single simile is heard for all [the objects] without distinction; or, when the objects of comparison are distinct, each one is compared individually.
Just as the term "Garuḍa" is employed with reference to a particular formation,
where by means of a single [element] there is a resemblance to Vainateya among elephants.
Even for a single [person], the distinct representation would be perceived simultaneously as "of Kāśyapa"; therefore, this [name] remains established with each individual.
When it is said, "The clouds are like a mountain," the similarity of all [the clouds] with the single mountain is understood; therefore, it is distinguished for each one individually.
The dependence on the suffix *cha* and its having that [suffix] as its object is not understood because of its being a predicate;
for in the expression "kākatālīya," the indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) is well-established.
Whether the object [of the verb] is a king, a horse, or something else remains undetermined;
therefore, prior to the application of the suffix *cha*, no designation [of it as such] exists.
In this case, the status of being a cause is perceived as belonging to two meanings:
by one [meaning], the constituent part is joined; by the other, the suffix is joined.
Caitra’s arrival there is like the arrival of a crow;
but the attack of a bandit is like the falling of a palm fruit.
Whatever action arises from the conjunction of those two in the object of comparison—
such as killing— it is by means of that [action] that the grammatical operation (vidhi) is intended for the object being compared.
When an action is inherent [in a substance], a word denoting a substance remains fixed;
likewise, the words *kāka* (crow) and *tāla* (palmyra palm) remain fixed in relation to the acts of falling and coming.
That sentence which serves as a grammatical exposition is thus postulated;
however, that which is a sentence used in common worldly practice is not employed in such a manner.
When the unexpected encounter of two things is observed, like that of the crow and the palm fruit,
the formation of a compound is accepted for those two as its primary basis.

Just as the killing of a crow by a palm fruit [is a cause for wonder], when another object of comparison (*upamya*) is rendered marvelous in that context, the suffix *cha* is desired there. (Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 3.14.615)
Others say that *cañcatprakāra*, *cañcatka*, and *bṛhatka* refer to gems, frogs, and fireflies, respectively, on account of their similarity [to those objects].
In that state, [the breath] is compared to a firefly by its opening and closing;
it is like a frog by its series of breaths; and like a gem with shimmering luster by its throbbing radiance.
Even if it is small, that gem which is perceived as having spreading radiance is designated by the term "large" in that context; such is the usage of the word in regard to the jewel.
Some maintain that similarity alone is the mode (*prakāra*) in all cases;
however, others accept that even when there is difference, it is designated as a "mode."
One [type of word] denoting a mode is established in that which possesses the mode;
another, having functioned in the mere mode, functions in that which possesses it.
In the sūtra, the mention of "similarity" (sādṛśya) is an indicator for "that which is similar" (sadṛśa).
In an avyayībhāva compound, the word *saha* denotes two things that are equal.
The occurrence of words denoting their literal meaning in the senses of distributive repetition (*vipsā*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*)—
this distinction [of the *yathārtha* class] has been shown separately within the category of *avyayībhāva* compounds.
Some maintain that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is fitness (*yogyatā*);
however, that which is a commonality residing in the physical form is designated by the term *sāha*.
Even in the case of "being thus" (itthaṃbhāva), similarity is based on the state of the cognition;
in that regard, when only the difference is grasped, another [cognition] is said to arise.
In the case of "The Vāhīka is a cow," similarity is cited as the basis for the dual number;
however, once [the quality] such as whiteness has been established, the Vāhīka is not spoken of in the dual.
Thus ends the Vākyapadīya composed by Bhartṛhari.
